Title: Negotiation impasses as meaningful outcomes: How AI is changing the cost structure of walking away
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is often expected to improve negotiation by strengthening information processing and analytical consistency. We argue that its effects on impasses are more selective. Extending the impasse cause, type, and resolution (ICTR) model, we distinguish two pathways. The first pathway is analytical augmentation: AI can reduce unwanted impasses caused by misunderstanding, poor option generation, and coordination failure. The second pathway runs through behavioral flexibility: Humans sometimes reach mutually acceptable agreements through aspiration adjustment, face-saving, and relational repair. Systems configured to apply stable decision thresholds and optimize focal-party outcomes without relational objectives reduce this flexibility and can thereby increase forced impasses. Which pathway dominates depends on AI's role as advisor or counterpart; its objective, training, and prompt; and whether agreement primarily requires analytical problem solving or interpersonal flexibility. These predictions concern system behavior, not whether AI experiences fatigue or social pressure: systems can be designed to respond to relational cues without experiencing them. Wanted impasses depend on both parties' underlying preferences, which AI does not change; AI instead helps negotiators recognize incompatibility sooner and justify walking away more openly. AI therefore changes the composition and meaning of impasses rather than uniformly increasing or decreasing agreement. Remaining impasses may reveal genuine incompatibility, but they may also reflect misspecified objectives or failures to encode principals' relational and economic costs. © 2026 The Authors

Title: When AI wears a face: How AI appearance shapes intentionality attributions in service success and failure
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Customer-facing AI agents are becoming frontline service interfaces, yet firms still face a consequential design question: should these agents look human-like or robot-like? This research examines how AI agent appearance shapes consumers' intentionality attributions in AI-mediated service encounters and how these inferences translate into satisfaction and future AI use intention. Drawing on attribution theory and anthropomorphism research, we propose that human-like and robot-like appearances do not have uniformly positive or negative effects; rather, their effects depend on consumers’ evaluations of service outcomes and their familiarity with AI. A 2 (AI agent appearance: human-like vs. robot-like) × 2 (service outcome: success vs. failure) between-subjects experiment was conducted with 350 U.S. participants in an airline customer-service chatbot context. Results reveal a reversal across outcome evaluations. When consumers experienced service success, robot-like AI elicited higher perceived intentionality than human-like AI, particularly among those with lower AI familiarity. When consumers experienced service failure, human-like AI elicited higher perceived intentionality than robot-like AI, although this effect weakened and reversed among consumers with higher AI familiarity. Perceived intentionality, in turn, increased satisfaction and future AI use intention, supporting a moderated mediation process. These findings reframe AI appearance as an attributional cue rather than a simple humanization strategy and demonstrate that consumers interpret the same AI appearance differently depending on how they evaluate the service encounter. Managerially, the results suggest that firms should not assume that increasing human likeness will universally improve customer responses. Title: When and why are negotiators overly pessimistic? The psychology of under-trust innegotiation
Abstract: Research on negotiation has devoted considerable attention to the risks of misplaced trust, particularly the possibility that negotiators may be exploited by deceptive counterparts. Less attention has been given to the opposite form of trust miscalibration: under-trust, and particularly, unwarranted pessimism regarding counterparts' honesty. This review focuses on such undue distrust and proposes a misperceived motivations account to explain its emergence. According to this account, negotiators' excessive distrust stems from an asymmetry between the motives that negotiators attribute to their counterparts and the motives that actually guide those counterparts’ behavior. When deciding whether to behave honestly, negotiators are driven not only by self-interest but also by concerns about moral self-image and anticipated moral emotions, which constrain dishonesty. However, when deciding whether counterparts are honest, negotiators assume that their counterparts are primarily motivated by self-interest and fail to foresee the constraining moral-identity concerns. We integrate evidence from the literature on negotiation, trust, and moral psychology to explain why pessimism is especially likely to emerge and persist in competitive bargaining contexts, highlight circumstances that may attenuate or amplify it, and identify implications for theory and research, alongside practical inferences for fostering truthful disclosure and credible honesty in negotiation. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Creative or uncreative partner: Comparing humans and AI in collaborative creative tasks
Abstract: Creativity is fundamentally a collaborative process. As generative AI becomes increasingly integrated into creative work, understanding how it reshapes collaboration becomes critical. This pre-registered study directly compares human-human and human-AI collaboration dynamics across two creative tasks: the Alternate Uses Task (AUT) and creative short story writing. Participants were randomly assigned to pairs in either human-human (N = 68 pairs) or human-AI (GPT-4o; N = 72 pairs) conditions, with partners alternating turns as first responders to examine how initiation order shapes the creative process. Our findings reveal that the apparent “AI advantage” in creative collaboration is illusory, driven primarily by increased AI verbosity rather than enhanced creativity. Critically, collaboration with AI partners negatively impacted humans' own creative responses compared to human-human partnerships, with human-AI collaboration failing to enhance idea originality or diversity relative to human-human collaboration. Human partners demonstrated higher collaborative creativity that strengthened over time, indicating that current generative AI systems, while producing more verbose outputs, do not replicate the collective creativity characteristic of human-human collaboration. These results challenge assumptions about AI's creative potential, with direct implications for AI system design and collaborative creative practice. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Documentor mindsets: Considerations when contributing learning resources for software development technologies
Abstract: Many volunteers contribute learning resources for software development technologies online. We interviewed 26 volunteer contributors, i.e. documentors, to understand why and how they design, create, and contribute software documentation. From a qualitative analysis of our interviews, we identified sixteen considerations that documentors have during the contribution process, along three dimensions, namely motivations, topic selection techniques, and styling objectives. We grouped conceptually related considerations to elicit five mindsets that documentors have during the creation of software documentation. We contribute a framework for describing documentor mindsets, and their associated considerations across the three dimensions. This framework provides a structure and vocabulary for reasoning about the documentation contribution process. Based on the framework, we surface the need to reconsider existing perspectives of the documentation creation process, including the role of the documentor and metrics to measure documentation quality. Our insights can inform software documentation creation tools and future research on user generated learning resources. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Title: The Resource, Users’ Socio-economic Status, and Governance in Coastal Marine Benthic Mollusk fisheries in Costa Grande, Guerrero, Mexico
Abstract: The mollusks caught by coastal fishing were analyzed as a resource, as well as the socioeconomic condition of the fishermen involved in this activity, who are members of the fishing cooperatives of the Costa Grande of the state of Guerrero. The objectives were to be acquainted with the list of species fished for human consumption, determine those of greatest economic importance, analyze the socioeconomic characteristics of the fishermen, and determine the current state of the mollusk resource based on the fishermen’s perception. The specimens were acquired from landing zones and restaurants, and a total of 27 surveys were conducted with fishermen, members of fishing cooperatives in the region. A total of 24 species of mollusks were identified; 10 were the target species for fishing, and seven species were not economically profitable for fishermen. Striostrea prismatica, Trochita trochiformis, and Hexaplex princeps generate more income annually. Five species have been excluded from the list of catches: Megapitaria squalida, Periglypta multicostata, Pinctada mazatlanica, Malea ringens, and the giant limpet Scutellastra mexicana. There was no evidence of generational replacement in the fishing activity. The fishermen’s income is sufficient to cover their basic needs and those of their families. The current regulations are insufficient. There is an urgent need to carry out technical-scientific and biological research to provide relevant information that can be used to implement measures for the appropriate use and regulation of mollusk fisheries in the region. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Title: Pursuit and burnout: How goal orientation influences academic pressure in students
Abstract: This study comprehensively investigated the relationship between students' goal orientation and their corresponding experience of academic pressure, emphasizing how distinct motivational frameworks impact psychological stress within modern academic settings. Recognizing that goal-driven behavior can simultaneously inspire exceptional achievement and inadvertently heighten emotional strain, this research aimed to shed light on how students' varied motivational orientations structurally align with their perceived academic demands. A descriptive-correlational research design was employed to capture these dynamics, involving a sample of 225 college students systematically selected through simple random sampling techniques. Data collection was facilitated using two standardized and highly reliable instruments: the Academic Stress Scale and the Achievement Goal Questionnaire-Revised (AGQ-R). Descriptive statistics were utilized to examine the general baseline trends in students' goal orientation and stress levels, while Spearman's rank-order correlation determined the exact nature, strength, and direction of the relationship between the two primary variables. Findings revealed that students generally demonstrated a high level of goal orientation, with a particularly strong emphasis placed on mastery-oriented goals. Concurrently, participants reported notable academic pressure stemming from intense personal expectations and the perceived social importance of academic success. Crucially, a significant positive correlation emerged between goal orientation and academic pressure, demonstrating that increased achievement motivation is frequently accompanied by heightened student stress. These results clearly indicate that while a strong goal orientation contributes positively to students' engagement and drive, it may also manifest as severe emotional strain if not properly balanced. Understanding this complex psychological dynamic is essential for designing supportive academic environments, offering vital insights for educators, counselors, and institutional policymakers aiming to cultivate a holistic learning climate that encourages high achievement without compromising long-term student health. Title: Decoupled semantic alignment and emotion-aware gated fusion for group emotion recognition
Abstract: Video-based group emotion recognition must resolve three coupled problems: semantic entanglement among multimodal cues, the loss of transient affective climaxes during temporal aggregation, and the propagation of noisy sensory features during fusion. We propose a Modality-Decoupled Language-Guided Framework that uses a vision-language model as an offline semantic engine to generate independent psychology-informed visual and acoustic narratives. The resulting modality-specific text anchors are aligned with CLIP visual features and CLAP acoustic features through a dual InfoNCE objective. A Soft Emotion-Aware Temporal Attention (SETA) module predicts a continuous emotion distribution and maps it to an affective query for frame-wise temporal weighting. The same distribution is projected into a fusion-specific query for Soft Emotion-Aware Gated Fusion (SEGF), which performs complementary channel-wise routing of the refined visual and acoustic features. The main novelty is the coordinated use of narrative-level modality decoupling and a shared soft affective hypothesis across both temporal localization and multimodal fusion. Across 10 independent runs, the framework achieves 77.69 ± 1.04% mean accuracy on VGAF and 97.87 ± 0.47% on GECV, with best-run accuracies of 80.03% and 98.52%, respectively. Interpretability, corruption, efficiency, narrative-decoupling, and failure-case analyses further characterize the behavior of the proposed modules. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Livelihood Diversification and Migration Amid Climatic Risk Perception in Slash-and-Burn Agroecology in Northeast India: A Case Study
Abstract: Slash-and-burn agriculture in tropical forests is widely debated in the context of net-zero carbon emissions and global warming. In India, approximately two million hill tribes practice slash-and-burn agriculture, locally called jhumming, across 11 million hectares, with a high concentration in Northeast India. The present study aims to assess climatic risk perception in jhumming in Northeast India, examine livelihood diversification and labor migration as part of livelihood strategies, and finally propose policy measures to address the crisis. This is a case study based on a field investigation of 352 tribal households in Manipur, one of the Northeast Indian states where jhumming is predominant. The study finds that soil erosion, declining soil fertility, monsoon vagaries, and summer temperatures are the predominant perceived risks in cultivation. There are also non-ecological issues, such as market inaccessibility and infrastructure deficits. Approximately 72% of households have ‘zero’ income diversification, specializing in a single activity—farming. Rural non-farm diversification is very challenging here; customary land rights and physiography are key bottlenecks. Labor migration—accounting for around 36% of households—to urban centers contributes substantially to non-farm income diversification. Vertical crop diversification—value addition to existing crops and market linkage—would be a policy suggestion. It will enhance farmers’ income and make farming sedentary, resulting in a longer fallow period and a well-developed secondary forest. Meanwhile, organized labor migration can be placed in the policy arena, which has double benefits—minimizing livelihood crises and reducing pressure on forest resources. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Title: Beyond financial literacy: The role of trust and neuropsychiatric symptoms in fraud vulnerability in dementia
Abstract: Background: Fraud vulnerability is an increasing concern in aging populations, particularly as financial activities shift to digital environments. Individuals with neurocognitive disorders may be especially vulnerable, yet the relative contribution of financial literacy, behavioral functioning, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and interpersonal factors remains poorly understood. This study examined these determinants in individuals with neurocognitive disorders. Methods: 290 individuals with neurocognitive disorders, including Alzheimer's disease, frontotemporal dementia, Lewy body dementia, semantic dementia, and mild cognitive impairment, were enrolled. Financial vulnerability was assessed using the Financial Frailty Battery, a caregiver-administered instrument evaluating financial behaviors before and after disease onset. Neuropsychiatric symptoms were assessed with the Neuropsychiatric Inventory. Regression models examined predictors of fraud occurrence, fraud type, and fraud frequency. Results: Behavioral changes in everyday functioning and interpersonal trust emerged as the strongest correlates of fraud vulnerability. Behavioral tendencies (OR = 1.10, 95% CI [1.01, 1.19], p = .030) and trust (OR = 1.11, 95% CI [1.04, 1.18], p < .001) significantly predicted fraud victimization. Higher trust predicted non-digital (OR = 1.12, p = .005) and mixed fraud (OR = 1.19, p < .001), but not digital-only fraud (OR = 1.08, p = .101). Trust was also associated with repeated victimization (χ2(2) = 42.2, p < .001). Conclusions: Fraud vulnerability in neurocognitive disorders appears to be driven primarily by behavioral and interpersonal factors rather than financial knowledge alone. Preliminary evidence suggests partially different vulnerability profiles for digital and non-digital fraud, highlighting the need for prevention strategies tailored to different forms of financial exploitation. © 2026

Title: When culture meets citizenship: The moderating role of instructional leadership
Abstract: This study aims to analyze the role of organizational culture and instructional leadership in shaping the organizational citizenship behavior (OCB) of high school teachers, as well as to explain the social mechanisms underlying this relationship. Specifically, this study answers questions regarding the extent to which organizational culture influences teachers' OCB, the role of instructional leadership in this relationship, and why statistically significant patterns emerge in the context of school organizations. The study uses a sequential explanatory mixed methods design, with the quantitative stage conducted through a survey of 285 public and private high school teachers in Gresik Regency, analyzed using AMOS-based Structural Equation Modeling (SEM). The qualitative stage was carried out through semi structured interviews to deepen and explain the quantitative findings. The results show that organizational culture has a significant effect on teachers' OCB, while instructional leadership has no significant direct or moderating effect. This indicates that cultural factors play a more dominant role than formal leadership practices in influencing teachers’ discretionary behaviors.Qualitative findings explain that teachers' OCB develops as a result of the internalization of collective values, trust, and peer relationships that are deeply rooted in school culture, while instructional leadership is perceived more as an administrative practice than an empowering pedagogical relationship. This study makes a theoretical contribution by repositioning organizational culture as the main mechanism of social exchange in the formation of teachers' OCB, as well as emphasizing the contextual and contingent nature of instructional leadership in educational organizations. In addition, the study highlights the importance of strengthening value-based school culture to sustain teachers’ professional commitment and collaboration. These findings enrich the study of OCB and instructional leadership through the epistemological integration of quantitative and qualitative approaches. © 2027, Malque Publishing. All rights reserved.

Title: What drives versus what is required: Sufficient and necessary conditions for consumer intention in an unfamiliar wellness service
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Despite the growing importance of wellness and health tourism, little is known about how individuals who have never experienced thermal spa treatments form intentions toward such services. This study addresses this gap by mobilizing an extended Theory of Planned Behavior framework enriched with subjective knowledge and expected health benefits. Based on a large-scale survey of French non-users, we combine Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling and Necessary Condition Analysis to examine both enabling and constraining mechanisms of intention formation. The results show that all predictors contribute positively to intention, with subjective norm emerging as the most influential factor. However, the necessity analysis reveals a markedly different causal structure: only subjective norm, expected health benefits, and perceived behavioral control establish threshold conditions that must be satisfied for higher levels of intention to occur. In contrast, subjective knowledge and attitude, although significant, do not operate as indispensable conditions. These findings reveal an asymmetry between the factors that raise intention and those that set the threshold for it. They suggest that, in this context, intention depends on socially mediated validation, not on individual evaluation alone. For managers, the priority is the conditions that must be met for intention to form - social legitimacy, credible health benefits, and feasibility - rather than interventions, such as information or persuasion, that intensify intention only once those conditions are in place. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Zhong W.; Luo J.; Yu S.; Lyu Y.; Guo J.
Title: Navigating AI affective support: The cognitive-affective pathway from appraisal to emotional well-being in learners
Abstract: As affective artificial intelligence becomes increasingly embedded in educational contexts, understanding how learners emotionally engage with such systems is both timely and critical. Grounded in cognitive appraisal theory and the theory of affective bonding, this research examines how students interpret AI-delivered affective support during academic stress. Across two preregistered experiments (N = 202; N = 394), we find that AI affective support enhances emotional well-being via affective resonance, the perceived emotional alignment between learner and agent. Study 1 shows that affective resonance mediates the effect of AI affective support on positive and negative affect. Study 2 advances a process model in which learners' appraisals of task value and perceived AI emotional affordance are associated with emotional valence, which in turn is associated with affective resonance. Preliminary evidence suggests this indirect effect is stronger when tasks are perceived as personally meaningful. Our findings indicate that emotional responses to AI are not passive reactions to expressive cues but are actively constructed through motivational and cognitive appraisal. By clarifying how learners perceive and internalize AI affective support, this study extends theoretical understanding of human–AI interaction in education and offers actionable guidance for designing emotionally attuned learning technologies that support engagement, resilience, and well-being. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Self-awareness and negotiations
Abstract: How does directing attention toward oneself, or self-awareness, affect one's performance in a negotiation? This article reviews recent research on self-awareness and discusses the implications of these findings for a negotiator's actions before, during, and after a negotiation. Before a negotiation, self-awareness may affect one's choice to negotiate in the first place, one's planned strategy, and one's preparedness to manage difficulties. During a negotiation, self-awareness may affect one's ability to adapt one's tactics and make ethical choices, and outward expressions of self-awareness may affect one's counterpart's perceptions of oneself. After a negotiation, self-awareness may affect one's self-reflection and ability to improve. Altogether, these findings shed light on a variety of possible effects of self-awareness on negotiations, and point to directions for future research. © 2026 The Author

Title: Why identity matters for development
Abstract: This paper argues that while development economics has moved beyond income-based metrics toward a broader capabilities framework, it remains insufficiently attentive to the role of social identity in shaping life chances. Identities such as caste, race, gender, and ethnicity structure access to resources, opportunities, and power in ways that conventional and multidimensional indices fail to capture. Drawing on evidence from global gender disparities and caste-based inequalities in India, the paper demonstrates how identity-blind policies risk reinforcing structural hierarchies. It concludes by advocating an identity-conscious development framework that centres historical injustice, targeted interventions, and inclusive governance to advance equitable development. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Clouds and crowds: A meta-analysis of air pollution and tourism demand-experience dynamics
Abstract: Empirical evidence on how air quality shapes tourist responses remains inconsistent. Drawing on a meta-analytical framework and cognitive-relational theory, this study synthesizes the effects of air pollution on demand- and experience-related outcomes across the travel process. The analysis pools 974 estimates from 58 demand studies and 92 estimates from 8 experience studies on destination-side pollution, as well as 483 estimates from 17 demand studies on origin-side pollution. After correcting for publication bias, air pollution has a mild, partly remediable adverse effect on tourism demand, while evidence for tourist experience is less consistent. The demand effect remains robust across destination-only and origin-destination settings, whereas origin-side air pollution has a negligible, statistically insignificant positive effect. Meta-regression results indicate that between-study heterogeneity is mainly driven by international tourism contexts, online word-of-mouth measures, PM2.5 or air quality index measures, and long-run effects. This meta-analysis provides actionable implications for scenario-based planning, forecasting and econometric practice. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: When does inconsistency help? The nonlinear effect of AI summary-rating inconsistency on consumer purchase intention
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: As generative AI becomes increasingly embedded in e-commerce platforms, AI-generated review summaries have emerged as an important information source for consumers. A growing concern is AI summary-rating inconsistency, defined as the degree to which the evaluative valence conveyed by an AI-generated review summary diverges from the aggregate product rating displayed on the same product page. However, prior research has paid limited attention to this specific form of cross-format evaluative cue conflict. This research investigates the nonlinear relationship between AI summary-rating inconsistency and consumer purchase intention and the psychological processes underlying this relationship. Using a mixed-method design, Study 1 analyzes 2654 product observations from Newegg and provides association-based marketplace evidence using nonlinear regression. Study 2 employs a 3 (AI summary-rating inconsistency: low vs. medium vs. high) × 2 (RIR feedback cue: high approval vs. high disapproval) between-subjects experiment to examine perceived trust in AI and cognitive load, as well as the moderating role of RIR. The findings show an inverted U-shaped pattern: moderate inconsistency is more persuasive than either low or high inconsistency. Perceived trust in AI and cognitive load operate as two parallel psychological processes, with trust transmitting a positive pathway and cognitive load transmitting a negative pathway. In addition, RIR serves as an important boundary condition by strengthening the trust pathway and weakening the cognitive-load pathway when summary-level user feedback is favorable. These findings contribute to research on AI-mediated review information, trust in AI, and consumer decision making, and offer practical implications for optimizing AI-generated review summaries in online retail. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: A combinatorial bidding based deep reinforcement learning approach for multi-agent job shop scheduling problem
Abstract: The multi-agent job shop scheduling problem has become a key challenge in demand-driven manufacturing systems, where multiple consumer agents with heterogeneous scheduling objectives share limited machine resources. This paper proposes a combinatorial bidding based deep reinforcement learning approach to solve this problem under the centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE) paradigm. In the proposed framework, combinatorial bidding allows each consumer agent to submit bundles of interdependent operations within a single round, enabling more expressive preference representation and effective resource utilization. A graph attention network based encoder is employed to capture interdependencies among unscheduled operations. An augmented pointer decoder is developed to generate coordinated operation bundles within each bidding round. Extensive experiments show that the proposed approach achieves competitive average social welfare and exhibits a scale-dependent performance pattern. Compared with evolutionary and reinforcement learning approaches, the simulation results indicate that combinatorial bidding enhances coordination efficiency and scheduling quality, particularly in larger multi-agent scheduling settings. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Event-centric human value understanding in news-domain texts: An actor-conditioned benchmark across multi-scope event contexts
Abstract: This work presents NEVU, a benchmark for actor-conditioned, event-centric, and direction-aware human value recognition in news-domain texts. NEVU evaluates whether models can infer values from event-structured evidence, attribute them to the correct social actors, and determine their aligned or contradictory direction. Built from 2865 English news articles, NEVU represents news at four semantic levels, from subevents to composite events and full articles. Using a hierarchical taxonomy of 54 fine-grained and 20 coarse-grained values, the benchmark contains 46,589 semantic units, 72,905 annotated unit–actor pairs, and 168,061 directed value instances. NEVU is constructed through a staged LLM-assisted annotation and verification pipeline, with targeted human verification for unresolved cases. Candidate-level acceptance and agreement are further examined through a multi-group assessment. The experiments show that prompting-only models remain limited, whereas LoRA-tuned open-weight models substantially improve performance, with overall Micro-F1 gains of 29.77 and 8.21 percentage points over the strongest prompting-only open-weight and proprietary baselines, respectively. These gains primarily reflect learnability under the NEVU reference-label setting. NEVU provides a structured benchmark for systematic evaluation and supervised adaptation of actor-conditioned human value recognition in English news. © 2026 The Authors. Published by Elsevier Ltd. Author full names: Sacco, Pier Luigi (35609660300); Fancourt, Daisy (55911947100)
Title: Operationalising the arts exposome
Abstract: A recent arts exposome framework identified 50 transdiagnostic causal mechanisms (emotional, cognitive, self-referential, arousal–stress, inflammatory–epigenetic, social, and behavioural) by which arts engagement may affect mental health, organised around patterned daily exposure to active ingredients across diverse modes of arts engagement. Translating this structure into testable predictions depends on two operational prerequisites that current research has under-addressed. First, the active ingredients must be decomposed into mechanism-aligned exposure dimensions: aggregating activities as varied as receptive consumption, active participation, and cultural attendance under “arts engagement” averages mechanistically different effects and yields findings that the framework cannot localise to specific processes. Second, mechanism tractability is unevenly distributed across measurement modalities. Stress–HPA–immune mechanisms are well-served by peripheral measurement, including transcriptomic markers such as the Conserved Transcriptional Response to Adversity. Aesthetic and reward mechanisms are tractable through central measurement and autonomic indices of aesthetic emotion, but not through peripheral biomarkers. Affiliative mechanisms face validity challenges in peripheral measurement that may require pharmacological probes or behavioural proxies. Neither prerequisite suffices alone: a valid biomarker linked to a heterogeneous exposure measures something the framework cannot interpret, and a well-specified exposure linked to an inappropriate modality deteriorates evidence quality. These refinements are best understood as minimum conditions for identifying the core ingredients that matter most for each mechanism, since individual and contextual variation continue to moderate activation in real-world settings. Together, they identify where mechanism research can deliver near-term advances, where alternative methods are needed, and how the framework can move from theoretical mapping toward ecologically grounded testable inference. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: A longitudinal study of supervisor support as a moderator in maintaining work engagement during working from home: A moderated moderated-mediation model
Abstract: Maintaining employee work engagement during extended periods of work from home (WFH) is essential for sustaining productivity. Although prior research highlights the detrimental effects of job stress and imbalanced work demands on burnout and engagement, few studies explore how supervisor support mitigates these effects over time. This study examines such relationships as WFH progresses. Panel data from 145 participants, collected at multiple time points over a 10-month period, reveal that as the WFH period extends, supervisor support becomes increasingly effective in alleviating the negative impact of job demands and perceived stress on burnout. This reduction in burnout subsequently contributes to the sustained work engagement of employees. These findings offer valuable insights into the role of supervisor support during extended WFH periods and provide recommendations for managing burnout and maintaining engagement in remote work environments. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Zhou C.; Yu Z.
Title: AI for guilt, human for encouragement? The interaction effects of creator type and emotional appeal on green purchase intention
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Green advertising inherently embeds emotional appeal to drive consumer responses. The proliferation of generative AI has shifted the creator from solely human-dominated to a hybrid landscape where AI-generated and human-generated coexist. Drawing on schema theory and attribution theory, this study investigates the interaction effects between creator type (AI-generated vs. human-generated) and emotional appeal (guilt vs. encouragement) in green advertising on consumers' green purchase intention. Three experiments, including two scenario-based lab experiments (one with a Chinese sample and one with an international English-speaking online sample) and a field experiment with actual purchase data from a live-streaming retailer, provide consistent support for our hypotheses. The results reveal that AI-generated guilt appeal elicits higher consumers’ green purchase intention than the human-generated one, mediated by reduced green moral pressure (a burden-alleviating pathway); conversely, human-generated encouragement appeal elicits higher purchase intention than the AI-generated one, mediated by green self-efficacy (a capacity-enhancing pathway). Furthermore, attribution focus moderates these interaction effects: behavioral attribution strengthens the advantage of AI-generated guilt appeal, whereas personal attribution strengthens the advantage of human-generated encouragement appeal. These findings move beyond the adversarial AI versus human comparison by demonstrating an interaction between disclosed creator type and emotional appeal in green advertising. The framework contributes to green advertising literature by integrating creator type and emotional appeal through an interaction logic, advancing schema theory and attribution theory in the green marketing context. The findings also provide actionable guidance for retailers on strategically collaborating AI and human in green advertising creation to maximize persuasive effectiveness. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: The impact of AI-based information system integration embedded with ESG considerations on perceived overall organizational performance
Abstract: This study examines how artificial intelligence (AI)-based information system integration, conceptualized as a perceived integration capability embedded in organizational workflows, is associated with perceived overall organizational performance. It focuses on the mediating roles of dynamic capability activities, employee AI action readiness, and environmental, social, and governance (ESG) practices, defined as routinized monitoring, disclosure, and governance activities. Using survey data from 496 employees in firms with AI systems, the proposed framework is tested through structural equation modeling and supplemented by machine-learning-based predictive analysis. The results indicate that AI-based information system integration is associated with perceived overall organizational performance mainly through indirect pathways. It is positively associated with employees’ awareness of AI-supported sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring activities and with their readiness concerning the practical applicability of AI-supported information in daily work, both of which are associated with stronger ESG practices and higher perceived overall organizational performance. Its direct association with ESG practices is positive but weaker than the indirect pathways through dynamic capability activities and employee AI action readiness. Bootstrapped analyses support parallel and sequential indirect effects, while multi-group analyses show that the overall relationship pattern is stable across small and medium-sized enterprises and large enterprises. This study contributes by shifting attention from AI adoption to the perceived integration of AI into organizational workflows and by identifying dynamic capability activities, employee AI action readiness, and ESG practices as complementary pathways linking AI integration to perceived overall organizational performance. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Evaluating land price effects of zoning policy adjustment in Bekasi's TOD area: A regression discontinuity design analysis
Abstract: The expansion of Transit-Oriented Development (TOD) and associated zoning adjustments in Bekasi, Indonesia, has reshaped urban land markets, yet their causal effects on land prices and social outcomes remain insufficiently examined in developing-city contexts. This study estimates the impact of zoning regulation changes on land prices around TOD areas using a sharp Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD) with dual distance cutoffs at 500 and 750 m. Based on 905 geo-referenced land price transactions from 2017 to 2024, the results reveal a statistically significant discontinuity at the 750-m threshold, corresponding to an average increase in land value of approximately 107 percent. In contrast, no significant effect is detected at the 500-m cutoff, suggesting that land prices in the immediate TOD core had largely internalized accessibility benefits prior to the formal zoning adjustment, resulting in a pre-existing price premium. Covariate balance and robustness tests support the validity of the causal estimates. The findings indicate that zoning-induced land value capitalization is most pronounced in transitional TOD zones rather than in fully matured TOD centers. While the results empirically support the use of a 750-m TOD planning radius, the magnitude of land value appreciation also raises concerns regarding housing affordability and potential gentrification. These outcomes highlight the need for complementary policy instruments to ensure that TOD-driven zoning benefits contribute to inclusive and socially balanced urban development. Copyright © 2026. Title: Chefs, kitchens, and stars: A literature review of fine dining in hospitality and management studies
Abstract: Fine dining represents a niche within the restaurant industry, yet it has garnered significant attention from both scholars and practitioners. Fine dining, due to its distinctive characteristics - such as extreme creativity and innovation, adherence to strict institutional logics, a rigorous system of social evaluation from customers and critics, and the juxtaposition of artistic logics and commercial logics - is a compelling setting for hospitality and management scholars. However, fine dining literature is quite fragmented. Drawing on a thematic analysis of 101 articles, this literature review provides scholars with five thematic clusters that emerged: (1) Work environment and career path; (2) Creativity and innovation; (3) Social evaluation and institutional logics; (4) Customer experience and engagement; (5) Entrepreneurship and business model innovation. Moreover, by presenting tensions among the clusters and illustrating gaps and opportunities in the methodological approach, this literature review develops a prospective research agenda for hospitality and management scholars. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Son J.
Author full names: Son, Jeyoung (58864629500)
Title: Michelin Key recognition and hotel evaluation: The roles of perceived transferred essence and travel distance
Abstract: This research investigates how Michelin Key recognition shapes consumer judgment in the hotel context. Across five experiments, participants evaluated fictitious hotels that either received or did not receive Michelin Key recognition, with variations in signal strength and travel distance. The results show that Michelin Key recognition increases attitude toward the hotel. This effect is consistently mediated by perceived transferred essence, defined as the belief that a hotel experience embodies a coherent and intentionally designed identity. This mediating role persists when perceived prestige and expected service quality are modeled as competing mediators. The mechanism emerges even in a mid-range hotel context designed to minimize explicit luxury cues, indicating that Michelin Key recognition operates beyond luxury-based inferences. The effect is further amplified when the hotel is framed as geographically distant, consistent with Construal Level Theory, through strengthened perceived transferred essence. Overall, Michelin Key functions as a meaning-oriented signal in pre travel hotel evaluation, shaping how consumers interpret the identity and coherence of the stay experience. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Identifying a dynamic information trading zone framework via insights from full-scale emergency exercises
Abstract: The article examines how the co-creation of a Common Operational Picture (COP) in multi-actor crisis response operations can be understood through the concept of Information Trading Zones (ITZ). The analysis is grounded in the theory of Situation Awareness (SA), including Endsley’s conceptualisation of individual, Team SA and Shared SA, and draws on Galison’s notion of trading zones as intercalation, the insertion of an intermediate concept or mechanism to bridge existing explanatory levels. In this study, ITZ is introduced as an intercalating construct linking information exchange, sensemaking, and coordinated action. Drawing on extensive qualitative analyses of five full-scale crisis exercises, the study traces the evolution of an operational framework that conceptualises ITZ as both a precondition for and an integral component of the co-creation of a COP. Within this framework, ITZ are positioned as socio-technical spaces where information is negotiated, interpreted, and stabilised across organisational boundaries, enabling the development of Shared and Team SA in the face of uncertainty. The article offers concrete recommendations for both researchers and practice, outlining how the interplay among ITZ, COP, and SA can inform the design of information systems that more effectively support coordination, sense-making, and decision-making in Emergency Management contexts. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Li B.; Kim N.; Zhang H.
Title: Virtual reality as a catalyst for change: Promoting communication intention, policy support and interaction with migrant workers in Singapore
Abstract: Migrant workers are vital to the host country's development, yet they often remain socially invisible and face barriers to social integration. Drawing on narrative persuasion and indirect contact perspectives, this research examines how immersive storytelling relates to empathy and supportive orientations toward migrant workers through two laboratory experiments in Singapore. Study One (N = 125) compared narrative delivery via virtual reality (VR), 360-degree video, and text. VR generated the highest immersion, and a sequential path indicated that greater immersion was associated with stronger identification with the protagonist, followed by greater empathy; empathy was associated with stronger willingness to interact with migrant workers, greater policy support, and higher future supportive behavioral intentions. Study Two (N = 87) focused on a key VR design choice, avatar perspective, by comparing self-versus other-embodiment in the VR experience. Self-embodiment increased self-presence, while greater self-presence was sequentially associated with immersion, identification with the protagonist, and empathy, followed by the same pattern of supportive outcomes. Together, the studies show that both modality and within-VR self-representation shape empathy-based pathways toward supportive orientations, offering actionable guidance for designing immersive interventions that promote understanding and support for marginalized groups. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Analysis of COVID-19 cases in India through machine learning: A study of intervention in the SIR model
Abstract: To analyse and predict COVID-19 cases from the prevalence of reported real COVID-19 cases, we propose a modified SIR (Susceptible-Infectious-Recovered) model that incorporates interventions using machine learning approaches. The SIR model is extended by introducing an intervention parameter, denoted by ρ, which collectively represents intervention measures such as complete lockdowns, partial lockdowns, quarantines, isolations, and social distancing. Further, we analyse the equilibrium points, local and global stability at the disease-free and endemic equilibria of SIR model with intervention. In addition, phase portrait plotting has been employed to visualize the qualitative dynamics of the system. Further, a supervised machine learning approach is used to estimate the transmission rate (β) based on real COVID-19 case data from the entire India and some states. Authors: Gong Y.; Huang J.; Bao L.; Li H.; Liu J.; Jing P.; Xiong J.; Tang X.
Title: Teacher emotional support, question openness and student oral participation: The role of positive emotion across stages in AI-observed STEM and non-STEM classes
Abstract: Background: Student oral participation is essential for engagement and learning, yet participation tends to decline in large-class and STEM contexts where social risk and cognitive demands are higher. Existing studies often relied on self-reported or small-scale observations, which may introduce subjective bias and are labor-intensive, limiting large-scale evidence on how instructional practices influence participation across contexts. Aims: This study examines how teacher emotional support and question openness influence student oral participation through student emotion, and whether these effects vary across educational stages and disciplinary contexts. Sample: Data were collected from 1455 face-to-face classes in China. Methods: Artificial intelligence-based techniques were used to capture fine-grained classroom interactions. Structural equation modeling and multigroup analyses were conducted to examine the mediating role of student positive emotion and to compare pathway patterns across educational stages and disciplinary contexts. Results: Teacher emotional support was primarily associated with student oral participation via student positive emotion, whereas question openness showed a more direct association with participation. The indirect role of emotional support through positive emotion became stronger across educational stages, suggesting a compensatory function in secondary education where baseline participation tends to decline. Students in STEM classes were less emotionally responsive to teacher support but showed a stronger association between positive emotions and oral participation. Conclusions: Emotional support is a context-sensitive intervention rather than a universally effective strategy. By combining large-scale AI-based observation with cross-stage and disciplinary comparisons, this study contributes methodological advances for classroom interaction research, although cross-cultural validation of AI-based measures is needed. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Understanding the mixed consequences of diversity practices: A typology of migrant employees
Abstract: Organizational diversity practices are widely implemented to support the workplace integration of international migrants (IMs), yet their outcomes remain inconsistent. Little is known about why IMs respond differently to the same initiatives offered by their organizations or why these practices sometimes fail or backfire. Drawing on signaling and attribution theory, we argue that IMs interpret diversity practices through the lens of two key disadvantages: unfamiliarity with the destination country and exposure to discrimination within this context. We develop a dual disadvantage typology of IMs and theorize how resource and nondiscrimination practices differentially affect organizational commitment depending on migrants’ disadvantage configurations. This typology refines existing diversity frameworks by introducing a configurational view of migrant diversity and explaining why identical practices may produce divergent outcomes. Using survey data from 394 IMs working in Germany, we find that while nondiscrimination practices are consistently positively associated with commitment, the effects of resource practices vary: some IMs view them as empowering, while others interpret them as stigmatizing or misaligned with their needs. In particular, training initiatives can backfire for IMs who are already familiar with the labor market and face discrimination. Our findings demonstrate the importance of tailoring initiatives to different migrant groups. We contribute a theory-driven framework that explains how diversity signals are differentially interpreted across migrant disadvantage configurations and when diversity practices produce intended versus unintended effects. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Rocky past, hazy future: Childhood adversity and adult prospection
Abstract: Two preregistered studies tested whether childhood adversity is associated with hazy future thinking, characterized by reduced clarity and detail in imagined future events and a more negative emotional outlook toward the future, and whether it is related to higher levels of intolerance of uncertainty. In Study 1 ( N = 232; 77.2% female, 22% male, 0.8% other or not specified), when asked to consider the future, participants with higher childhood adversity reported less vivid, detailed, and optimistic future thoughts, with more hopelessness and negative emotions. In Study 2 ( N = 262; 79.4% female, 19.8% male, 0.8% other or not specified), higher adversity was related to lower confidence, persistence, and commitment regarding goals. Separating adversity into harshness and unpredictability revealed that unpredictability was more consistently associated with both cognitive and emotional aspects of hazy future thinking, even when controlling for harshness. Also, higher childhood unpredictability was associated with higher intolerance of uncertainty in both studies. These findings provide evidence that early-life unpredictability is related to less cognitively clear and more emotionally negative visions of the future. Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Wang H.; Chen Z.; Zhang S.; Zhang M.; Pang H.
Title: Linking need for cognitive closure to cyberchondria among health information seekers: Disentangling the roles of uncertainty discrepancy, health worry and information processing evaluations
Abstract: Despite growing research on online health information seeking behaviors, the psychological factors through which dispositional characteristics are linked to maladaptive information outcomes such as cyberchondria remain underexplored. Drawing on the Theory of Motivated Information Management (TMIM), this study establishes a conceptual framework to examine how the need for cognitive closure is associated with cyberchondria through interpretive constructs (i.e., uncertainty discrepancy and health worry) and evaluative assessments (i.e., perceived health information overload and self-efficacy). The study examines the pattern of associations among these information management constructs as theorized by TMIM. Analysis of data from 581 adults using structural equation modeling demonstrates that the need for cognitive closure was directly associated with cyberchondria and was also positively associated with uncertainty discrepancy and health worry. Uncertainty discrepancy and health worry were associated with perceived information overload and self-efficacy, and perceived information overload and self-efficacy were associated with cyberchondria. This research offers insights into the information management constructs associated with cyberchondria by illustrating how dispositional factors are linked to maladaptive information management outcomes in a pattern consistent with the structure theorized by TMIM. Because the data are cross-sectional, this structure reflects a theoretical ordering assumed by the framework rather than an empirically established temporal sequence. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Research on the mechanism of linking time pressure to career growth among hotel employees
Abstract: Research overlooks how and why identical cognitive appraisals of time pressure translate into divergent coping behaviors. Drawing upon the cognitive appraisal theory of stress, this study investigates the mechanisms linking time pressure to the career growth of frontline hotel employees. Utilizing a three-wave time-lagged design, we collected survey data from 323 frontline hotel employees in China and analyzed it using PLS-SEM via SmartPLS 4.0. The results reveal that challenge appraisal and hindrance appraisal play differentiated mediating roles between time pressure and career growth, with job crafting serving as a crucial behavioral bridge in the transformation from stress appraisal to career growth. Furthermore, achievement motivation significantly moderates this transformation from stress appraisal to job crafting behavior. This study provides empirical evidence for the hospitality industry to implement differentiated stress management and employee development interventions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: The power of noticing the good: The mediating role of reward perception in the effect of mindfulness on depression and suicidal ideation

Abstract: Background: Although dispositional mindfulness is inversely associated with mental health problems and suicidal ideation, the behavioral mechanisms underlying this relationship remain unclear. Method: In a cross-sectional study of 407 Colombian adults, Kendall’s tau correlations and bootstrapping mediation analysis with 5,000 resamples and bias-corrected 95% confidence intervals were used to estimate indirect effects. Title: Artificial general intelligence architectures and evaluation methodologies: A comprehensive review and future research roadmap
Abstract: Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) seeks to create machines with broad, human-like cognition. However, rapid advances in narrow AI make it clear that general intelligence remains unresolved. This systematic review synthesises AGI research in five dimensions: definitions, enabling technologies, envisioned applications, evaluation methodologies, and open challenges. We performed a systematic search of major academic databases and search engines up to January 2026. After deduplication, two reviewers independently screened 927 records and included 393 studies that met the predefined criteria. We extracted data to address five research questions for each dimension and conducted a qualitative synthesis, as the evidence base did not support a meta-analysis. Across the literature, AGI is primarily characterised by broad adaptability and cross-domain generalisation. The main approaches include symbolic knowledge-based methods, machine learning, cognitively inspired architectures, hybrid neuro-symbolic systems, and brain-inspired or theoretical models Raman et al. (2025) [302]; each contributes partial capabilities, but exhibits limitations in isolation. The proposed application areas include healthcare, education, finance, transportation, smart cities, defence, scientific research, and more. Evaluation practices span multidimensional scales, cognitive test batteries, and safety-oriented benchmarks for alignment and autonomy. However, many benchmarks are saturated rapidly and do not fully capture real-world generality. Persistent challenges include the absence of a unified empirical theory of intelligence; the integration and scalability of heterogeneous methods; symbol grounding and embodiment; value alignment and control of highly capable agents; and the development of rigorous yet comprehensive evaluation protocols. In general, AGI research remains fragmented, with no approach that demonstrates the full spectrum of general cognitive competence. We operationalise “integration” as a system-level property in which learning, reasoning, memory, and social-ethical constraints are coupled through shared representations and closed-loop control so that each component can shape the others during task execution. We also describe two integrative candidate architectures proposed in the literature: (i) a Self-Evolving Binary-Symbolic AGI framework and (ii) the Cohomological Active Inference Architecture (CAIA). Whether a proposed architecture achieves this integration can be measured empirically using multidimensional AGI benchmarks and safety or alignment evaluations discussed in AGI assessment methodologies. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Authors: Liu X.; Geng Y.; Liu Y.; Ye Q.
Title: When more becomes less: Cumulative eWOM volume and automobile sales
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Consumers increasingly rely on electronic word-of-mouth (eWOM) when purchasing high-involvement products, yet whether an expanding stock of accumulated reviews continues to benefit product performance remains unclear. This study investigates the relationship between cumulative eWOM volume and automobile sales using a panel dataset from the Chinese automobile market covering 2013 to 2025. Contrary to the conventional view that more reviews are always beneficial, we find that cumulative eWOM volume is negatively associated with subsequent automobile sales. A 1% increase in cumulative eWOM volume is associated with approximately a 0.206% decrease in automobile sales. This negative association is stronger when accumulated ratings exhibit greater heterogeneity, measured by both cumulative rating variance and entropy, providing evidence consistent with an information overload explanation. In addition, greater cumulative eWOM volume is associated with fewer newly generated reviews, which partially mediates its negative association with automobile sales. The negative association is weaker when cumulative eWOM ratings are higher, when a larger proportion of cumulative reviews is recent, and for higher-priced automobiles. Additional analyses show that the association persists when recent reviews are excluded from the cumulative measure, across automobile age groups and sample periods, and is stronger for domestic and conventional vehicles. These findings extend the eWOM research by showing that the value of accumulated reviews depends not only on their availability but also on their composition and processing demands. The findings also suggest that manufacturers and platforms should encourage recent reviews and emphasize recent evaluations and aggregate ratings in review presentation. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: The role of deontological morality in shaping demand within the sharing economy
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: This study examines how deontological and consequentialist appeals in Airbnb host self-descriptions relate to trust-related attention and marketplace performance. Study 1 combines a five-city listing panel with third-party New York property-month records; Study 2 analyzes a behavioral highlighting task. In the five-city models, deontology was negatively associated with Expected Demand and Expected Income, but its interactions with deontological sentiment were positive, indicating a framing-dependent pattern. In a six-month New York DID-style pre/post comparison under conditional parallel trends, entropy-balanced ATT weighting indicated 18.6% higher monthly revenue for positive deontological but not positive consequentialist baseline framing relative to neither-positive framing (nominal p = .038). The corresponding ATO estimate was 14.0% for the covariate-overlap population (nominal p = .042), not an independent replication. In Study 2, participants identified trust-eliciting content more often in deontological than consequentialist descriptions; the retained data support differential attention, not a causal effect on trust or booking behavior. Title: Immunohistochemical evidence of glutamatergic modulation of Nesfatin-1 neurons in the rat supraoptic nucleus during inflammatory stress
Abstract: Background: Stress triggers a complex network of neuroendocrine, immune, and behavioral responses aimed at maintaining homeostasis. Nesfatin-1, a hypothalamic peptide initially identified for its anorexigenic effects, has also been increasingly implicated in stress-related processes. Methods: This study investigated whether acute inflammatory stress induced by lipopolysaccharide (LPS) activates Nesfatin-1 neurons in the supraoptic nucleus (SON) and examined the modulatory role of glutamatergic receptor antagonists. Female and male Sprague–Dawley rats were assigned to control, LPS, MK-801 + LPS, and CNQX + LPS groups. Neuronal activation was assessed using dual immunohistochemical staining for c-Fos and Nesfatin-1, followed by quantitative analysis of co-localized neurons in the SON. Results: LPS administration significantly increased the proportion of c-Fos-positive Nesfatin-1 neurons in both female and male rats compared to controls (p = 0.001). Pretreatment with MK-801 and CNQX attenuated this activation (p < 0.01), indicating the involvement of both NMDA and non-NMDA glutamatergic pathways. Conclusion: Acute inflammatory stress activates Nesfatin-1 neurons in the SON, and this response is modulated by glutamatergic signaling. Title: Fostering institutional trust and organ donation: Evidence from a randomized informational intervention in Tunisia
Abstract: Organ transplantation saves lives and improves the quality of life of patients who would otherwise depend on costly and invasive treatments. The technology is becoming available in low- and middle-income countries, but the gap between the demand for and the supply of organ transplants remains large. In a randomized controlled trial at a Tunisian university, we evaluate an expert-led intervention designed to inform about organ donation and strengthen trust in medical institutions. The intervention consists of a short video testimonial from a heart transplant survivor, a presentation led by a medical doctor and a short Q&A session. We find that the intervention significantly increases deceased donor registration, with suggestive evidence of positive spillover effects on the control group. The survey data provides little support for changes in attitudes and social expectations as potential mechanisms. Instead, it reveals large and statistically significant increases in medical and legal knowledge, religious beliefs supportive of donation, and institutional trust among treated students. Finally, we show that treatment effects on organ donor registration are driven by male students and those whose families likely support organ donation. Targeting older segments of the population may further increase the impact and cost-effectiveness of this intervention. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Hart E.
Title: Post-negotiation behavior and attitudes: We have a deal, now what?
Abstract: Negotiators often equate “winning” with securing favorable agreement terms, yet the agreement is only one outcome of the negotiation process—and may not be the most important, particularly when interactions continue after the deal. This review broadens the lens to encompass post-negotiation outcomes, including emotions, satisfaction, relational perceptions, contract implementation, and subsequent behaviors. Considering a wider range of outcomes deepens understanding of the costs and benefits of negotiation, and can shed light on negotiation initiation and strategy. Integrating post-negotiation behavior also reveals when and why economic and relational motives collide. By treating agreements as the beginning, rather than the endpoint of negotiation, individuals can better align economic and relational objectives and ultimately maximize value beyond the bargaining table. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Valuing the ecosystem service gap in private forestland management: evidence from Texas and Louisiana
Abstract: Private forestlands generate substantial ecosystem services that function as positive externalities, often requiring private operations to bear costs. This market failure creates a gap between private incentives and socially optimal forest stewardship, which leads to chronic underinvestment in sustainable forestry management practices. Using the contingent valuation method, we measure the divergence in forest stewardship by evaluating five practices across NIPF operations in Texas and Louisiana. Results show that thinning requires the highest average cost-share at around 53%, while prescribed burning presents the lowest barrier at around 30%. When translated to monetary terms, establishment commands the highest private valuation at around $308 per acre, whereas prescribed burning shows the lowest Implied WTP at around $42 per acre. We find that the willingness to pool management with neighboring operations is associated with lower required cost-share percentages across all practices. Land size is associated with lower required cost-share percentages for establishment, but shows limited evidence of association for the other practices. These findings illuminate the economic mechanisms underlying the market failure in ecosystem service provision and demonstrate how practice-specific incentive design and landscape-scale collaboration can more efficiently align private operation behavior with social objectives for forest-based natural capital stewardship. © 2026 The Authors. Title: Whose story do we live? Experiential authorship threat in AI-mediated hospitality journeys and its consequences for meaning, memory, and engagement
Abstract: AI now functions as hospitality's concierge, curating itineraries, wellness plans, and trip narratives at scale. While such systems boost efficiency and personalisation, they raise a symbolic concern central to hospitality: when algorithms pre-write the journey, do guests still feel like the authors of their own experiences? This research introduces and validates Experiential Authorship Threat (EAT), defined as the perceived loss of agency, ownership, and self-authored meaning when AI curation displaces the guest's narrative role. Across six studies (scenario-based, embedded-field, and interface experiments; total n = 2073), AI (vs. human) curation elevates EAT, especially under rigid itineraries (Study 1), and EAT, rather than adjacent constructs, drives symbolic and behavioural disengagement through diminished psychological ownership, particularly among guests high in narrative identity (Study 2). Framing AI as a co-creator rather than a curator, and offering editable rather than pre-filled itineraries, restores autonomy and authorship and improves engagement and satisfaction (Studies 3 and 4). The cost of EAT is greatest for symbolic, identity-relevant trips and high-identity-salience guests (Study 5) and persists in impoverished post-trip memory (Study 6). Theoretically, the research integrates self-determination, narrative identity, and meaning-maintenance perspectives to position EAT as a distinct psychological mechanism in hospitality. For managers, preserving guest authorship through framing, interface design, and symbolic sensitivity emerges as a design priority alongside accuracy and speed. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Spatial perspective on perceived fairness of climate-related fuel tax increases
Abstract: We explore the perceived fairness of fuel tax increases from a spatial perspective. Actions in transport sector are needed to meet climate change mitigation targets, but such policies may disproportionately impact rural and urban residents, leading to spatially varying experiences of injustice. Perceived fairness is the most important determinant of public opinion towards mitigation policies, but perceived fairness of these policies itself has been understudied. We combine our inquiry of perceived fairness regarding fuel tax increases with considerations of spatial justice. We explore, whether residential area type, region, and variables such as climate concern, trust in climate policies, political orientation and use of fossil-fuelled car, are associated with perceived fairness of increasing fuel tax, and whether there are regional differences in these variables. Data were collected via a survey in June 2022 in three regions with different characteristics in Finland: Helsinki, Finland Proper, and Northern Ostrobothnia. Our results reveal that residents in rural areas and sparsely populated regions perceive fuel tax increases as less fair. Climate concern, trust and political orientation were found to influence fairness perceptions. Moreover, climate concern and trust were lower in sparsely populated regions. Considerations of fairness perceptions are important for successful climate mitigation policy. © 2026 The Authors. Published by Elsevier B.V. Title: The complex role of perspective taking in negotiations
Abstract: To reach an agreement, successful negotiators typically need to understand two things: what they themselves are willing to accept, and what the other side is willing to accept. Understanding the other party's threshold requires perspective taking. In negotiations over goods or services, these judgments shape perceptions of the bargaining zone: the range of outcomes both parties would prefer to walking away without an agreement. The present paper examines how negotiators form perceptions of the bargaining zone. These perceptions have important downstream consequences, influencing everything from the offers negotiators make to the agreements they reach. We review work on how negotiators form perceptions of what their counterpart is willing to accept. Perspective taking can help negotiators estimate the lowest price a seller would accept or the highest price a buyer would pay. However, it can also lead negotiators to erroneously internalize the other party's perspective as if it is relevant to their own valuation. As an example, we demonstrate that buyers are willing to pay more for the same good when the seller gives up an entire endowment rather than only part of it, although the seller's end state should not affect buyer's willingness to pay for the good. These findings show how taking the other party's perspective can shape valuations, fairness judgments and negotiations outcomes. We conclude by discussing implications for multi-issue bargaining and strategic framing, highlighting how psychological heuristics and social context interact to shape outcomes in complex real-world situations, such as salary negotiations and real estate transactions. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: How Sociodemographic Factors Shape Community Well-Being in Sustainable Tourism Destinations
Abstract: Tourism significantly contributes to the livelihoods of host communities, influencing their social, environmental, and economic development. However, residents’ diverse demographics and attitudes often shape their perceptions of tourism, affecting the level of support or opposition within these communities. Such demographic factors may influence how individuals perceive tourism’s benefits and drawbacks, leading to regional variations in engagement. This study examined the relationship between sociodemographic factors, New Silk Road (NSR) infrastructure, community well-being, and tourism sustainability in destination areas. Specifically, it analysed correlations among NSR infrastructure, demographic variables, tourism impact (TI), quality of life (QOL), place image (PI), and support for tourism development (STD). Data were collected during the NSR infrastructure project in Turkistan, Kazakhstan. The findings indicated that 24 of 28 relationships between variables were statistically significant, demonstrating strong associations. Additionally, post-hoc analysis revealed significant differences in satisfaction with non-material aspects of life—affected by respondents’ income, occupation, and parental status—providing valuable insights for policymakers to develop targeted strategies. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Title: Factors associated with perceived frugal-innovation capability in traditional craft villages: A respondent-level PLS-SEM study in Hanoi, Vietnam
Abstract: Frugal innovation is increasingly treated as a capability for developing affordable, resource-efficient, and context-appropriate solutions, yet its antecedents remain fragmented across the literature and are insufficiently examined in community-embedded craft production. This study evaluates two connected sets of respondent-level associations in traditional craft villages in Hanoi, Vietnam. The resource-recombination route links perceived empowering leadership, knowledge management, organic innovative culture, and network embeddedness with bricolage and, in turn, perceived frugal-innovation capability. The institution-market route links network embeddedness with perceived government support, perceived customer requirements, customer participation, and frugal-innovation capability. A cross-sectional survey produced 432 returned questionnaires; 416 retained cases were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). All constructs are interpreted as respondents’ perceptions of practices and conditions in their focal production or business units rather than as objective organization-level measures. Bricolage had the largest direct association with perceived frugal-innovation capability (β = 0.441), and empowering leadership had the largest association with bricolage (β = 0.492). Network embeddedness was associated with several specific indirect routes, while perceived government support was associated with frugal-innovation capability both directly and through customer-facing constructs. The model explained 52.5% of the adjusted variance in perceived frugal-innovation capability. The findings support a resource-conversion interpretation centered on bricolage, but the cross-sectional, single-source design does not establish temporal mediation or causal effects. Title: Selecting a project-delivery structure for Indonesia's first nuclear power plant: an expert AHP-weighted anchored-rating analysis of the bankability–strategic-control trade-off
Abstract: Indonesia's energy policy and supply plan include nuclear generation, shifting attention from adoption to delivery. This study evaluates five case-anchored delivery configurations against 14 criteria covering ownership, contractual risk allocation, strategic national value, and financing feasibility, using a hybrid AHP-weighted anchored-rating model: 19 purposively selected Indonesian experts derived criterion weights by pairwise comparison and rated each configuration on an anchored nine-point scale; each respondent's weights and ratings were combined before aggregation. All 95 pairwise matrices met CR ≤ 0.10 under software-enforced consistency requirements, whereas agreement on dimension priorities was weak (Kendall's W = 0.187). Within this panel and under the administered profiles, a host-majority public–vendor joint venture scored highest (0.710), ahead of a state-utility configuration (0.638); its margin arose from perceived bankability, construction-risk allocation, and funding access, not from strategic national value, the largest-weighted dimension (34.4%). Priority heterogeneity alone reversed the group choice for no respondent; assessment heterogeneity reversed it for five. A1 led in over 98% of resampling and weight-variation draws, but the lead reversed when its seven contracting and financing ratings were lowered together by more than about 1.2 points. Newcomer delivery choices should weigh the risk bearer's control rights, exposure, and loss-absorption capacity, not nominal allocation alone.
