Title: Mother tongue as a tool for africanization of the curriculum
Abstract: This paper explores the prospects of mother tongue education as a tool for the Africanization of the curriculum by addressing the research gap on the decline in the use of the mother tongue in educational institutions. The deliberation is targeted at promoting a more inclusive and culturally responsive education system in which the linguistic identity of learners is respected. Africanization in education aims at recentering African perspectives, values, and knowledge systems, challenging Western-dominated views that have long sidelined African cultures and languages in learning spaces. While many African countries continue to prioritize colonial languages such as English and French in education, the mother tongue remains a vital tool in assisting learners, as colonial languages often hinder learners’ academic success and reduce their engagement in the learning process. However, the African mother tongue remains at risk of becoming extinct as people continue to migrate in hopes of better economic opportunities. This paper reviewed the language policies of selected African countries, emphasizing the urgent need to prioritize mother tongue teaching and to develop African languages as effective instructional media across all subjects, going beyond just language classes to utilize it as a tool to Africanize the curriculum. The implications for the basic school curriculum are discussed, stressing that mother tongue integration not only supports language preservation but also enhances academic achievement and identity formation. The paper calls for curriculum designers, policymakers, and educators to collaboratively embed African languages and knowledge systems into the curriculum. This approach builds an education system that genuinely embodies and supports the values, cultures, and needs of African communities. The insights emerging from this discourse promise to nurture culturally grounded learners who are capable of addressing African challenges through an Afrocentric lens. © 2027, Malque Publishing. Title: Navigating blue economy research conflicts for improved societal outcomes
Abstract: The Blue Economy aims to balance economic prosperity, environmental stewardship, and social equity through sustainable ocean development. Its rapid expansion—spanning fisheries, aquaculture, maritime transport, and energy—has intensified competition for marine resources and space, often generating conflict and cumulative impacts on ecosystems and communities. These tensions are driven by uncertainty about outcomes, as well as differing stakeholder values and perceptions. To realize the goals of the Blue Economy, robust research is needed. However, research institutions working in contested marine spaces may face reputational, ethical, and strategic risks. These include navigating tensions among ocean users, developers, policymakers, and the public. From an organisational perspective, deciding whether to engage in such research requires balancing potential benefits against risks to integrity, partnerships, and long-term goals. This paper introduces the Conflict Navigation Grid, a decision-support framework that enables research organisations to systematically evaluate the risks and benefits of proposed projects. The Grid helps identify initiatives that provide strong organisational, community, environmental, and policy value while also assessing whether reputational, operational, or personal risks are manageable. It distinguishes projects that align with institutional values and capacities from those where the potential harms outweigh uncertain returns. By adopting this systematic decision framework, organisations can confidently make decisions in the face of conflict, thereby managing risk and achieving improved societal outcomes. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Consumer egg washing and handling practices in Southeast Asia: a mixed-method study
Abstract: Egg washing at home is generally discouraged in some regions because it can damage the egg's natural protective cuticle and increase the risk of bacterial penetration. However, little is known about how consumers in Southeast Asia wash and handle eggs in domestic settings. This study aims to investigate egg washing and handling practices among consumers using a mixed-method approach. A cross-sectional online survey was conducted with consumers from Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Thailand, and Vietnam. This was followed by 24 domestic kitchen observations and semi-structured interviews in Malaysia, Indonesia, and Thailand. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, Kruskal-Wallis tests, and logistic regression. Qualitative data were analysed thematically. The majority of participants reported washing eggs before cooking. More than half of those who washed eggs indicated that they would still wash eggs even when they appeared visually clean. Eggs were commonly rinsed under tap water, often to remove dirt, faeces, slime, or feathers. Respondents from Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines and those with greater perceived risk of Salmonella contamination in eggs were more confident in following the message. Observations revealed appropriate handwashing after handling or cracking eggs was rare and cross-contact opportunities were frequently observed. Semi-structured interview findings showed that egg washing was closely linked to perceived beliefs about cleanliness and safety, habitual practice, and uncertainty about how eggs had been handled before purchase. Some participants also described wiping as an alternative cleaning strategy, while informal information sources appeared to influence views on egg washing. Practical guidance should emphasise washing only visibly dirty eggs, cooking them immediately after washing, handwashing hands with soap and water after handling or cracking eggs and preventing cross-contamination during preparation. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Hierarchical DEMATEL-based key risk identification for urban public safety within grid management
Abstract: With the acceleration of urbanization, urban public safety risks have exhibited characteristics of diversification, complexity, and linkage. Based on the grid-based governance concept of “comprehensive horizontal coverage and hierarchical vertical stratification” and combined with the hierarchical DEMATEL method, this paper constructs an urban public safety Grid Risk System for Urban Public Safety (GRSFUPS) and a risk analysis framework. GRSFUPS takes grids as the minimum governance units and progressively refines four types of A-level risks—natural disasters, public health, social security, and accident disasters—into B-level and C-level risks, forming a complex system with clear hierarchies and close linkages. Subsequently, using Kunming as a case study, a case application study was conducted on its critical public safety risks. Combined with centrality ranking and the Pareto principle, 55 critical risk factors were identified from 258 risk factors. Research results indicate that public health incidents and accident disaster risks occupy a dominant position in Kunming City, while natural disaster risks such as meteorological and flood hazards repeatedly appear across multiple districts and exhibit significant amplification effects. Theoretically, this paper enriches the urban public safety risk identification framework from a grid-based perspective. Practically, it provides a new analytical paradigm and methodological support for Kunming City and other similar cities to conduct risk governance under grid-based management models. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: An adaptive methodology for determining the optimal transition point and reuse lifespan of photovoltaic panels considering degradation-adjusted energy yield
Abstract: End-of-Life (EoL) management of Photovoltaic (PV) panels is an emerging concern for waste managers and policymakers, given the high rates of PV deployment worldwide. Existing studies emphasize the benefits of PV recycling, but there are few assessments of panel reuse. Identification of the appropriate transition point from reuse to recycling that balances economic and environmental trade-offs is much needed. Studies that do engage with this domain fail to account for the operational and maintenance (O&M) and EoL costs incurred during the reuse phase. With the aims of sustainable waste management, the present study develops a dynamic techno-economic and environmental optimization framework for PV reuse, based on a scalarized multi-objective analysis, referred to as the Reuse Time Span Optimization Model (RTOM). RTOM integrates degradation-adjusted energy generation and monetized environmental benefits into an economic optimization model while accounting for O&M and EoL costs. Results indicate that, after a first life of 25 years, PV panels can be optimally reused for up to 13 years, yielding substantial net benefits. It shows that reuse boosts PV panel benefits by eight times (8×) compared to recycling. The study concludes that reuse is beneficial only within an optimal reuse duration; beyond which, it is no longer advantageous. A Monte Carlo-based sensitivity analysis is used to capture parameter uncertainty and evaluate robustness. The developed RTOM is a decision-support framework that is adaptable and transferable by modifying region-specific parameters. Overall, this work advances the discourse on PV waste management by repositioning reuse as a viable and preferable strategy. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Ethics, economics, and environmental stewardship: Religious moral frameworks as constraints for rational policy choice
Abstract: Environmental policy often embeds ethical judgments implicitly in discount rates, welfare weights, prices, or informal constraints. This paper develops a constraint-based framework that makes major ethical commitments explicit before economic optimization begins. Drawing on convergent principles in Jewish, Islamic, Christian, Indigenous, Buddhist, and secular traditions, it identifies stewardship, restraint of waste, intergenerational responsibility, ecological limits, and institutional responsibility as candidate non-compensatory constraints. Economic analysis then compares costs, trade-offs, and institutional feasibility only among policies that satisfy the adopted constraints. Title: Molecular detection of Paenibacillus larvae, Melissococcus plutonius and Vairimorpha spp., in historical honey samples from South Brazil
Abstract: Honey bee colonies are threatened by several pathogens, including Paenibacillus larvae , Melissococcus plutonius , Vairimorpha apis , and Vairimorpha ceranae . Those infections affect bee health, survival, and productivity. The social behavior of the bees facilitates the spread of these pathogens, making disease management a significant challenge in apiculture. This study aimed to assess the historical presence of Paenibacillus larvae , Melissococcus plutonius , Vairimorpha apis , and Vairimorpha ceranae in honey samples from Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil. A total of 125 archival honey samples collected from 2011 to 2022 were retrospectively evaluated. The samples had previously been analyzed for physicochemical and botanical origins. DNA was extracted from honey and spores, followed by PCR assays targeting the four pathogens. Sequencing was performed to confirm the results. M. plutonius was the most frequently detected pathogen, identified in 112 samples (89.6%), followed by V. ceranae , which was present in 67 samples (53.6%). In contrast, P. larvae were identified in only six samples (8.8%), and V . apis was absent. The high detection rate of M. plutonius suggests its widespread distribution in South Brazilian apiaries. The absence of V . apis suggests that V . ceranae has displaced this specie in the region. The presence of P. larvae spores emphasizes its resilience through the ability to persist for extended periods in the environment. Additionally, the simultaneous detection of multiple pathogens raises the concern for synergic effects or interactions, which could further increase colony losses. Title: When regulatory-focus language matches the product category: A within-person computational analysis of reviews from an online retail platform
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Online review platforms use helpfulness votes and related signals to rank and solicit reviews. This study tests whether regulatory-focus-related language is associated with helpfulness in a category-sensitive manner. We analyze 391,047 Amazon reviews from eight product categories classified a priori as promotion-oriented or prevention-oriented. Promotion language concerns gains, aspirations, and enjoyment. Prevention language concerns safety, reliability, and problem avoidance. Category assignments and language measures were benchmarked against human ratings of 800 products and 1136 reviews, respectively. The primary analyses compare within-reviewer deviations in 153,655 reviews from 20,787 reviewers represented in both category types, thereby accounting for additive time-invariant reviewer differences under the specified model. The same reviewers used a higher density of promotion language in promotion-oriented categories and a higher density of prevention language in prevention-oriented categories, with paired Cohen's d values of. 20 and. 14, respectively. Within reviewers, matched-language count was positively associated with log(1 + helpful votes), and its coefficient exceeded the mismatched-language coefficient, p <. 001. Category-specific count estimates were positive in all eight categories, although their magnitudes varied. The median count-based double/debiased machine-learning point estimate across five seeds was also positive. The association was small. A one-standard-deviation within-reviewer difference in matched-language count corresponded to a 2.39% difference in the model-implied geometric mean of 1 + helpful votes. Adding promotion and prevention density terms and their category interactions increased internal five-fold cross-validated R2 by ΔR2 =. 0002. The hypothesized response-surface pattern did not characterize the central data region. The findings are associational and do not distinguish regulatory fit from informational attribute relevance. They warrant prospective tests of whether category-congruent language measures improve review ranking or solicitation. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: When AI meets DEI: Employee AI-beliefs and their implications for workplace diversity, equity, and inclusion
Abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes the workplace, its impact on diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) has been examined primarily through the lens of what AI actually does (i.e., system design, outputs). This review shifts the focus to humans' subjective beliefs about AI, identifying mechanisms through which three dimensions of AI-beliefs (competence, warmth, and morality) may affect DEI goals: improving representation of underrepresented groups, closing career gaps across groups, and fostering inclusion. Our synthesis shows that, independently of what AI does, AI-beliefs can disadvantage underrepresented groups in some contexts, while creating opportunities for bridging human subgroups in others. Title: Drought, women's time poverty, and the development costs of water collection in Sub-Saharan Africa
Abstract: Drought can impose development costs that are not fully captured by income, production, or formal water access indicators. This paper examines one such hidden cost in Sub-Saharan Africa by focusing on women's time poverty arising from household water collection. Combining harmonized Demographic and Health Surveys with geocoded drought exposure measured at the survey cluster level, we estimate how local drought conditions are associated with women's annual water collection burden and broader household adjustments. We find that drought exposure is associated with higher water-collection time for women, with larger estimated increases among women living in poor households, women with no formal education, and women living in households without piped-water access. Intermediate-outcome evidence shows that drought is associated with lower local water availability and a higher likelihood of very long collection trips, particularly journeys exceeding 60 minutes. These water-time burdens are also associated with greater engagement in flexible, household-based, family-based, and self-employed forms of work among women rather than with a simple expansion of protected paid employment. In addition, higher community water burdens are associated with poorer schooling outcomes among girls, including a greater likelihood of being out of school and larger grade-for-age gaps. Household-linked evidence further shows that poorer girls’ schooling outcomes are associated with larger household shares of adult women in unpaid or in-kind work, self-employment, and family work. The findings suggest that drought-related water insecurity can redistribute adaptation costs within households, making women's unpaid time a key margin through which climate stress produces hidden development costs. © 2026

Authors: Li Q.; Chen H.; Lin Y.
Title: Trust begins at home: The role of psychological distance in trust transfer for emerging technology
Abstract: The widespread adoption of emerging technologies holds substantial potential to benefit societal development. However, fostering public trust and acceptance of emerging technologies, which involve complex underlying principles and are in pre-commercialization stages, remains a critical multifaceted challenge. To address this issue, this study draws on trust transfer theory to identify an effective mechanism for enhancing people's trust in emerging technologies. Specifically, we propose and test that trust in emerging technologies can be transferred from that in familiar institutions of the public by reducing psychological distance to such technologies. Analyzing quota-sampling data, we find that greater consumption of news about local brain–computer interface (BCI) achievements was associated with greater trust in local technology institutions. Institutional process and purpose trust were, in turn, associated with lower psychological distance to BCI, which was associated with greater general trust in BCI and, subsequently, stronger BCI use intention. The corresponding pathway was not supported for performance trust. These findings extend trust transfer theory by introducing psychological distance as a vital mechanism. Practically, this study demonstrates a route through which practitioners can promote public acceptance of unfamiliar and emerging technologies. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Students’ perceptions of learning management systems for academic essay writing and creative expression
Abstract: This study investigates students’ perceptions of the use of Moodle-based Learning Management System (LMS) in supporting essay writing skills as a form of creative expression in higher education. The study was conducted at Universitas PGRI Palembang, where the LMS was integrated into academic writing instruction. Although digital learning platforms have increasingly transformed writing pedagogy, empirical studies focusing on students’ perceptions of LMS use for creative academic writing in Indonesian higher education contexts remain limited. Addressing this gap, the study examines how the Moodle-based LMS supports the development of essay structure, language accuracy, and idea expression from the learners’ perspective. A mixed-methods research design was employed. Quantitative data were collected through a questionnaire administered to 50 undergraduate students (n = 50), while qualitative data were obtained from semi-structured interviews with 20 selected participants (n = 20). In this study, Moodle functioned as the primary learning platform for essay writing activities, including the distribution of instructional materials, assignment submission, and instructor feedback. The findings indicate that students generally perceive the use of Moodle positively in supporting their essay writing development. LMS use was associated with perceived improvements in essay organization, grammatical accuracy, and clarity of ideas. Its flexibility and accessibility allowed students to learn at their own pace and revisit learning materials, contributing to deeper understanding and enhanced creative confidence. Additionally, the availability of diverse learning resources supported students’ creativity in developing written ideas. However, challenges such as limited personalized feedback and technical issues were reported, which negatively affected student engagement. Overall, the study concludes that a Moodle-based LMS can effectively support essay writing development and creative expression when pedagogical implementation and technological reliability are optimized. © 2027, Malque Publishing. Authors: Zhou L.; Wang S.; Zhou Y.; Wan S.
Title: Flying low for greener farms: Configurational pathways linking the low-altitude economy to agricultural green total factor productivity in China
Abstract: The low-altitude economy is increasingly viewed as a new technological frontier for agricultural transformation, yet its relationship with agricultural green total factor productivity remains poorly understood. This study examines how low-altitude economy-related conditions are associated with high agricultural green total factor productivity in China. We develop an institutional-technological-scenario framework and apply a sequential mixed-method design that combines qualitative coding, necessary condition analysis and dynamic fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis. The empirical analysis uses a balanced panel of 30 Chinese provinces from 2014 to 2022, covering 270 province-year observations. The period is treated as a formative and pre-consolidation stage of the low-altitude economy rather than as a fully mature integrated system. The results show that no single condition constitutes a statistically supported necessary condition for high agricultural green total factor productivity. Exploratory bottleneck analysis nevertheless reveals descriptive threshold patterns at higher outcome levels. The dynamic configurational analysis identifies three pathways associated with high agricultural green total factor productivity, namely technology-application coupling, institution-innovation coupling and scale-application diffusion. The non-high productivity configuration further shows that enterprise development, policy support and market support may fail to translate into green productivity improvement when industrial application is absent. Regional and temporal analyses reveal substantial spatial and temporal heterogeneity. The findings suggest that the low-altitude economy is better understood as an emerging socio-technical enabling system rather than as a single UAV-based technology, and that agricultural green transformation depends on the configuration of institutional support, technological capacity and application scenarios. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: RumorGAL: Graph-anchored LLM for domain-generalized rumor detection
Abstract: Rumor detection models must remain robust to breaking events that are unseen during training. Although large language models (LLMs) offer strong generalization potential, their text-centric nature makes them vulnerable to spurious textual patterns in noisy social media discussions and leaves them without explicit awareness of how rumors propagate through conversation threads. To address these limitations, we propose RumorGAL, a graph-anchored LLM framework for domain-generalized rumor detection. The framework first employs a graph neural network (GNN) to derive graph-anchored structural prefixes from the propagation graph, providing structural guidance for the LLM. It then identifies high-quality textual evidence from noisy discussions through an evidence density-guided mining strategy. Finally, a hierarchical reasoning mechanism organizes both the structural prefixes and textual evidence into a unified reasoning process, enabling the LLM to ground its predictions in both propagation patterns and informative content. Across the three transfer settings, RumorGAL achieves robust performance, improving average accuracy over the strongest baseline, zero-shot GPT-4.1, by 5.27 percentage points under the domain generalization setting. When compared with domain adaptation methods, it surpasses the best domain adaptation method in two out of three tasks, with improvements of 3.1 and 0.5 percentage points in F1 score for the rumor class, respectively. These findings suggest that an LLM-as-primary, GNN-as-auxiliary design, which couples structure-aware guidance with evidence-grounded reasoning, is a promising approach to robust and interpretable rumor detection. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Who gets to negotiate? Tracing gender gaps in structural empowerment with people analytics

Title: Pathogen evolution under strategy changes in vaccination campaigns: A game-theoretic framework
Abstract: In existing models of pathogen evolution under voluntary vaccination, vaccination behaviour is typically assumed to be static, overlooking the conflicts between individual and collective interests. To address this, we develop a multi-scale model within a game-theoretic framework that couples the dynamic processes of disease transmission, vaccination decision-making, and pathogen evolution. By reformulating vaccine uptake as a time-dependent strategic choice and incorporating a heterogeneous update mechanism, we establish the evolutionary model of vaccination strategies. Numerical results show that heterogeneous updating rules will capture autonomous population decision-making. The co-evolutionary dynamics are highly sensitive to the evolutionary adaptation rates and exhibit an asymmetric relationship between population and evolutionary dynamics. At the early stage of a vaccination scenario, we observe that imitation behaviour dominates due to limited information. Enhancing vaccine uptake is effective in limiting the emergence of detrimental variants, and the long-term evolutionary outcome may favour the emergence of specialist variants. This framework provides quantitative methods and key methodological advancements for multi-scale mathematical modelling in the context of pathogen evolution. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: Crowding and green choice: Understanding a U-shaped relationship in China's organic food market
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Organic food represents a product category in which safety-and-health attributes and environmental attributes are both salient, making it an appropriate context for examining how retail situations shape sustainable consumption. This study investigates the nonlinear effect of shopping crowding on organic food purchase behavior and purchase intention, and further examines whether different crowding levels activate different organic food attribute cues. First, transaction records from a large supermarket chain in China provide associational evidence of a statistically supported U-shaped relationship between shopping crowding and organic food purchase behavior, with the turning point located in the upper portion of the observed crowding distribution and modest changes in predicted purchase probability. Second, a randomized scenario experiment provides causal evidence for the low–moderate–high nonmonotonic pattern in organic food purchase intention and identifies distinct indirect-effect structures involving positive emotion and perceived loss of control. Third, a 2×2 experiment compares the two crowding endpoints and shows that environmental-responsibility cues are relatively more effective under low crowding, whereas safety-and-health cues are relatively more effective under high crowding. Taken together, the findings extend crowding research and sustainable consumption research by identifying a nonlinear crowding effect, integrating compensatory control theory with consumer emotion theory, and showing how the match between retail situations and product attribute cues shapes organic food choice. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Tell me what you read, and I will tell you what you remember: Evidence for personalized embeddings in memory modelling
Abstract: Computational models of memory have achieved considerable success by formalizing how traces are encoded, cued, and retrieved. However, the role that individual linguistic experience plays in shaping representational structure has been relatively understudied. Where the issue has been examined, most models assume that a common population-level semantic space suffices, effectively treating individual variation in language experience as noise rather than signal. Participants reported their reading habits across the eight genres, and personalized semantic representations were constructed by weighting genre-specific corpora proportionally to each participant's reading profile. Two complementary analyses were conducted. In a model-free analysis, cosine similarity computed within each participant's personalized semantic space predicted recall and omission outcomes more reliably than similarity derived from generic semantic spaces. In a computational analysis, substituting personalized representations into the embedded Computational Framework of Memory improved cue–target-level predictions over generic alternatives, accounting for approximately 4 percentage points more explained variance. These findings provide proof of concept that variation in individual linguistic experience shapes semantic structure in ways that are both behaviourally detectable and computationally tractable. Title: Governance and renewable energy adoption: Assessing the state's role in solar energy uptake in Iran
Abstract: This study investigates how government managers in Golestan Province, Iran, interpret and respond to national directives aimed at promoting solar energy adoption. Title: The role of psychological factors on the mathematics achievement among alternative learning students in the Philippine context
Abstract: This study examined the role of key psychological factors such as self-efficacy, self-regulation, and time management in explaining the mathematics achievement among students enrolled in an alternative learning system (ALS) at selected public high schools in the school districts of Cebu, Philippines. Title: Reframing artificial intelligence as an observable market signal: Extending Signaling Theory in luxury fashion retail

Abstract: Artificial intelligence is transforming luxury fashion retail; however, existing research primarily views AI as an operational technology that enhances efficiency and personalization. Title: From smart cities to smart villages: Evolution, domains, and policy implications for smart rural development
Abstract: Smart villages have evolved from early parallels with urban smart city models into a comprehensive, multidimensional framework that integrates digital infrastructure, agriculture, local enterprises, tourism, and sustainability. This expanded framework recognizes the unique characteristics and potentials of rural areas, moving beyond the urban-centric logic of technology adoption. This review aims to examine the conceptual evolution of smart village research, track emerging methodological trends, and analyze global implementation trajectories. In the early stages, many studies concentrated on definitional debates and approaches that were primarily centered on technology. However, more recent perspectives have begun to emphasize the importance of integrating technological innovation with social innovation, community empowerment, participatory governance, and environmental stewardship. Methodological approaches have also advanced significantly, shifting from conceptual reflections and single-case studies toward more diverse methods including comparative studies, bibliometric mapping, and participatory action research. These evolving methods enable a deeper and more nuanced understanding of smart village dynamics. Regional approaches demonstrate distinct emphases: European initiatives focus on service revitalization and smart specialization; Asian and African strategies prioritize connectivity, renewable energy access, and digital inclusion; while Latin American programs increasingly integrate climate-smart agricultural practices. Despite regional differences, common challenges remain, including the persistent rural digital divide, fragmented coordination among multiple stakeholders, issues of financial sustainability, and the emergence of new forms of inequality. Policy directions increasingly stress the importance of place-based strategies, building local capacities, establishing supportive governance structures, and fostering inclusive participation. The review concludes by identifying critical areas for future research, such as the creation of unified evaluation metrics, conducting longitudinal impact assessments, and embedding smart village initiatives within broader rural development and climate resilience agendas. Overall, smart villages represent dynamic and promising pathways for driving innovation-led, inclusive, and sustainable rural transformation. © 2027, Malque Publishing. All rights reserved.

Title: Psychological vulnerability in conversational AI: How incentive and urgency manipulations alter trust formation and privacy behaviour across healthcare, financial, commercial, and security contexts

Abstract: Users increasingly interact with conversational AI systems in sensitive domains, yet little is known about how psychological manipulation techniques systematically alter privacy decision-making and trust formation across different contexts. Title: Reputation and value signals as moderators of advertising spend efficiency in E commerce search advertising
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: China hosts the world's largest e‑commerce search advertising market, yet merchants persistently misallocate advertising budgets by treating ad spend as a monotonic driver of sales efficiency. Drawing on the Resource‑Based View (RBV) and Information Overload Theory, this study investigates how advertising spend intensity (ASI) affects two core efficiency metrics—the Ad‑to‑Sales Ratio (ASR) and Return on Ad Spend (ROAS), as well as the moderating roles of two structural market factors. Keyword Specificity (KS) reflects the semantic breadth of keywords ranging from generic terms to long‑tail queries, whereas Category Competition Intensity (CCI) captures the density of competing products within each keyword market. Based on keyword‑level panel advertising data from a home appliances and household goods retailer operating on China's leading business‑to‑consumer platform, alongside supplementary observational data on competing products, this study identifies an inverted‑U‑shaped relationship between ASI and both ASR and ROAS: advertising efficiency improves with greater spending initially but declines after crossing a category‑specific threshold. KS shifts the efficiency peak toward higher spend levels, meaning long‑tail keywords can maintain efficiency under greater advertising investment. By contrast, CCI compresses this optimal spending range and triggers earlier efficiency deterioration in highly competitive categories. These findings extend the RBV and Information Overload Theory to sponsored‑search research and provide keyword‑type and competition‑dependent spending benchmarks for practitioners in Chinese e‑commerce. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Can natural capital accounting bring accountability for nature?
Abstract: With increasing global ecosystem degradation, new ways of governing the relationship between people and nature are needed. As Western societies increasingly turn to the emerging practice of Natural Capital Accounting (NCA), this is a critical time to consider its institutional role. In this paper we consider the effectiveness of NCA in bringing accountability for nature. This study theorises the link between accountability and NCA practice and explores this link empirically through quantitative and qualitative analyses of four methods of practice - the Capitals Coalition, Integrated Reporting, the System of Environmental Economic Accounting – Ecosystem Accounting, and Accounting for Nature®. The study found that NCA methods employ a range of technical mechanisms for delivering accountability, including data processes, external audit, and participation of, and transparency with, stakeholders; however, there were substantial limitations for their effectiveness. Our results highlight five challenges for NCA in delivering accountability for nature, underpinned by the broader governance environment in which this institution operates. We discuss governance options for bringing accountability for nature both with, and without, NCA. Title: Integrating human–stream interactions into ecological stream assessment: A novel rural–urban socioecological sustainability framework
Abstract: Current assessment tools for streams and rivers focus on ecological functioning while ignoring the social dimension, which varies across rural and urban ecosystems. This study presents the rural–urban socioecological stream sustainability index (hereinafter, RU-SESSI) for assessing stream function across the rural–urban continuum. This index is based on the stream ecosystem services (ES) and biodiversity index (SESBI), which was developed in our previous study to assess stream health. The SESBI was extended into a sustainability subindex by adding two economic indicators, and the framework was complemented by a stream–society interaction subindex comprising accessibility, public safety, and community involvement. Together, these subindices capture stream function through both sustainability performance and human–stream interaction patterns. The framework was refined and validated using the Delphi method, revealing significant differences in the relative importance of most RU-SESSI indicators between rural and urban segments. Applied to the Yarkon Stream in central Israel, the index revealed higher biodiversity and regulating services scores in the rural reach, whereas economic, recreation, and accessibility scores were higher in the urban reach, while public safety and community involvement were comparable between reaches. The urban reach achieved a slightly higher RU-SEES score than the rural reach (6.22 vs. 5.76), with no significant difference in the distribution of weighted indicator scores. Title: Audit fees under accounting and auditing standards: A communicative action perspective
Abstract: This study investigates audit fee determination under accounting and auditing standards by moving beyond dominant economic and agency-based explanations toward a critical, normative perspective. The study conceptualizes audit fees as a social construct shaped by the interaction between professional judgment, regulatory systems, and market forces by using Theory of Communicative Action developed by Jürgen Habermas. Using a semisystematic literature review (SsLR), this research synthesizes empirical audit fee studies published between 2010 and 2024 and analyzes them through a Habermasian lens to explore the tension between the auditors’ professional lifeworld and the systemic logic embedded in accounting and auditing standards. A comprehensive search of the Scopus database resulted in a final sample of 33 empirical studies. These studies were then used as the basis for an analysis examining how accounting and auditing regulations contribute to the colonisation of audit fee-setting practices. The findings indicate that standards such as IFRS, auditing standards, and regulatory oversight regimes function as steering mechanisms. These standards orient audit fee determination toward instrumental rationality, compliance, and risk mitigation. While these standards enhance transparency and comparability, they also increase audit complexity, documentation requirements, and litigation risk. The limitation of this study is that it depends on empirical literature with quantitative data. Nevertheless, this study contributes by expanding audit fee research into a normative-communicative framework, highlighting audit fees as a guiding medium in modern audit systems. Title: The relationship between intolerance of uncertainty and fear of missing out: Evidence from network analysis and a daily diary study
Abstract: Intolerance of uncertainty (IU) and fear of missing out (FoMO) are common psychological vulnerabilities during emerging adulthood, yet their item-level organization and daily temporal associations remain underexplored. Study 1 ( N = 875) used item-level network analysis in an undergraduate sample to examine the conditional association structure of IU and FoMO. Study 2 ( N = 235) used a 14-day diary design and dynamic structural equation modeling to examine their within-person temporal associations at the construct level. In Study 2, both constructs showed autoregressive continuity and positive bidirectional cross-lagged associations. Higher daily IU was associated with higher next-day FoMO, while higher daily FoMO was associated with higher next-day IU. Together, the findings describe complementary aspects of the IU-FoMO relationship: Study 1 identifies candidate item-level interface domains, whereas Study 2 independently shows temporal coupling between daily IU and daily FoMO at the construct level. Authors: Khan H.; Knight G.; Khan Z.
Title: Mechanisms for digital business model innovation in international new ventures from developing economies
Abstract: Digital international new ventures (DINVs) increasingly leverage ecosystem partnerships to drive digital business model innovation (DBMI) and navigate global markets. However, research to examine how such partnerships contribute to DBMI is limited, particularly in resource-constrained firms from developing economies. Drawing on the dynamic capabilities view, organizational learning theory and an ecosystem-based digital learning perspective, we investigate the role of ecosystem partnerships in enabling DBMI through the development of digital learning capabilities. Based on survey data from 147 DINVs in a developing economy, findings suggest that ecosystem partnerships enhance digital learning, which in turn facilitates DBMI. Moreover, foreign market turbulence tends to positively moderate the relationship between ecosystem partnerships and digital learning capability. In addition to demonstrating how DINVs build innovation capacity under volatile conditions, findings help to extend perspectives on capabilities, learning, and ecosystems. Leveraging ecosystem partnerships, digital learning, and digital business model innovation appears to enhance the performance of DINVs. Ecosystem partnerships appear to be especially valuable to DINVs when market turbulence is high. The study offers theoretical and practical insights into the mechanism through which DINVs from developing economies can achieve digital innovation, and provides policy implications for supporting their international growth. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Self-construal and the three flows of compassion: The role of dialectical thinking
Abstract: Compassion for self, others, and from others is increasingly understood as culturally embedded. This study examined the relationships between self-construal and the three flows of compassion and explored dialectical thinking as a potential process linking self-construal to compassionate experience. Caregivers of older adults in Hong Kong ( N = 210; 75.2% women) completed an online survey including the Compassionate Engagement and Action Scale, Self-Construal Scale—Short Version, and the attitude toward contradiction subscale of the Analysis–Holism Scale. Independent self-construal was positively related to dialectical thinking, which was associated with self-compassion and compassion for others, but not compassion from others. A significant indirect effect of independent self-construal on self-compassion via dialectical thinking was observed, with a positive but non-significant indirect effect for compassion for others. Dialectical thinking may link independent self-construal to compassion, particularly self-compassion, while other mechanisms may underlie the association between interdependent self-construal and compassion for others. Title: The attractor model of political competition and the resilience of democracy
Source title: International Journal of Modern Physics C
Abstract: We introduce an attractor model of political competition in which the distribution of voters’ ideal points is endogenous. Two candidates for office select policies they intend to pursue while in office. They also select a range of voters whom they will attempt to persuade of the merits of their policies. Finally, the opinion formation process, wherein each voter is influenced by neighboring opinions, determines the distribution of ideal policies. Our main insight in this paper is that despite the endogeneity in the distribution of voters’ ideal points, candidates will adopt policy positions equivalent to the median voter’s ideal point before the communication processes take place. This outcome is termed the “median attractor” result and shows that democracy possesses inherent resilience. We also show that candidates choose smaller influence ranges to attract voter groups, as such strategies will trigger the most favorable shift in ideal voter distribution toward the candidates’ policy positions. © 2027 World Scientific Publishing Company.

Title: Perceived need and measured well-being: How well do subjective rankings capture relative poverty?
Abstract: Subjective well-being rankings are widely used to target social protection programs, yet their ability to capture relative welfare and wealth remains debated. Subjective rankings also better reflect relative deprivation among households exposed to covariate shocks. A composite index combining all three modestly improves concordance with standard metrics. Title: Modelling the macroeconomic impact of Brazil's ecological transformation plan: a stock-flow consistent approach
Abstract: In 2023, the Brazilian government launched the Ecological Transformation Plan (ETP), a new development strategy aimed at promoting environmentally sustainable economic growth while enhancing productivity and social equity. This paper evaluates the macroeconomic impacts of the ETP's financial policy mix, by developing a stock-flow consistent model.The analysis focuses on representing the policy mix embedded in the ETP—particularly its financial instruments—and evaluating its implications for investment, growth, and macroeconomic stability. Title: Technology acceptance and student experience with a web-based school management system in Philippine higher education
Abstract: The integration of digital management systems has become a critical strategy for enhancing administrative efficiency and service delivery in higher education institutions. Title: Journey to the bargaining table: Signaling, seeking, and screening
Abstract: Negotiation scholarship has focused extensively on what happens at the bargaining table—how parties make offers, manage conflict, and reach agreements. Far less attention has been paid to how parties get to the table in the first place. In this article, we argue that the journey to the table deserves greater scrutiny. Title: Online collective aggression in algorithmic environments: The roles of algorithm awareness, moral outrage, and negative descriptive norms
Abstract: In algorithmic social media environments, filtering, ranking, and recommendation systems shape which online events, comments, and group reactions become visible. However, little is known about whether awareness of these algorithmic processes can reduce online collective aggression. Drawing on a focused application of value-added theory and a multidimensional framework of algorithmic literacy, the present research tested a moderated mediation model in which algorithmic awareness may reduce aggressive participation through attenuated moral outrage, with negative descriptive norms as a boundary condition. Title: Multi-objective multi-task optimization using decomposition collaboration mechanism and adaptive differential evolution
Abstract: Multi-objective multi-task optimization (MOMTO) is a key research direction in evolutionary computation, widely used to address complex trade-offs among multiple objectives and tasks. In recent years, numerous algorithms have been proposed and demonstrated promising performance. However, with the increasing scale and complexity of real-world problems, especially in high-dimensional settings, existing methods face major challenges such as slow convergence, high computational cost, and loss of population diversity. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an innovative many-objective and multi-task optimization algorithm (MaMTO/D-ADE). Furthermore, an enhanced differential evolution approach is developed, which integrates adaptive parameter control with hybrid mutation operators to effectively balance global exploration and local exploitation. A flexible offspring updating mechanism is also introduced to accelerate convergence while maintaining population diversity. Title: Applications of Artificial Intelligence in Disaster Management: Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses
Abstract: This study presents an examination of artificial intelligence (AI) in the disaster management (DM) cycle to support human decision-making systems. There is an urgent need for holistic application strategies that support disaster risk reduction given the increasing frequency and severity of disaster events. This stems from the growing adoption of AI technologies, including machine learning (ML), deep learning, and natural language processing in transforming disaster management. This is to enable the development of high-performance tools for assessing disaster impacts and addressing un-met human needs. This study reviewed journals and conference proceedings articles from three different academic databases: Web of Science, PubMed, and IEEE Xplore. Article selection and query refinement were conducted in accordance with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines to support methodological approach. The review explored scholarly perspectives on AI application in DM phases to support human-centered decision-making processes in reducing disaster impacts on human lives. Findings from the review indicate that most existing studies focus primarily on the AI application in the response phase. Despite its potential, integrating AI into disaster management remains challenging, particularly due to widespread misconceptions about adoption of AI, as well as ongoing ethical, trust, and security concerns. This study emphasizes the comprehensive application of AI to enhance planning, encourage proactive measures, and improve response and recovery efforts during disaster events. © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

Title: How do children intervene in transgressions? The influence of apology and intervention costs
Abstract: When norms for maintaining cooperative networks are violated, humans try to cope in various ways. However, knowledge is limited regarding how children respond to transgressions. Across two experiments, we examined how 82 six-year-olds, predominantly of Japanese ethnicity (97.6%), choose among punishment, forgiveness, and non-intervention when addressing transgressions from a third-party perspective using a novel paradigm. In addition, we examined how an apology from the transgressor and intervention costs influence children’s moral intervention behaviors. In Experiment 1, Japanese children (N = 41) were presented with a transgressor who either did or did not apologize. Contrary to the previous assumption that children are highly inclined to moral intervention even when it is costly, punishment was the least selected option and non-intervention was the most selected. Children who initially showed reluctance to intervene in transgressions then flexibly adjusted their choice to show forgiveness in response to the transgressor’s apology. In Experiment 2, as in Experiment 1, Japanese children (N = 41) avoided costly punishment and predominantly chose non-intervention. However, when punishment involved no personal cost, children were more likely to choose punishment and less likely to choose no intervention. These findings demonstrate that, when presented with multiple options, 6-year-olds engage less actively in punishment or forgiveness than previous work has suggested, and their intervention strategies are sensitive to social cues and personal costs. This research provides novel insights into the development of moral decision-making in early childhood. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: “The Right to Repair”: A systematic literature review and research agenda for an emerging interdisciplinary field
Abstract: The Right to Repair (R2R) is an important arena in which restrictive repair practices, including limits on access to spare parts, manuals, software, and specialised tools, as well as product designs that inhibit repair, are being contested. Although scholarly interest in R2R is growing rapidly, research remains fragmented across disciplinary and empirical domains, limiting the development of a coherent understanding of its implications for technology-society relations. In response, this paper presents a systematic literature review that maps and synthesises existing research on R2R. Specifically, it (1) consolidates empirical evidence on the implications of R2R; (2) examines how the concept has been theorised across disciplines; and (3) identifies key conceptual and methodological gaps that constrain theoretical and empirical advancement in the field. By organising this literature into coherent thematic domains and tracing the relationships between them, the review argues that the effective realisation of R2R depends on a socio-technical capacity: the practically exercisable ability to repair produced through the interaction between legal entitlements, technological architectures, economic arrangements, and social capabilities. It also reveals disciplinary and geographical imbalances and identifies four tensions structuring future research: formal ownership versus effective control, legal entitlement versus practical repair capacity, universal frameworks versus situated repair practices, and systemic transformation versus continuity. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: Transformative learning strategies in health education: Health Literacy and Information Discernment among tertiary students
Abstract: This study evaluated the impact of transformative learning strategies on the health literacy and information discernment of tertiary students at North Eastern Mindanao State University (NEMSU) – Cantilan Campus. While conventional health education often focuses on the passive transmission of factual knowledge, this research explored the effectiveness of pedagogical strategies grounded in Mezirow's Transformative Learning Theory (TLT), which emphasize critical reflection and the deconstruction of personal health assumptions. A quasi-experimental matching pretest-posttest control group design was implemented, involving 200 participants divided into experimental and control cohorts. The experimental group utilized reflective journals, collaborative case studies, and thematic health modules, while the control group received traditional didactic instruction. Data were gathered through a validated 50-item instrument designed to measure health knowledge and reflective insight. Findings revealed that the experimental group's mean scores improved from 22.10 (SD=4.12) to 37.70 (SD=3.45), whereas the control group's scores increased from 21.50 (SD=4.30) to 32.10 (SD=4.05). Statistical analysis, including an independent samples t-test (p=0.037) and a normalized gain (N-gain) test (t=5.894, p < 0.001), indicated a statistically significant difference in learning outcomes between the two groups with a large effect size (d =1.45). Observations from student journals further suggested an increased capacity for the critical evaluation of health information. These results indicate that integrating reflective teaching practices into the curriculum can significantly enhance health literacy and analytical discernment skills among tertiary students. This study aligns with Sustainable Development Goals 3 (Good Health and Well-Being), 4 (Quality Education), and 10 (Reduced Inequalities), suggesting that transformative pedagogical approaches provide a viable framework for addressing contemporary health literacy challenges in a university setting. Authors: Chen R.; Gao M.; Gao W.; Jin W.; Sun Y.
Title: The Olympic effect revisited: 1950–2019
Abstract: Rose and Spiegel (2011) identified a positive trade-promoting effect of hosting the Olympic Games, yet they did not account for multilateral resistance terms in their analysis, which are emphasized in the structural gravity model by Anderson and van Wincoop (2003). This paper revisits the trade effects of the Olympics using a nonparametric matching method developed by Chang and Lee (2011), analyzing a comprehensive gravity dataset encompassing 187 economies from 1950 to 2019. Our findings suggest that hosting the Olympics is positively associated with bilateral trade. For pairs in which both countries have hosted, the matching estimate corresponds to a long-run trade difference with an implied increase of approximately 15 times relative to matched nonhost pairs. Under an assumed trade elasticity of 4, this estimate corresponds to an illustrative trade-cost equivalent of approximately 50%. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Artificial intelligence is not enough to enhance organizational performance
Abstract: This study examines the relationship between Artificial Intelligence (AI), supply chain visibility, supplier integration, and organizational performance through the lens of Organizational Information Processing Theory (OIPT). Drawing on empirical data from UK-based organizations that have adopted AI technologies, we employ structural equation modeling along with mediation and moderation analyses to test our hypotheses. The findings indicate that AI does not have a significant direct effect on performance; instead, its impact is fully mediated through supply chain visibility and supplier integration. This supports the view that AI-driven supply chain visibility acts as an information-processing mechanism that enhances firms' ability to coordinate, collaborate, and integrate with supply chain partners, thereby improving organizational performance. Furthermore, supply uncertainty positively moderates the relationship between supplier integration and performance, amplifying the benefits under conditions of higher uncertainty. This study contributes to the literature by clarifying AI's indirect role in driving performance and highlighting the importance of embedding AI within broader organizational capabilities. It also offers practical insights for managers seeking to leverage AI to enhance supply chain integration and organizational effectiveness. © 2026

Authors: Liu Q.; Ma N.; Zhang X.
Title: Your recommendation and my choice: The impact of algorithmic recommendation convergence on consumers’ algorithmic recommendation aversion
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Personalized recommendation features launched by integrated online shopping platforms with multi-brand competition trap consumers in the dilemma of product choice constrained by algorithmic recommendation convergence, and induce consumers' algorithmic recommendation aversion. Against this backdrop, this article systematically examines the existence, antecedents, and boundaries of consumers' algorithmic recommendation aversion. The results show that algorithmic recommendation convergence significantly triggers consumers' algorithmic recommendation aversion and suppresses their purchase intentions. Specifically, in addition to perceived lack of self-control affecting algorithmic recommendation aversion, consumers' state of choice overload caused by homogeneous recommendation convergence is the key reason for perceived lack of self-control and the emergence of algorithmic recommendation aversion. Meanwhile, the results further demonstrate that in multi-brand markets with multi-oligopolistic brand coexistence, brand agglomeration further narrows consumers' brand and product choice scope, making it more likely to induce consumers' algorithmic recommendation aversion. In contrast, in a single-brand-dominated market structure, the core brand effect can leverage its dominant market position and market recognition to mitigate the impact of algorithmic recommendation convergence on consumers' algorithmic recommendation aversion. These findings expand the research perspective on consumer algorithmic bias, emphasize the importance of brand strategies, and provide timely and critical insights for understanding and alleviating consumers’ algorithmic recommendation aversion. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Phygital pop-up stores: Measuring immersion, novelty, and post-visit purchase behavior using eye-tracking and biometrics
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Phygital pop-up stores hybrid retail environments fusing physical spaces with digital layers represent an accelerating frontier in contemporary retailing. However, the precise cognitive mechanisms through which these sensor-driven environments translate immediate sensory engagement into durable long-term consumer choices remain under-theorized. Drawing upon the Technology Acceptance Model, Expectation Confirmation Theory, and Trust Theory, this study develops an integrated model positioning consumer trust as a critical mediator between phygital experiential antecedents and downstream purchasing commitments. Primary data were collected from 612 adult consumers across the United Kingdom and Australia via a stratified intercept sampling protocol. Objective measures of consumer immersion were captured using eye-tracking metrics and galvanic skin response indices embedded within a structured self-report survey. Partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) reveals that while immersive experiences, novelty, interactivity, and enjoyment associate positively with retrospective post-visit purchase behavior within a 30-day window (R2 = 0.482), consumer trust functions as the dominant direct predictor (β = 0.274, p < 0.001) and an essential gatekeeper mediating the immersion–purchase pathway. Multi-group analysis indicates that tech experience significantly moderates immersion and interactivity tracks, whereas gender exhibits structural invariance. This biometrically validated framework offers strategic resource-allocation priorities for experiential retail developers. © 2026

Title: Carbon trading in community-based forest management: A bibliometric mapping of scientific publications from 2000 to 2025
Abstract: Carbon trading in community-based forest management (CBFM) has emerged as a promising mechanism for simultaneously addressing climate change mitigation and improving the welfare of rural communities. This study presents a bibliometric analysis of 203 scientific publications obtained from Scopus, covering the period 2000 to 2025, with an analytical focus on the period 2010-2024. Using VOSviewer v.1.6.20 and Scopus's built-in analysis, this study analyzes publication trends, author participation patterns, geographic distribution, journal sources, and thematic structure through author collaboration, co-occurrence of keywords, and bibliographic linking networks. Results show a sharp acceleration in publication growth following key climate policy milestones, including the Warsaw Framework for REDD+ (2013), the Paris Agreement (2015), and COP26 (2021), with a record 21 articles published in 2024. Nepal and Indonesia emerged as dominant knowledge producers, collectively contributing 42.4% of total publications. Thematic mapping identified three main research clusters: carbon governance in CBFM, carbon measurement and quantification, and multifunctional forest landscape ecology. A critical knowledge gap was identified: while the supply side of carbon measurement of forest carbon stocks and biomass has been well documented, the demand side of how communities access, negotiate, and fairly obtain benefits from carbon markets remains largely unexplored. These findings underscore the urgent need for interdisciplinary research that links technical carbon measurement with institutional, economic, and social dimensions of equity to promote fair and scalable carbon trading within the framework of community forest governance. © 2027, Malque Publishing. Title: ICU onboarding, boot camp, and procedural readiness curricula as entry-phase competency development for residents and fellows entering adult critical care: A scoping review
Abstract: Introduction Entry into an adult intensive care unit (ICU) requires adaptation to unstable physiology, invasive support, local workflows, team roles, and supervision practices. We mapped onboarding, orientation, boot camp, and procedural-readiness curricula for residents and fellows entering adult critical care. Methods We conducted a prospectively registered scoping review (OSF DOI: 10.17605/OSF.IO/H2SN4 ). PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, CINAHL Plus with Full Text, and ERIC were searched on April 25, 2026 and updated through September 10, 2026. Embase was searched on September 10, 2026 to address its omission from the initial search. Supplementary citation and gray-literature searches were conducted. Records were independently screened by two reviewers, with third-reviewer adjudication when required. Intervention and landscape/needs studies were synthesized separately. Results Following database updates, the corrective Embase search, and eligibility re-adjudication, 31 reports representing 26 independent studies and five linked reports were included. Twenty-three studies evaluated interventions and three were landscape/needs studies; 20 interventions were entry-window and three were entry-anchored longitudinal. Non-mutually exclusive outcome mapping identified Level 1 outcomes in 14 studies, Level 2a in 15, Level 2b in 14, Level 3 in 2, Level 4a in 1, and Level 4b in 1. Twelve independent studies were conference-abstract-only. Conclusions Adult critical care entry curricula were heterogeneous and predominantly US-based. Technical and respiratory readiness were the largest evidence clusters, although nonprocedural transition domains were also represented. No superior curriculum model was identified; workplace-transfer evidence was uncommon, and patient-level evidence was limited to one uncontrolled airway-program evaluation. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: The effects of adolescents' digital and environmental literacy on parents’ green consumption: A reverse intergenerational socialization perspective
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Drawing on reverse socialization theory, this study examines how adolescents' digital and environmental literacy influence parents' green consumption behavior (GCB). Using matched adolescent–parent survey data, we employ PLS-SEM to test net and mediating effects and fsQCA to identify configurational pathways leading to high levels of parents' GCB. The results show that adolescents' digital literacy and environmental literacy are both positively associated with parents' GCB. Parents' decision-making confidence mediates the relationship between adolescents' digital literacy and parents' GCB, reflecting a capability empowerment pathway, whereas parents' personal norms mediate the relationship between adolescents' environmental literacy and parents' GCB, reflecting a norm activation pathway. The fsQCA results further identify nine configurational pathways, indicating that parents’ GCB is characterized by equifinality and conditional substitution. This study extends reverse socialization theory to the context of family green consumption and offers practical implications for promoting green consumption within families. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Ethical considerations in establishing reference population DNA databases of Indigenous peoples in Southeast Asia
Abstract: Reference population DNA databases are essential for accurate forensic statistical calculations, yet Indigenous populations remain significantly underrepresented in most forensic genetic repositories, limiting the scientific accuracy of allele frequency distributions and population genetic parameters in affected countries. This gap is particularly acute in Southeast Asia, where Indigenous peoples comprise substantial populations but are largely absent from forensic databases. This paper reports ethical and governance principles that should be considered in establishing and maintaining Indigenous reference population DNA databases to generate empirically derived allele frequency distributions, characterize population structure, and calculate population-specific theta (θ) values for forensic applications. We propose that such databases should be governed by policies discussed with and approved by authorized Indigenous representatives, with independent academic or government institutions serving as custodians. Effective governance requires culturally informed ethical policies, defined organizational structures, standardized operational procedures, and well-trained staff. Drawing on international precedents from Singapore (Health Science Authority), Malaysia (Jabatan Kimia Malaysia), New Zealand (the New Zealand Institute for Public Health and Forensic Science), and the Philippines (Filipino Genomes Research Program, DNA Analysis Laboratory, Natural Sciences Research Institute, University of the Philippines Diliman), we demonstrate that reference population DNA databases can be successfully managed by universities or government agencies that maintain institutional independence from law enforcement while supporting calculations of random match probabilities and likelihood ratios. We identify critical ethical gaps regarding informed consent, community engagement and/or partnership, data ownership, and restrictions on secondary use. We recommend adopting dynamic consent models consistent with Indigenous data sovereignty and the CARE (Collective Benefit, Authority to Control, Responsibility, Ethics) principles. The Philippines is presented as a case study, demonstrating how free, prior, and informed consent (FPIC) frameworks and stakeholder engagement enable the collection of Indigenous population genetic data while respecting Indigenous rights, albeit with their own challenges. Our findings demonstrate that ethical inclusion of Indigenous peoples in forensic database development is essential for generating accurate, population-specific genetic parameters and advancing forensic science that encompasses both broad general populations and smaller Indigenous communities. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Title: Don't promise me, prove it: Leveraging blockchain affordances to reduce uncertainty and build consumer purchase confidence in sustainable fashion
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: While the role of blockchain technology in shaping sustainable consumer behaviors is increasingly examined, empirical understanding of its capability to reduce uncertainty and enhance consumers' purchase confidence remains limited, particularly within the sustainable fashion context. In addressing this gap, the current study examines how blockchain affordances, including transparency, traceability, and immutability, contribute to sustainable product uncertainty reduction (SPUR) and strengthen consumers’ purchase confidence. PLS-SEM results reveal that blockchain affordances indirectly affect purchase confidence, primarily through PID and PSPQ rather than SPUR, with IL exhibiting mixed moderated mediation effects. Title: PhDGPT: Measuring bias in academic mental health across quantised and uncensored LLMs
Abstract: We investigate bias in academic mental health as reflected by Large Language Models (LLMs). This synergy of scores and texts offers a dual, comprehensive perspective on the emotional well-being of simulated academics, e.g. male/female Ph.D. students or professors. We find that both GPT-3.5 and GPT-OSS produce higher levels of mental distress when impersonating Ph.D. students compared to professors, a direction that aligns with humans’ recent results about mental health in academia. Compared against more than 39,000 human psychometric responses, GPT-3.5 reproduces the canonical structure of anxiety, stress and depression, whereas GPT-OSS does so only under vLLM inference and not under the GGUF quantisation analysed here. This specific instance of GPT-OSS, run via LM Studio under GGUF quantisation, also produces markedly fewer linguistic patterns correlating with psychological dimensions of distress than GPT-3.5. Authors: Xiao Y.; Liu Y.
Title: Intervention scope and crowd evacuation reliability under panic contagion
Abstract: Evacuation planning under exit failure is conventionally posed as a routing problem, in which the decision that matters is where each occupant is sent. This paper shows that once panic contagion couples crowd density to its own collapse, a control action becomes a load on the crowd it protects, and its reliability is decided by how many occupants it sets in motion. Three decisions that prior work confounds, the exit assignment, the release schedule and the scope of the repair applied when an exit closes, are varied independently in a validated social-force simulator with SIR-type contagion, across three station geometries with 40 paired seeds per cell. Metering the release into three batches is worth 20 to 36 percentage points. Redirecting only the occupants whose exit closed is worth 7.5 to 9.5 points on a linear-program plan and leaves the number of frozen occupants unchanged, whereas a re-solve that also releases the remaining crowd falls 43.5 to 43.9 points below that targeted repair wherever a cascade can develop. Optimizing the assignment yields no dependable gain. Every occupant ends the run evacuated, stranded or frozen, and the value of an intervention is its balance of stranding recovered against freezing induced. Copyright © 2026. Title: Computational models of hedonic evaluation: An explanatory–predictive framework
Abstract: Hedonic evaluation underlies preferences across domains ranging from food and social stimuli to art. Increasing evidence suggests that these diverse judgements rely on common computational and neurobiological principles, motivating a unified perspective on how hedonic value is constructed. Computational modelling has become central to this endeavour by transforming conceptual theories into quantitative, testable accounts of how sensory information, prior experience, internal states and contextual factors give rise to subjective value. However, the rapid expansion of computational approaches has produced a heterogeneous landscape of models that differ in their assumptions, computational principles, explanatory ambitions and predictive performance. Here, we propose an explanatory–predictive framework for organising, comparing and evaluating computational models of hedonic evaluation. The framework characterises models according to two complementary dimensions: mechanistic explainability and empirical predictive performance. We also organise models into six broad families defined by their dominant computational principles. Finally, we argue that progress will depend less on competing modelling traditions than on integrating complementary computational principles into a general computational theory of hedonic evaluation. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: Adaptive fusion heterogeneous graph attention network for detecting review spammer groups
Abstract: Detecting review spammer groups is important because coordinated fraudulent reviewers can jointly manipulate product reputation at a scale that single-review spam detectors often miss. On three benchmark datasets, AFHGAN achieves the best P@1000, R@1000, and F1@1000 under the adopted protocol. Relative to original Louvain, S-Louvain improves F1@1000 by 10.8 %, 8.5 %, and 40.0 % on Amazon, YelpChi, and Yelp_four, respectively. Title: Shaping tastes: Context- and task-dependent correspondences between basic tastes and visual forms
Abstract: Crossmodal correspondences refer to systematic associations between features across sensory modalities, such as gustatory sensations and visual shapes. The current study examined associations between three basic tastes (sweetness, sourness, and bitterness) and two visual dimensions (angularity and symmetry), focusing on their dependence on taste contrast, mapping direction, and measure explicitness. In Experiments 1–3, separate participant groups were assigned to one of three taste contrasts (sweet–sour, sweet–bitter, sour–bitter) and completed either taste/shape matching tasks or an Implicit Association Test (IAT). Experiment 4 assessed all contrasts within participants using taste/shape rating tasks or the IAT. Across matching and rating tasks, sweetness was associated with rounded and symmetrical shapes, whereas sourness and bitterness were associated with angular and asymmetrical shapes; however, less consistent mappings in the sour–bitter contrast suggest that sweetness served as a key reference. IAT results showed the most consistent evidence for the sweet–sour contrast, with weaker and less consistent effects for the other contrasts. These findings demonstrate that taste–shape correspondences are context-dependent and modulated by the direction of mapping and the explicitness of the measure. Title: Training emotion regulation in Preschoolers: Preliminary evaluation of a Researcher–Teacher co-constructed program aligned with usual classroom practices
Abstract: This study evaluated the effects of a research-based, innovative training program targeting emotion regulation in preschool children. The program was co-constructed with teachers to ensure its integration into everyday classroom practices. Its effectiveness was evaluated using tasks assessing emotion comprehension, recognition, and identification, as well as Theory of Mind and emotion regulation (ERC-vf checklist; Nader-Grosbois, 2014, completed by teachers). The results indicated improvements in teacher-rated emotion regulation and reductions in teacher-rated emotion dysregulation associated with the intervention, as well as gains in the identification of emotional intensity (particularly at the highest levels). Across these domains, pre- to posttest gains were greater in the Intervention group than in the Non-Intervention group, with differences in emotion regulation and dysregulation between groups emerging only among older children (5–6 years) in the classroom-adjusted analysis, although the effect for emotion regulation was at the threshold of statistical significance. The potential role of emotion regulation in supporting emotional and non-emotional competencies is discussed.
