Authors: Wang Q.; Tong W.; Wei T.Y.; Fan X.Q.; Zhang W.
Title: How should conversational recommendation agents organize candidate products? Matching recommendation set granularity with time pressure
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: With the widespread application of conversational recommendation agents (CRA) on e-commerce platforms, an increasing number of consumers use a CRA to support product choices. Existing research has mainly focused on the accuracy of CRA recommendations, with limited attention paid to how candidate products should be organized and whether this organization should be adapted to consumers' current decision contexts. Drawing on the product set granularity perspective and the heuristic–systematic model, this study examines the matching effect between recommendation set granularity (coarse vs. fine) and time pressure (high vs. low) on consumers' intention to adopt CRA recommendations and investigates the underlying psychological mechanisms. The results of three online scenario experiments reveal that consumers show higher adoption intention toward CRA recommendations featuring coarse recommendation set granularity under high time pressure and toward those featuring fine recommendation set granularity under low time pressure. The two matching effects operate through perceived fluency and perceived attractiveness, respectively. Furthermore, consumer knowledge affects the relative effectiveness of the two matching strategies: the match between coarse recommendation set granularity and high time pressure is more effective for consumers with low product knowledge, whereas the match between fine recommendation set granularity and low time pressure is more effective for consumers with high product knowledge. These findings extend CRA research from recommendation content to the organization of candidate products and provide guidance for retail platforms to adjust recommendation set granularity according to consumers’ time pressure and product knowledge. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: The automation paradox: Efficiency gains vs. workforce concerns in human-AI collaboration
Abstract: Human-AI collaboration (HAC) has attracted growing attention in operations and supply chain management due to its potential to enhance decision-making and organisational performance. Despite this promise, automation preferences remain uneven across organisations. This study examines preferences for full, partial, and no automation using a discrete choice experiment. Data were collected from 398 managers, generating 1592 choice sets and 4776 alternative-level observations. Alternative-specific conditional logit results show that automation preferences are primarily shaped by a trade-off between performance gains and workforce concerns. Operational efficiency and accuracy significantly increase the likelihood of selecting automation, whereas job insecurity exerts a strong negative influence. Anthropomorphism generates positive but context-dependent utility, while social interaction and investment cost are not statistically significant in the overall model. Managers prefer collaborative human-AI arrangements, choosing partial automation in 55.7% of scenarios and selecting no automation in only 3.4% of choice scenarios, indicating that the central decision concerns the degree of automation rather than its adoption. Further subgroup analyses reveal context-specific patterns across gender, sector, and organisational size, indicating subgroup-specific associations between socio-technical attributes and automation preferences. By identifying subgroup-specific patterns in the utility of AI attributes, this study extends socio-technical systems and contingency perspectives on technology adoption and highlights the need for context-sensitive automation strategies that balance efficiency gains with workforce security. © 2026

Title: Municipal utilities and SDG adoption: Evidence from Austria and Germany
Abstract: This paper explores how municipal utilities (MUs) in Austria and Germany adopt and integrate the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) into their strategies, strategic projects and management controls (MCs). MUs have a long tradition of delivering public infrastructure services, such as energy, water, and public transport, in the two focus countries. As important municipal enterprises, MUs must position themselves on a continuum between their public mission and their business orientation, and therefore act in a financially sustainable manner. Taking SDG adoption seriously is in line with the public mission orientation. Drawing on legitimacy theory, the study investigates whether MUs engage with the SDGs symbolically or substantively. The research is based on nineteen semi-structured interviews conducted with representatives from sixteen MUs, allowing for an in-depth qualitative analysis of strategic alignment, project implementation, and related MCs. The findings reveal considerable variation in SDG integration, showing that most MUs are still in an early, emerging stage of adoption, which is still at a symbolic level. By providing empirical insights from two countries with long-standing traditions of municipal service provision by local government-owned public utilities, the study contributes to the limited literature on SDG adoption in municipal enterprises and enhances understanding of the legitimacy dynamics shaping SDG practices in local state-owned entities. © 2026 The Authors. Authors: Yin H.; Zhu J.; Wang G.; Ni P.
Title: Debunking decisions for dynamically emerging topic-associated rumors
Abstract: In public emergency events, topic-associated rumors typically erupt in a streaming, multi-wave fashion, requiring authorities to continuously produce debunking decisions as new rumors keep emerging, all under unknown diffusion-model parameters. Inspired by Planck’s blackbody radiation law, we propose the Topic-associated Rumor Dynamic-emergence Competitive Cascade (TRDCC) model with a cognitive-fatigue effect, cast dynamic debunking as an online learning problem under the query–decision regression paradigm, and develop the Topic-associated Rumor Dynamic Control (TRDC) algorithm. Theoretically, we establish the NP-hardness of the problem and the submodularity of the objective, and derive a probabilistic approximation bound for the score function as well as a generalization-error upper bound that accounts for state distribution shift. On four real-world networks, TRDC attains time-averaged Performance Ratio (PR) values of 0.859, 0.891, 0.657 and 0.713 even under fully unknown diffusion parameters. Across all four networks, it outperforms the best-performing heuristic, learn-and-optimize and deep reinforcement learning baseline by margins of at least 0.23, 0.25 and 0.28 in PR, respectively, and remains stable throughout the entire decision stream. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Author full names: Ren, Zhiying (Bella) (57791675000); Collins, Hanne K. (57200137409)
Title: Good listening as a wise negotiation tactic
Abstract: Listening is a foundational interpersonal skill. Effective listening is central to managing the dual demands of negotiation: competing over limited resources while sustaining cooperation and trust. Nevertheless, limited research has shed light on how to listen effectively in negotiation. Integrating research from psychology, communication, and negotiation, we identify three common listening traps that undermine negotiation effectiveness: negotiators tend to focus too much on: (1) the self (and too little on others); (2) resolving disagreement (and too little on exploring it); and (3) what is said (and too little on what remains unspoken). We propose three approaches for effective listening in negotiations: (1) listening to understand rather than persuade; (2) listening for movement and change; and (3) making listening observable through concrete verbal and nonverbal behaviors. We argue that high-quality listening improves both informational and relational outcomes by facilitating deeper information exchange, increasing trust, and supporting integrative agreements. By highlighting high-quality listening as a wise negotiation tactic, this article illustrates how negotiators can better navigate the tension between cooperation and competition in mixed-motive interactions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Assessing Urban Flood Resilience through the Lens of a Dynamic Flood Resilience Index: Systematic Review
Abstract: Urban flooding is becoming more frequent and damaging due to the combined effects of climate change and rapid urbanization, exposing the limitations of conventional risk-based flood-management approaches. Consequently, resilience-based strategies have gained attention for managing uncertainty, system complexity, and recovery capacity in urban flood contexts. Flood-resilience index (FRI) frameworks are widely used to operationalize resilience by integrating social, economic, infrastructural, institutional, and environmental dimensions into composite indicators. However, many existing FRI frameworks rely on static or snapshot-based assessments that inadequately represent feedback mechanisms, temporal evolution, and nonstationary flood regimes. This study presents a systematic literature review examining how geographic information systems (GIS), multicriteria decision-making (MCDM), and system dynamics modeling (SDM) have been applied individually and in combination to support urban flood-resilience assessment. Seventy-six peer-reviewed studies published between 2010 and 2024 were analyzed using qualitative content analysis and frequency-based quantitative synthesis. The review synthesizes dominant methodological practices and identifies recurring limitations related to indicator aggregation, weighting, spatial representation, uncertainty treatment, and temporal dynamics. The findings show that GIS-MCDM approaches enable spatially explicit and structured resilience assessment but are commonly constrained by static assumptions and criterion independence. SDM applications offer strong potential for capturing feedback-driven system behavior and for the long-term evolution of resilience, yet are rarely integrated with GIS-based MCDM FRIs. The paper proposes a formalized synthesis-based framework that integrates GIS, MCDM, and SDM to support spatially explicit and dynamically informed urban flood-resilience assessment. Title: When and why women ask (or do not): Taking stock of research on gender differences in negotiation propensity, behavior, and outcomes
Abstract: Evidence first emerged several decades ago that women are less likely than men to initiate negotiations and perform less competitively than men in negotiations. Researchers also have discovered moderators of these effects, including structural ambiguity, representation role, and gender salience and relevance. Furthermore, the anticipation of backlash has emerged as a potential mechanism to explain gender differences in negotiations. Yet, more recent research has revealed varied findings concerning whether gender differences, underlying mechanisms, and moderators have shifted, as well as the role of intersectionality. We review the research in this area and find that the nature of gender differences in negotiation is complex, with some recent research replicating certain past findings (e.g., gender gaps in negotiation behavior) but not others (i.e., gender gaps in negotiation propensity or moderation by representation role). Still other recent research has even revealed a reversal of gender gaps in negotiation propensity, with women being more likely than men to negotiate in certain cases, and that female negotiation counterparts are liked more than male negotiation counterparts, leading to greater counterpart satisfaction. We also consider the role of statistical power given the small-to medium-sized effects typically reported: Sample size may be another important reason for inconsistent findings in the gender and negotiation literature. Finally, we consider the potential for changing gender roles. Overall, we conclude that gender differences in negotiation performance outcomes persist and are influenced by situational nuances, but that these differences have been mitigated for propensity to initiate negotiations. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: AI guest personalization as driver of hotel performance and hotel guest behavior: A dual-model analysis
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)–driven personalization is reshaping hotel operations, yet evidence on its financial effects and guest acceptance mechanisms remains limited. This study adopts a dual-perspective design combining hotel-level performance modeling with guest-level behavioral analysis. Study 1 examines revenue dynamics using Interrupted Time Series (ITS), SARIMA forecasting, and TOPSIS, comparing AI-driven and non-AI-driven hotels based on publicly documented implementations of AI personalization. Findings indicate heterogeneous short-term responses but more consistent differences in long-term revenue stability and predictability. Study 2 develops a Diffusion of Innovation–based structural model extended with trust in AI as a mediator, using survey data from 1396 hotel guests. Relative advantage and compatibility increase trust and adoption intention, whereas complexity reduces them; trust partially mediates these effects. Authors: Li Z.; Hu Q.; Huang H.
Title: Unveiling the effects of multidimensional urban shrinkage on urban flood resilience: A case study of the Yangtze River Basin, China
Abstract: Climate change poses growing flood-management challenges for cities undergoing economic, demographic, and spatial decline. Using 1921 city-year observations for 113 prefecture-level cities in China’s Yangtze River Basin (YRB) from 2007 to 2023, this study develops a six-subsystem urban flood resilience (UFR) framework encompassing socioeconomic conditions, ecological environment, infrastructure, institutional support, spatial structure, and climate stress. The analysis integrates CRITIC-TOPSIS, coupling coordination analysis, GeoShapley, mechanism tests, and probabilistic scenario simulation. The results reveal four main findings. (1) Both UFR and subsystem coordination improved significantly, with Sen slopes of 0.0023 and 0.0059 per year, respectively. (2) Drainage infrastructure, economic activity, and fiscal capacity made the largest predictive contributions, whereas the associations of population and spatial shrinkage were smaller, more heterogeneous, and more dependent on local context. (3) The mechanism tests further indicate partial pathways through population density and impervious surface. (4) The expansion scenario produces the highest projected coordination level, followed closely by SSP1, whereas SSP3 yields the lowest trajectory. Economic shrinkage remains below the baseline, whereas population- and spatial-shrinkage trajectories are not clearly separated from it in several comparisons. These findings identify robust associations and scenario-dependent pathways rather than causal effects. The analysis is subject to data constraints relating to event-level inundation, damage, and infrastructure condition, suggesting that future research should incorporate finer-scale hazard and asset-condition information and extend validation to other river basins. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Li W.; Liao H.; Teng M.
Title: Extreme weather and human capital formation: evidence from Qing China
Abstract: Weather shocks can constrain educational investment and human capital formation. In Qing China, education spending rose and fell with weather-sensitive farm income. Using a two-century panel (1646–1904) covering 234 prefectures, we find that a drought occurring one year before the examinations and additional droughts within the past five years reduce jinshi (the highest degree in the imperial examination system) density by approximately 6 % and 2.6 % per period, respectively. Adaptive measures such as the introduction of sweet potatoes, savings from surplus years, and flexible pricing mechanisms prove effective in mitigating drought effects. For robustness, we proxy regional recording capacity with the word count of meteorological entries and augment the baseline with controls for social unrest and epidemic shocks, with results remaining stable. Title: Capability, opportunity, and motivation for healthy eating: Exploring gender-specific pathways
Abstract: Women generally consume a healthier diet than men; however, both fall short of dietary guidelines. Health behaviour theories are often applied in a gender-neutral manner, implicitly assuming that explanatory models operate similarly across groups. This conceptual replication tested the Capability, Opportunity, Motivation and Behaviour (COM-B) model for dietary behaviour, originally evaluated in a female-dominant sample, in a male-dominant sample (N = 1358; 67% male). Using the same measurement battery and a closely aligned analytic approach, structural equation modelling indicated acceptable overall fit, with the COM-B model explaining 22% of the variance in diet quality. As in the original study, capability and opportunity were associated with behaviour indirectly through motivation, which was the strongest predictor of diet quality. At the indicator level, the male-dominant model retained action control and habits (capability), descriptive norms and the home food environment (opportunity), and self-efficacy, intentions, affective attitudes and perceived behavioural control (motivation), whereas identity, decision-making barriers, instrumental attitudes and the shopping environment indicator were not retained during trimming. These differences, relative to the female-dominant model, suggest potential variation in how COM-B constructs are operationalised across gender-dominant samples and should be treated as hypothesis-generating. Discriminant validity concerns (habits–action control; self-efficacy–intention) further indicated overlap between conceptually distinct constructs in the male-dominant sample. Overall, findings support the stability of the higher-order COM-B pathway while highlighting potential group differences in indicator contributions, with implications for measurement and population-sensitive intervention design. © 2026 The Authors. Title: Affordances and paradoxical engagement in virtual immersive learning platforms: A configurational analysis across demographic groups

Authors: Deng G.; Ye T.; Liu J.; Xu Y.
Title: Synergy or backfire? Adding virtual influencers to advertisements featuring human influencers: The roles of sensory cues and temporal framing
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: In recent years, virtual influencers (VIs) have emerged as a salient presence in brand communication. Firms are increasingly featuring them alongside human influencers (HIs) in advertising campaigns. Yet whether such HI–VI co-endorsement creates synergy or instead backfires remains unclear. Drawing on cue utilization theory and the elaboration likelihood model, this research examines how endorsement format, defined as advertisements featuring only HI(s) versus HI–VI co-endorsement, and advertising sensory cue type (distal vs. proximal) jointly shape consumers’ purchase intentions, and how this relationship varies across temporal frames (past vs. future). Results from four experiments (total N = 1293) show that advertisements featuring both an HI and a VI are more effective than advertisements featuring only HIs when distal sensory cues are emphasized, but less effective when proximal sensory cues are highlighted. These effects operate through two distinct mechanisms: perceived novelty explains the synergy associated with HI–VI co-endorsement under distal sensory cues, whereas perceived authenticity explains the advantage of advertisements featuring only HIs under proximal sensory cues. Moreover, future-oriented framing strengthens the novelty-based effectiveness of HI–VI co-endorsement, whereas past-oriented framing favors advertisements featuring only HIs through authenticity-based evaluations, particularly when proximal sensory cues are emphasized. Title: Academic self-handicapping in education: reconceptualizing it as a central psychological mechanism through a systematic review
Source title: Journal of Behavioral and Cognitive Therapy
Abstract: This study synthesizes empirical findings on academic self-handicapping (ASH) in educational contexts using a systematic literature review (SLR) of 30 articles retrieved from major international databases. The review aims to identify antecedent factors, examine the role of ASH as a psychological mechanism, and analyze its impact on academic and psychological outcomes. The findings indicate that ASH is a complex and multidimensional phenomenon shaped by the interaction of psychological, motivational, and contextual factors, including academic anxiety, low self-control, performance-avoidance orientation, weak self-regulation, and social pressure. More importantly, ASH operates as a core psychological mechanism that links antecedent variables to outcomes, functioning as a psychological bottleneck that constrains positive resources and as a risk-amplifying mechanism that intensifies negative academic and psychological consequences. Although intervention-based research remains limited, preliminary intervention evidence suggests that cognitive- and emotion-focused approaches, including CBT, REBT, and ACT, may help reduce academic self-handicapping; however, the limited number of intervention studies precludes firm comparative conclusions. This study contributes by shifting the understanding of ASH from a variable-based construct toward a process-oriented psychological mechanism within the academic system. Title: Why travelers prefer humans over artificial intelligence (AI): Developing and testing an AI aversion model in tourism
Abstract: As tourism businesses increasingly adopt artificial intelligence (AI) to enhance traveler decision-making, a persistent reluctance to rely on AI-generated recommendations has emerged as a critical barrier. This research addresses this gap by developing and validating an AI aversion model that identifies the factors driving traveler resistance to AI-generated recommendations. Using a mixed-methods approach, this research uncovered five core drivers rooted in the perceived absence of human nature attributes: lived experience, emotional engagement, contextual understanding, domain specific knowledge, and proactive engagement in communication. Title: Development of flood fear scale and investigation of psychometric properties
Abstract: This study aimed to develop a flood fear scale. The study was designed as a methodological and cross-sectional study. The study was conducted with 1158 participants aged 18–65 residing in Türkiye’s Black Sea Region between February 15, 2025, and May 15, 2025. SPSS 25 and Amos 21 programs were used to analyze the data. The flood fear scale consists of four dimensions and 26 items. The Cronbach’s alpha coefficient was 0.948, and the scale explained 62.644% of the total variance. The model fit indices were χ2/ df = 3.444, RMSEA = 0.065, SRMR = 0.056, CFI = 0.921, IFI = 0.922, NFI = 0.893, and TLI = 0.912. The findings indicated that the flood fear scale provided valid and reliable for adults aged 18–65 residing in Türkiye’s Black Sea Region. The total scores obtainable from the scale range from 26 to 130, with higher scores indicating an increased level of flood fear. Scale can be used to assess flood fear in community-based disaster risk reduction efforts. It is recommended that validity and reliability studies of the scale be conducted in different cultures and geographical regions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Munir K.; Nand A.
Title: Circular economy approaches to sustainable food waste management in the hospitality and food services sector
Abstract: The Circular Economy (CE) as a model has become a widespread approach to promoting sustainability through the restoration and regeneration of products and materials within production and consumption. Despite the plethora of work done, research on the application of CE principles for food waste management in the hospitality and food services (HaFS) sector remains scarce. This study adopts a conceptual review approach and follows the PRISMA-ScR guidelines to address this gap through exploring the role of CE in reducing and managing food waste in the HaFS sector through a review of papers between 2015 and 2026. The findings indicate that collective efforts of both actor-internal (hospitality managers and staff) and actor-external (customers, local authorities and government) stakeholders are essential to achieve sustainable and circular practices. Additionally, a framework that supports managerial decision-making by aligning with external stakeholders to enable circular food waste management is proposed for adoption in the HaFS sector. Title: Terror management and antagonistic personality: A network analysis of the dark tetrad, self-esteem, and fears of death and dying
Abstract: Terror Management Theory (TMT) posits that self-esteem buffers death anxiety, but TMT is rarely explored in antagonistic personalities. In a university sample ( N = 571), we estimated a Bayesian Gaussian graphical network linking Dark Tetrad traits (D4; Machiavellianism, grandiose narcissism, psychopathy, sadism), self-esteem, and fears of death and dying (FoDeath-Self, FoDeath-Others, FoDying-Self, FoDying-Others). Self-esteem connected negatively to FoDying-Self and FoDeath-Others, but positively to FoDeath-Self, complicating simple TMT accounts. It also showed comparatively high strength but near-zero expected influence due to offsetting positive and negative edges. D4 traits showed distinct TMT-related profiles: Machiavellianism connected negatively to self-esteem and positively to FoDeath-Others, with lower strength and intermediate expected influence; narcissism connected positively to self-esteem but no fears, and showed the highest D4 expected influence; psychopathy connected negatively to self-esteem, FoDying-Self, and FoDeath-Others, but positively to FoDeath-Self, showing the highest D4 strength but lower expected influence due to offsetting positive and negative edges; sadism was unrelated to self-esteem and connected negatively to FoDying-Others, showing lower strength and intermediate expected influence. An exploratory directed acyclic graph yielded a tentative FoDeath-Others → Machiavellianism orientation, motivating a speculative “personality-as-terror-management” hypothesis. Overall, self-esteem was not uniformly associated with lower mortality-fear, and D4 traits showed distinct mortality-fear signatures. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Actionable Weather Communication Recommendations for Hard-to-Reach Populations Using Topic Modeling and Thematic Analysis
Abstract: Language barriers, geographic isolation, and limited digital access are some of the obstacles that hard-to-reach populations in the United States face when trying to access weather and climate information. These conditions restrict equitable access to the public benefits mandated by federal weather policy and public warning systems. We identified actionable, evidence-based strategies for strengthening hazard communication for these populations. We conducted topic modeling on 7,705 peer-reviewed article abstracts and an in-depth thematic analysis of 129 peer-reviewed studies documenting effective approaches for engaging groups with differentiated information needs. The thematic analysis produced four integrated recommendations: community-embedded communication, hybrid and redundant communication systems, cross-sector coordination, and inclusive and actionable communication. Across these themes, studies emphasized strategies such as mobile service delivery, low-tech communication channels, culturally specific messages, trusted messengers, and participatory design. The results show how broader federal priorities for improving forecast communication and public response can be advanced and hazard communication improved through practices validated in health and social services. When taken as a whole, these insights provide communicators, emergency managers, and legislators with scalable ways to create more resilient and inclusive hazard information systems.  © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

Title: Energy equity under crisis pricing: the vulnerability-responsiveness paradox in Norwegian residential electricity consumption during the European energy crisis
Abstract: Dynamic electricity pricing is widely advocated for demand-side management, yet its distributional consequences under crisis conditions remain poorly understood. We examine the equity implications of hourly spot pricing during the European energy crisis using metered consumption from 1136 Norwegian households (October 2020–March 2022) linked to socio-demographic surveys. Southern Norwegian wholesale prices nearly tripled (+192%), and mean household electricity costs rose from 484 to 1785 NOK/month. Energy poverty emerged from a zero baseline: no household exceeded the conventional 10% income-burden threshold before the crisis, versus 1.2% during it, and 6.8% exceeded a 6% burden. Impacts were steeply regressive: the mean burden of the lowest-income group reached 7.4%, against 1.9% for the highest — a fourfold gap. SHAP analysis shows that housing characteristics dominate income and price as predictors of consumption, indicating that vulnerability is structural, rooted in the building stock, rather than purely economic. We term this the vulnerability-responsiveness paradox: the households facing the greatest welfare exposure have the least structural capacity to adjust. Counterfactual simulations show that a 1.0 NOK/kWh price cap cuts poverty to 0.3%, and that pairing the cap with targeted retrofits of high-consumption detached homes performs best across cost, poverty, and inequality simultaneously. Crisis pricing policy should combine short-term price caps with structural building-efficiency programmes. Title: What drives happiness in 15 European Union countries? The role of income inequality, democracy, and environmental quality
Abstract: This study examines happiness as a key dimension of sustainable development by focusing on its socio-economic, political, and environmental correlates. In recent years, it has become increasingly accepted that happiness cannot be explained solely by economic prosperity but is strongly influenced by structural factors such as income distribution, democratic institutions, and environmental conditions. Despite growing interest, empirical studies examining the simultaneous effects of these three fundamental factors on happiness are scarce. This creates a noteworthy gap in the literature. This study aims to fill this gap by empirically examining the effects of income inequality, democracy, and environmental degradation on happiness in 15 European Union countries, including the United Kingdom for comparability, between 2011 and 2022. Per capita income and health expenditure are included as control variables. Methodologically, the study employs MMQR and assesses the robustness of the findings using FGLS, PCSE, and HPJ approaches. The findings suggest that income inequality and environmental degradation are negatively associated with happiness, whereas democracy is positively associated with individuals' happiness. Furthermore, it is found that per capita income and health expenditure are found to be positively related to happiness. The results point to the need for sustainable development goals to be addressed within a holistic framework rather than independently, offering important implications for policymakers. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Title: Research on multi-behavior recommendation model via relational graph attention networks based on knowledge graph
Abstract: In practical recommendation scenarios such as social media and e-commerce, users engage in diverse interactions with items, including browsing, favoriting, adding to cart, and purchasing. However, traditional recommendation techniques still face limitations: (1) the neglect of differential values across diverse interactions; (2) the persistent challenge of user cold-start problems; and (3) the blurring of individual preference boundaries caused by an over-reliance on group-level characteristics, which leads to inadequate modeling of individualized preferences. To address these challenges, we propose the Multi-behavior Recommendation Model Based on Knowledge Graph and Relationship Graph Attention Network (MBRGAT). First, we construct a dual-layer attention architecture: at the micro level, node-level attention precisely captures the intensity of user preferences for different items; at the macro level, behavior-level attention dynamically learns the contribution weights of diverse behaviors to purchase prediction. This facilitates end-to-end quantification of behavioral significance, resolving the issue of uniform interaction weighting. Second, we design a cold-start preference transfer framework based on Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) clustering. By modeling preference groups through multiple Gaussian distributions, the framework assigns cluster membership probabilities to users, establishing reliable carriers for preference transfer to cold-start users. Finally, we implement a contrastive learning mechanism with a dual-layer intra-group and inter-group architecture. Training is optimized through dynamic sample-weight allocation, enhancing individual expression while accounting for group commonality. Comprehensive experiments across three public datasets–Yelp, Tmall, and Taobao–demonstrate that our framework offers significant advantages over state-of-the-art methods. Authors: Fan Y.; Wang M.; Zhang X.; Shi R.
Title: When products speak: The effects of product-as-subject anthropomorphic communication on consumer responses to carted products
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Shopping cart abandonment is a pervasive challenge in e-commerce, with more than 70% of online shopping carts failing to convert into purchases. In this context, this research examines whether and how anthropomorphic communication directed at carted products influences consumers' responses to shopping cart reminders. Across five experiments, we find converging evidence that product-as-subject anthropomorphic communication enhances consumers' purchase-related responses to carted products. Study 1 shows that product-as-subject anthropomorphic communication generates stronger responses than both non-anthropomorphic and brand-as-subject anthropomorphic communication, while Study 2 demonstrates that these effects are robust across different levels of pity conveyed in the message. Study 3 identifies state empathy and perceived interestingness as parallel mediators. Study 4 further demonstrates that these indirect effects are stronger among consumers with an emotional (vs. rational) decision-making style. Finally, Study 5 extends the findings to behavioral responses, showing that product-as-subject anthropomorphic communication increases behavioral cart re-engagement and reduces consumers’ reported likelihood of cart abandonment. This research advances understanding of anthropomorphic communication in shopping cart contexts and offers actionable guidance for the design of shopping cart reminders. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Walther D.B.
Author full names: Walther, Dirk B. (56921553200)
Title: The sweet spot of seeing: A categorization-based account of visual aesthetic pleasure
Abstract: Aesthetic pleasure is shaped by many visual attributes, including prototypicality, fluency, complexity, symmetry, and self-relevance, but it is unclear why such diverse factors all influence liking. I propose that a major component of visual aesthetic pleasure is an epiphenomenon of categorization in the visual system, constrained by the metabolic cost of neural activity. In this view, successfully recognizing a stimulus as a member of a category is intrinsically rewarding because it supports perception, generalization, and planning, and aesthetic pleasure partly reflects the summed effect of many local rewards for successful categorization across the visual hierarchy. At the same time, neural activity costs energy, so that strongly driven, cluttered, or statistically extreme displays incur costs that can make them aversive even when they are easily interpretable. The “sweet spot of seeing” (3S) model formalizes visual pleasure as a compromise between categorization-based reward and metabolic expense. It offers a unifying explanation for prototype effects, fluency and mere exposure, mid-level regularities such as symmetry and good continuation, and visual discomfort. The model links classic inverted-U relations between complexity and liking to a concrete trade-off between information and cost, and it makes specific predictions for how aesthetic preferences change due to expertise or fatigue. While integrating recent evidence that lower-cost representations in categorization-trained neural networks and human visual cortex predict higher aesthetic ratings, the 3S model leaves room for later, reflective, self-relevant, and culturally informed forms of aesthetic experience that recruit broader neural systems. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: Dual roles of higher-order interactions in temporal cooperation dynamics

Title: Comparative morphology and chemical profile of the metapleural gland in two ants: Paraponera clavata and Pachycondyla crassinoda
Abstract: Ants possess a pair of metapleural glands whose secretions are associated with antimicrobial defense and colony hygiene. Despite their importance, comparative studies integrating morphology and chemical characterization of these glands remain limited, particularly among poneromorph ants. This study investigated the hypothesis that species belonging to different ant lineages exhibit differences in the morphology and chemical composition of the metapleural glands. These features were evaluated in workers of Paraponera clavata (Fabricius, 1775) (Paraponerinae) and Pachycondyla crassinoda (Latreille, 1802) (Ponerinae), two phylogenetically distant species with distinct ecological habits. Histological and morphometric analyses were conducted to describe gland structure, including secretory cells, reservoir, and sieve plates, and gland extracts were analyzed by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC-MS) to identify chemical compounds. The metapleural glands of both species share the same general organization but differ in ostiole morphology, the number of sieve plates, and reservoir size, with the latter being larger in P. clavata. GC–MS analyses revealed both shared and species-specific compounds, with P. clavata exhibiting a greater chemical diversity, including the long-chain alcohols 1-octacosanol and 1,30-triacontanediol. Notably, 1-octacosanol has rarely been reported in ants, whereas 1,30-triacontanediol appears to have not been previously documented in the family Formicidae. These results demonstrate that the metapleural gland shows some morphological and chemical variation between phylogenetically distant species and provide new data that contribute to the understanding of the diversity and evolution of exocrine glands in Formicidae. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Multi-view aligned fused representation clustering network for unsupervised community detection

Authors: Zhou D.; Gong Z.
Title: Organizational responsibility attribution: Public responses to AI versus human failures in government services
Abstract: Existing research provides only limited insights into whether, compared to traditional human service failures, artificial intelligence (AI) failures in government services lead the public to attribute more responsibility to the service organization, and whether outsourcing necessarily alleviates organizational responsibility attribution. To advance this debate, this study conducted three pre-registered survey experiments. Study 1 (N = 1112) reveals that citizens attributed more responsibility to the service organization for AI service failures than to human service agents. The effect was mediated by the perceived service provider's controllability, rather than by counterfactual thinking. Study 2 proposed and tested two distinct pathways, namely the responsibility-transfer and controllability-transfer pathways. The objective was to explain how diminished controllability perceived at the individual service provider level increases the attribution of responsibility to the organization. Empirical evidence (N = 1084) supports the responsibility-transfer pathway. When citizens perceive that AI agents have less control over services than humans, they assign less responsibility to the AI agent and transfer more responsibility to the service organization. Study 3 (N = 1007) examines whether disclosing that the AI agent was externally developed mitigates the attribution of organizational responsibility. Compared to in-house AI systems, outsourcing to either a state-owned enterprise or a private enterprise, rather than to other government organizations, reduced organizational responsibility. In this study, this reduction was substantial enough to eliminate the disparity between AI and human service failures. This study advances theories of responsibility attribution in the digital era, highlighting the nuanced role of outsourcing transparency and the responsibility-transfer mechanism. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Effects of psychosocial interventions on emotional health outcomes in parents within one year after paediatric intensive care: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Abstract: Background: Post-intensive care syndrome in paediatrics affects the physical, cognitive, emotional, and social health of children and their families. Although psychosocial interventions are increasingly advocated, evidence regarding their effects on parental emotional health after paediatric intensive care unit (PICU) admission remains uncertain. Objectives: To determine the effects of psychosocial interventions on emotional health outcomes in parents of critically ill children within one year after PICU discharge. Research methodology and design: This systematic review and meta-analysis included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating psychosocial interventions for parents of children admitted to a PICU. Five databases were searched from inception to January 2026. Eight RCTs were included, and all eight contributed PICU-specific data to at least one meta-analysis. Outcomes included post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), depression, anxiety, and stress. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool. Setting: Studies were identified through searches of PubMed, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, PsycINFO, and CINAHL from database inception to January 2026. Main outcome measures: Parental PTSD, depression, anxiety, and stress symptoms assessed within one year after PICU discharge. Results: Eight RCTs involving 470 participants contributed PICU-specific data to the quantitative synthesis. Psychosocial interventions were associated with small reductions in PTSD symptoms (eight studies, n = 467; SMD = −0.30, 95% CI −0.53 to −0.07, p = 0.017) and depression symptoms (seven studies, n = 448; SMD = −0.13, 95% CI −0.24 to −0.02, p = 0.029). The pooled effect on anxiety was not statistically significant (eight studies, n = 470; SMD = −0.08, 95% CI −0.28 to 0.12, p = 0.380). General stress was reported by one study and was not pooled. Conclusion: Psychosocial interventions may produce small reductions in PTSD and depression symptoms in parents after their child's PICU admission, whereas the anxiety estimate remained compatible with benefit and no effect. Interpretation is limited by the small number and size of trials, variation in intervention characteristics, and risk of bias. Implications for clinical practice: Accessible evidence-based psychoeducational support, distress screening with appropriate referral pathways, and planned follow-up may help address parental emotional distress after PICU admission. Title: Influencer beware: The buffering role of sponsor–influencer fit in the commercialization-authenticity trade-off
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: As social media influencers (SMIs) increasingly commercialize their online presence through sponsored content, understanding how sponsorship intensity shapes consumer responses has become important. Drawing on attribution and congruence theories and the entity-referent correspondence (ERC) framework, this study examines how sponsorship levels influence audience engagement and purchase intentions through perceived personal authenticity (PPA) and whether these effects depend on sponsor–SMI fit. Three experimental studies were conducted to test the proposed relationships. The results show that higher sponsorship levels reduce consumers’ intention to follow influencers and share their content. Sponsor–SMI fit attenuates the negative effect of sponsorship intensity on PPA. Thereby mitigating its adverse effects on consumer engagement and purchase intentions. We further demonstrate that sponsorship level affects consumer responses indirectly through PPA and that this indirect effect is contingent on sponsor–SMI fit. These findings advance the influencer marketing literature by applying the ERC framework to distinguish the different authenticity types and their impact on consumer behavior. Title: Navigating housing system complexity – Part II: Quantitative analysis of the Housing System Abstraction Hierarchy (HSAH)
Abstract: Housing is a key component of urban systems, playing an essential role in shaping sustainable development and enhancing the resilience of cities. To achieve adequate housing, governments must adopt a systemic, integrated perspective on the housing system's structure, considering its complex interdependencies. Part I of this two-part study (the accompanying paper) introduced the Housing System Abstraction Hierarchy (HSAH), a conceptual framework for capturing the structural complexity of housing systems. Part II quantifies the HSAH, consisting of 176 nodes and 7822 interconnected links, using advanced network analysis metrics to identify the most influential components of the housing system and their functional dependencies. The results reveal that nodes with high Eigenvector Centrality, primarily within the economic, environmental, and technical domains, represent the most structurally influential parameters, whereas governance and social-related nodes with high Betweenness Centrality act as critical bridges facilitating cross-sectoral coordination within the housing system. Understanding these leverage points and network hubs provides policymakers with targeted entry paths for improving housing outcomes and driving system-wide transformation. Furthermore, the analysis traces cascading effects and systemic vulnerabilities, demonstrating how weaknesses in lower-level functional parameters can propagate and influence the system's higher-level objectives. Finally, the study highlights key insights from the policy paper on achieving adequate housing in Iran, developed based on the HSAH analysis, offering transferable insights for other developing and rapidly urbanizing contexts worldwide. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Nature sells: How visual biophilia influences promotional effectiveness of service firms
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Amidst the crowded media environment and growing consumer disconnection from nature, leveraging biophilia - the innate human tendency to connect with nature - offers a compelling way for service firms to attract and engage consumers. Although biophilia in service environments has been studied, its comprehensive application in service-firm promotions - both direct and indirect - remains underexplored. This research advances service literature by examining the effects of direct and indirect biophilia in service advertising using schema congruity theory. Across two studies, we show that indirect biophilia led to more favorable ad evaluations compared to direct biophilia and no biophilia (control). Although direct biophilia is known for restorative effects, we show that indirect biophilia in service advertising (i.e., abstract depictions of natural scenes, nature-like materials, and color schemes) outperforms direct biophilia by eliciting perceived novelty and mystery, which in turn enhance ad evaluations and behavioral intentions. Furthermore, our findings indicate biophilia yields the greatest benefits when the service is conceptually aligned with nature. Authors: Zhang J.; Cheng B.; Peng Y.; Tian J.; Chen M.
Title: Comparing applicants’ self-presentation in artificial intelligence versus human interviews: The role of opportunity to perform and contingency-based interactivity
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly embedded in employment interviews. Although AI interviewers may enhance the efficiency and standardization of personnel selection, their effects on applicants’ authentic and inauthentic self-presentation remain insufficiently understood. Drawing on impression management theory, this study examines how AI interviewers, relative to human interviewers, shape applicants’ self-presentation and why differences arise. Across four studies, we find that applicants facing AI interviewers perceive fewer opportunities to perform than those facing human interviewers. This reduced opportunity to perform, in turn, weakens not only exaggerated self-enhancement but also authentic self-presentation and authentic self-enhancement. These findings indicate that AI interviewers do not constrain deceptive impression management. They also dampen the expression of genuine strengths and self-relevant information. The results also show that contingency-based interactivity can mitigate this disadvantage by enhancing applicants’ perceived opportunity to perform and narrowing the gap between AI and human interviewers. By identifying both the constraining effects of AI interviewers and the design conditions that can reduce them, this study advances the research on AI interviews and offers practical implications for the design of more effective AI-enabled interview systems. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: A blockchain-enabled distributed service configuration approach for distributed smart manufacturing systems
Abstract: In the era of Industry 4.0, distributed manufacturing (DM) paradigms, exemplified by cloud manufacturing (CMfg), have garnered significant attention from both academia and industry. However, existing research on service configuration predominantly relies on centralized information architectures, which pose critical challenges such as single point of failure (SPoF), data privacy leakage risks, and limited scalability. Authors: Lin X.; Yang M.; Liu C.; Agag G.
Title: How retailers build authenticity over time: A longitudinal study of transparency, frontline brand enactment, customer-company identification, and sales growth
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Retailer authenticity is treated as a commercial asset, yet its relevance may depend on identity conversion. This longitudinal study separates retailer-controlled evidence from customers' higher-order authenticity judgments and from the self-definitional response that follows. Retailer transparency supplies informational evidence concerning disclosure, clarity, accuracy, and candor, whereas frontline brand enactment supplies behavioral evidence that employees embody the retailer's professed identity. Three waves of matched survey data from 10,214 loyalty customers nested in 208 stores in China are linked to a 12-month archival comparable-sales-growth window beginning during the closing month of Time 3. Multilevel longitudinal structural equation modeling indicates temporally ordered positive associations from Time 1 transparency and frontline brand enactment to Time 2 authenticity, from Time 2 authenticity to Time 3 customer-company identification, and from store-level identification to follow-up sales growth. The direct authenticity-growth association is not reliable after identification is modeled. The authenticity-identification association is stronger at higher prestige, recorded frontline interaction frequency, and brand familiarity, consistent with proposed conditions of cue diagnosticity and identity relevance. The study's central contribution is an evidence-judgment-identity-performance account: the observed pattern links authenticity with commercial performance through identification, without establishing that this is its only pathway or that a direct premium is absent. Title: Political Ideology Shifts in Large Language Models
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in politically sensitive contexts, raising concerns about their susceptibility to ideological biases. In this work, we examine how synthetic persona conditioning shapes ideological expression across seven open-weight instruction-tuned models (7B–72B parameters) using the Political Compass Test (62 statements) as a standardized behavioral probe. Across three studies involving 200,000 synthetic personas and more than 260 million model responses, we analyze implicit and explicit malleability, as well as theme-associated variation. We find that: (i) larger models exhibit broader implicit ideological coverage, increasing from 14%–35% for 7–8B models to up to 49% for 70B+ models; (ii) explicit ideological priming induces large and statistically significant shifts, with right-authoritarian cues moving all models in the intended direction and generally producing larger shifts than left-libertarian cues across model-axis comparisons; (iii) left-libertarian priming produces more heterogeneous responses, with counter-directional economic shifts in three of four 7–8B models and intended-direction shifts across all 70B+ models; and (iv) theme-associated semantic content in persona descriptions is linked to systematic and interpretable directional shifts in ideological space. While our results identify an upstream mechanism through which persona conditioning can alter model responses under a standardized ideological probe, we do not test whether such shifts affect users’ beliefs, decisions, or political behavior. Our findings are best understood as evidence of ideological malleability at the generation layer, highlighting the need to account for interactional factors when evaluating political neutrality, fairness, and safety in English-prompted, persona-conditioned language models. © 2026 The Authors. Title: The impact of digital marketing on consumer attitudes and behavioural responses: The role of perceived value and financial considerations in the decision-making process
Abstract: Digital technologies influence consumers across need recognition, information search, evaluation, purchase, and post-purchase activity. This study examines how six features of digitally mediated promotion—informativeness, personalisation, interactivity, entertainment, credibility, and electronic word-of-mouth (eWOM)—shape attitudes and subsequent behavioural responses among Albanian consumers. It also evaluates attitude as a mediator, media literacy as a moderator, and differences across decision-journey stages. Methods: A quantitative cross-sectional survey yielded 487 valid responses from adults residing in Albania who had recently used online channels in purchase-related activity. The conceptual model integrates the Stimulus–Organism–Response framework, the Theory of Planned Behaviour, and the customer-journey perspective. Measurement and structural relationships were assessed using partial least squares structural equation modelling with 5,000 bootstrap subsamples; supplementary analyses tested mediation, moderation, age-group differences, and stage-specific effects. Results: Credibility was the strongest predictor of attitude (β = 0.291), followed by positive eWOM (β = 0.245) and informativeness (β = 0.230). Attitude positively predicted purchase intention (β = 0.597), online engagement (β = 0.467), and recommendation intention (β = 0.517), while purchase intention predicted self-reported purchasing (β = 0.553). Attitude mediated the effects of all six promotional features on purchase intention. Media literacy strengthened the informativeness–attitude relationship (β = 0.109), whereas age-group differences were not significant. Influence was greatest during information search and alternative evaluation. Conclusion: Effective online communication depends more on usefulness, credibility, and authentic social evidence than on entertainment alone. The findings extend evidence from a Southeast European setting and show that favourable attitudes translate into purchases only when perceived value, affordability, payment, and delivery conditions permit conversion. Title: Nuclear ship Mutsu and the 1974 radiation leak Incident: Technical background and management lessons
Abstract: During its experimental voyage in September 1974, Japan’s first nuclear-powered ship, Mutsu, experienced abnormal radiation during a low-power reactor test conducted approximately 800 km east of Cape Shiriya in Aomori Prefecture. The immediate technical mechanism involved fast-neutron streaming and secondary gamma-ray generation caused by an inadequate shielding configuration. Although the event did not involve major fuel damage or a large release of radioactive material, it developed into a serious operational and political problem, leading to resistance to the ship’s return and to a government investigation. This paper reconstructs the incident and reviews the technical and organizational conditions that shaped its occurrence and subsequent handling. Drawing on official reports, technical records, and prior studies, it examines how inadequate project integration, limited design review, contractual separation, and communication failures complicated what began as a shielding-design problem. Using action system theory of management as a heuristic framework, we organize key task-level findings and relate them to recurrent patterns in major public technology projects. The case indicates that, in prototype nuclear systems, technical adequacy alone is insufficient: integrated review, clear responsibility, and effective communication are also essential to safe development and testing. Authors: Jing C.; Gao H.; Chen Y.; Gao T.
Title: DPIR: Dynamic propagation inconsistency reasoning for explainable fake news detection with large vision-language models
Abstract: With the rapid dissemination of multimodal content on social media, fake news detection faces increasingly complex challenges. Although existing methods can leverage textual and visual information for multimodal analysis, they often focus on static cross-modal consistency while overlooking the temporal-aware semantic divergence between news content and propagation evidence during information diffusion. To this end, this paper proposes an explainable fake news detection model based on Dynamic Propagation Inconsistency Reasoning (DPIR). Specifically, a temporal permeation strategy is introduced to dynamically fuse multimodal information and capture temporal-aware semantics within propagation sequences. Local semantic communities are leveraged to identify inconsistency patterns, and evidence-aware semantic aggregation is performed from a dynamic defense perspective. Finally, multi-source information is integrated to generate robust news representations. Extensive experiments conducted on three real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms the comparison methods in detection performance, achieving a 2.9% improvement in accuracy on the PHEME dataset, while providing reasonable and interpretable explanations for the detection results. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Stamkou E.; da Silva Pinho A.
Author full names: Stamkou, Eftychia (57217604327); da Silva Pinho, Ana (57705708800)
Title: Out of the picture: A multilevel framework of gender disparities in art
Abstract: Why do women artists remain a minority in museum collections and art markets, decades after becoming the majority in art schools? Talent does not explain it, since creative ability shows no meaningful gender differences, and audiences cannot tell an artist's gender from the work itself. The gap persists, we argue, because it is produced by a system rather than at any single stage of artwork production, selection, and reception. We therefore introduce a multilevel framework that treats the art world as an ecosystem. Artists, gatekeepers, and audiences act on artworks within three embedded levels of analysis (individual, institutional, and societal), and gender enters the ecosystem not only through these actors but also through the gendered content of artworks and the norms of the wider society. Actors, artworks, and norms interact across levels and over time. Societal beliefs in male artistic genius are internalized by artists and audiences and enacted by gatekeeping institutions; biased selections accumulate into a male canon; and the canon feeds that belief back to the next generation. The ecosystem is thus recursive, reproducing inequality without requiring discriminatory intent. Yet the same loop invites contestation, and excluded artists have answered with concealment, counter-institutions, and activism. Integrating evidence scattered across disciplines, this review derives a research agenda that treats the feedback loop, rather than any single stage, as the unit of analysis and as the lever of change. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: Data-centric AI in disaster management: Scalable Named Entity Recognition via LLM-based stacking and pseudo-label generation
Abstract: This study presents a scalable Teacher–Student architecture for Named Entity Recognition (NER) that enables automatic information extraction from Turkish disaster-related social media texts. To reduce labeling costs, the collective intelligence of three large language models (Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5) is combined through a learnable stacking meta-classifier. On a 500-tweet manually annotated dataset, stacking reached a token-level Macro F1 of 0.9313 (0.9219 under leakage-free tweet-level grouped cross-validation), on par with the strongest individual model (0.9245) and clearly above a BERT baseline trained on the same data (0.8335). It was selected as the Teacher for its learnable per-class weighting, its stability across meta-classifiers and its robustness to single-provider outages. The Teacher’s discrete predictions were transferred to a more efficient BERT Student through hard-label pseudo-labeling, and this Student was then used as a zero-cost proxy labeler to scale the corpus to 17,000 tweets. On a fully isolated 300-tweet blind test set, the final model obtained an entity-level Macro F1 of 0.9160, against 0.8648 for the baseline trained only on manual labels. A size-matched controlled experiment isolates the source of this gain: labeling the same 3000 tweets with the model ensemble instead of a self-training labeler improves entity-level Macro F1 by 0.033 in all five random seeds ((Formula presented) ), whereas scaling from 3000 to 17,000 instances adds only 0.006. Title: Exploring digital culture: A bibliometric review using keyword co-occurrence and performance analysis
Abstract: Digital culture has become a central organizational phenomenon shaping how firms navigate digital transformation, emerging technologies, and sustainability pressures, yet prior research remains fragmented across disciplines and contexts. This study provides the first large-scale bibliometric mapping of digital culture research from an organizational perspective. Using the Scopus database, we analyzed 212 publications published between 2008 and 2025. Bibliometric techniques and VOSviewer were applied to examine (i) annual publication trends, (ii) thematic structures through keyword co-occurrence networks, (iii) influential knowledge producers across authors, affiliations, and countries, and (iv) document type distribution to infer field maturity. The results show a clear acceleration after 2020, culminating in more than 60 publications per year by 2025, indicating that digital culture has shifted from a niche conceptual topic to a consolidated research stream. Keyword co-occurrence reveals eight interconnected thematic clusters, with “digital culture” and “digital transformation” acting as the primary conceptual anchors and linking strongly to (1) digitalization and Industry 4.0 in SMEs, (2) performance and dynamic capabilities, (3) sustainability/ESG-oriented transformation, (4) digital strategy and structural alignment, (5) AI and IoT as emerging technological drivers, (6) the digital economy, (7) marketing and consumer interaction, and (8) leadership-driven innovation. Country production patterns highlight a recent geographic diversification, with rapid growth from emerging economies alongside established contributors. Document type analysis further indicates a field dominated by journal articles (68.0%), supported by book chapters (18.5%) and conference papers (11.0%), while reviews remain scarce, suggesting strong empirical expansion but limited synthesis. Overall, the study clarifies the intellectual structure, growth trajectory, and research frontiers of digital culture, offering a structured knowledge map to guide future theory building and research agendas. © 2027, Malque Publishing. Title: River tourism based on community participation and regional linkages for sustainable livelihoods: The case of Can Tho City, Vietnam
Abstract: This study examines the role of community-based river tourism and regional linkages in supporting sustainable livelihoods in Can Tho City, Vietnam. A convergent mixed-methods approach was employed, combining surveys of 385 tourists, 47 local households, and 18 tourism officials and community representatives with 36 semi-structured interviews. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, exploratory factor analysis (EFA), cluster analysis, and multiple regression, while qualitative data were integrated through thematic coding, triangulation, and SWOT analysis. The findings indicate that community-based river tourism contributes to livelihood diversification, income generation, skill development, and social capital formation. Participating households reported relatively high livelihood stability (mean = 3.87) and moderate government support (mean = 3.59), whereas regional linkage participation remained low (mean = 1.79). EFA results revealed a common factor linking government support, regional cooperation, and livelihood outcomes, with factor loadings ranging from -0.64 to -0.51. For tourism officials and community representatives, EFA identified two governance dimensions—regional coordination and community-enterprise synergy—which explained 84.83 of the total variance. Tourists reported high overall satisfaction (mean = 4.35), strong community interaction (mean = 4.61), positive perceptions of cultural preservation (mean = 3.71), and willingness to pay for tourism services (mean = 3.98). Regression analysis showed that cultural preservation perception was the only statistically significant predictor of tourist satisfaction ( β = 0.146, p = 0.004 ). Open-ended responses highlighted key development priorities, including reducing crowding ( 29.6 ), increasing the availability of tour guides ( 26.8 ), enhancing cultural activities ( 23.9 ), and extending tour duration ( 19.7 ). Overall, sustainable livelihood outcomes depend not only on community participation but also on effective governance, cultural preservation, and stronger regional integration. Title: Escaping the AI cage: construction workers’ perceived risk with AI gives rise to unsafe behaviors
Abstract: Reducing unsafe behavior among construction workers remains a central concern in construction management. While artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are increasingly adopted to replace or monitor workers, the negative perceptions workers hold toward the promotion of such technologies have largely been overlooked. This study introduces the concept of perceived risk with AI, defined as workers’ subjective perception of the potential negative consequences associated with AI adoption. Drawing on self-determination theory, which emphasizes individuals’ core psychological needs, we propose an inside-out theoretical model. This model explains how construction workers’ perceived risk with AI triggers unsafe behavior through two internal psychological pathways: emotional exhaustion and organizational identification. We further identify AI failure as a critical boundary condition that amplifies these effects. Data were collected from 343 frontline workers at 3 smart construction sites where AI actively interacts with human labor. Results indicate that perceived risk with AI increases unsafe behavior, and this relationship is mediated by both heightened emotional exhaustion and weakened organizational identification. Notably, these effects are significantly amplified when AI malfunctions occur. Our findings not only extend the application scope of self-determination theory but also contribute to the knowledge base on workers’ unsafe behavior in the context of human-AI coexistence. Practically, the study offers actionable insights for managers to mitigate the unintended side effects of AI implementation on worker safety. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Beyond circularity: Topological and temporal limits of the circular economy
Abstract: The circular economy has established itself as a dominant sustainability paradigm, yet the formal properties of its foundational metaphor, the circle, remain unexamined. This paper identifies two analytically distinct constraints embedded in the dominant circular imaginary. The first is topological: when the operative metaphor functions as a single closed loop, it reproduces the cycle graph, a one-dimensional structure with zero redundancy and minimal resilience. The second is temporal: the assessment apparatus associated with circularity operates within quantitative, sequential time (chronos) and renders qualitative, heterogeneous temporalities (kairos) structurally invisible. The claim defended here is specific. Sustainability paradigms generally pose time as a problem left open; the circular economy's founding metaphor figures time as resolved (return, cycle, regeneration) while its apparatus operationalizes only chronos. This blindness is not general ignorance but performative contradiction. Empirical evidence from three continents (African solar projects, Mexican circular assessment, Peruvian extraction) substantiates the diagnosis. We propose a polyrhythmic completion structured as a wheel, with Doughnut Economics as the rim, regeneration as the hub, and ArtefactKairos (institutional devices for temporal composition) as the spokes, operationalized through the Temporal Composition Diagnostic (TCD), a four-step governance protocol. The TCD is applied to a published sugar beet pulp biorefinery assessment that models feedstock as a fixed daily input without addressing the seasonal harvest sustaining it, then calibrated ex ante against the Antamina mining region in Peru. In both settings it reveals what standard assessment cannot detect and specifies the institutional clauses it would generate. © 2026 The Author. Published by Elsevier B.V. Title: Gender differences in early semantic trajectories and academic career persistence
Abstract: Gender disparities in academia are well documented in publication output, citations, and career attrition, yet relatively little is known about whether male and female scholars differ in the semantic development of their research. On average, male scholars exhibit greater semantic expansion, whereas female scholars show higher research coherence and semantic alignment. These differences persist across career stages and productivity levels. Discrete-time hazard models further indicate that early semantic trajectories are associated with subsequent publication-based career persistence. Greater early semantic expansion is associated with a lower risk of dropout for both genders, whereas greater research coherence and semantic alignment are associated with a higher dropout risk, with stronger associations among female scholars. These patterns are consistently observed across major scientific disciplines. Together, our findings suggest that gender differences in academia are reflected not only in research productivity and career outcomes but also in the semantic organization of research development, and that early semantic trajectories are associated with subsequent patterns of career persistence. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Investigations of the cascading effect of hotel entrepreneur's optimism on employees’ work behaviors and customers evaluations in small and medium hospitality enterprises
Abstract: Given the significant proportion of small and medium hospitality enterprises (SMHEs) in the hospitality and tourism industry, this study focuses on the influential role and the power of entrepreneurs. Title: Shaping street rhythms: Spatial context and the temporal patterns of pedestrian activity
Abstract: Urban streets provide spatial contexts in which pedestrian activity unfolds over time, yet previous research has seldom examined how these street rhythms differ across space or how they are associated with local street conditions. This study addresses this gap by examining street-level pedestrian rhythms across Seoul's commercial streets. Using mobile phone signal–based estimates of pedestrian presence for 110,574 street segments in 2022, we extract 11 temporal features from weekday pedestrian time series and apply fuzzy C-means clustering to identify five street rhythm types. Multinomial logistic regression evaluates how these rhythms relate to 16 indicators of commercial hierarchy, physical scale, accessibility, functional mix, and surrounding populations. The findings show that street rhythm types are systematically associated with multiple dimensions of spatial context, rather than reflecting simple differences in pedestrian-presence levels or land-use intensity. Even among commercially active streets, evening-peak rhythms were distinguished by concentrations of retail, leisure, and entertainment-oriented functions. Midday- and afternoon-peak rhythms, despite their similar daytime profiles, were also differentiated by their spatial contexts: midday-peak rhythms were associated with office- and institution-based workday districts, whereas afternoon-peak rhythms were linked to production-related commercial areas. Title: Leveraging big data analytics for sustainable competitive advantage: A model of operational performance
Abstract: Big Data Analytics (BDA) has become an important organizational capability for strengthening firm performance and sustaining competitive advantage. OPBDA, in turn, significantly improves management's decision-making and organizational efficiency, while its relationship with Increased Innovation and Agility is not statistically significant. Title: Aesthetic perception is an embodied experience
Abstract: For at least the past century, philosophers have proposed a role for the human body in aesthetic perception. Scholars from experimental psychology, empirical aesthetics and human neuroscience joined in this endeavour in earnest at the start of the 21st century, following on from the establishment of neuroaesthetics as a formal scientific discipline as well as neuroscientific discoveries advancing our understanding of action–perception coupling in the human brain. Title: Enhancing Agricultural Extension Access: The Role of Different Extension Media in Climate-Vulnerable Areas of Bangladesh
Abstract: Enhancing rural productivity and resilience depends heavily on agricultural extension services, which support farmers in climate-vulnerable regions. This research examines how different farmer characteristics affect access to agricultural information through three channels: individual, group, and mass media. A cross-sectional survey of 820 farm households across the High Barind Tract and the southwest coastal and southeastern hilly regions of Bangladesh used random sampling for data collection. Age negatively influenced engagement, while farming experience enhanced contact. The majority of farmers relied on informal networks, including progressive farmers and neighbors, but showed minimal interaction with official extension agents and digital resources. Older and less-educated participants displayed restricted use of mass media. The study establishes that effective extension strategies require educational development, organizational engagement, and demographic adjustments. Title: Consumers and local short food supply chains: Critical purchasing factors

Abstract: Short food supply chains (SFSCs) are considered an effective way to promote greater sustainability in agri-food production. Despite their importance, limited research on consumers and SFSCs is available in emerging countries. It was found that socio-economic characteristics of the consumers, such as age range, level of education and income level, are factors that determine the purchase of food through L-SFSCs. Title: From disposition to action: The role of trait and state reactance in pro-choice protest participation in Poland
Abstract: Governmental restrictions on individual freedoms often elicit heterogeneous public responses. While some individuals mobilize collectively, others remain passive. The present study examines whether stable personality differences in trait reactance explain variability in protest engagement in response to abortion restrictions in Poland. Autonomy orientation and frustration with injustice were included as related dispositional variables to test the specificity of the proposed trait–state relationship. A sample of 586 participants completed measures of trait reactance, autonomy orientation, frustration with injustice, state reactance, and self-reported protest behavior. Structural equation modeling revealed that trait reactance positively predicted state reactance, which was strongly associated with favorable protest attitudes and higher participation. The indirect effect of trait reactance on participation via state reactance and attitudes was significant, whereas the direct effect was not.
