Authors: Guo N.; Chen L.; Guo L.
Title: Modeling pedestrian evacuation in ships: an enhanced heuristic-based approach accounting for oscillation and falling
Abstract: Passenger ship motion, characterized by periodic oscillations (pitching and/or rolling) induced by wind, waves, and currents, critically influences pedestrian behavior and crowd dynamics during evacuations. Severe oscillations can significantly impede movement or even cause falls, elevating the risk of stampedes and fatalities. This study examines how ship motion parameters—oscillation direction, amplitude, and period—affect pedestrian evacuation. We first analyze pedestrian desired speed on an inclined ramp by balancing gravitational, frictional, and driving forces. This model is then extended to simulate dynamic shipboard conditions by incorporating the effects of transient weightlessness and overweight accelerations. The analysis reveals that ship motion reduces desired speed. This modified desired speed is subsequently integrated into a heuristic-based pedestrian flow simulation model. Additionally, falling behavior is modeled by comparing real-time speed to the maximum achievable desired speed. Simulation results demonstrate that ship motion reduces evacuation efficiency in both room and corridor. Larger oscillation amplitudes and shorter periods further prolong evacuation times. Shifting the oscillation direction from pitching to rolling can partially mitigate efficiency losses. Critically, excessive oscillations trigger falls, drastically increasing evacuation time. This research enhances understanding of evacuation dynamics under ship motion and supports the development of effective crowd management strategies for large passenger vessels. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Trends and directions in military professionalism research: A scopus-based bibliometric analysis
Abstract: The current bibliometric analysis examines the evolution of research related to professionalism in the military based on the Scopus database. Author contributions, country-based production, institutional engagement, and co-occurrence analysis were reported. The biblioshiny in the R language was used to examine the data, and the Garza-Reyes was utilised to ensure the validity and reliability of the data. In this case, a total of 35 relevant publications were selected to be reported in the bibliometric analysis. Based on the finding, the USA is the most contributing country and has a steady increase in the number of publications, which peaked in 2023. However, even though the USA was indicated as the country with the most publications in this research theme, the United Kingdom was found to have the most impactful and influential publication, with a total cited score of 49. In terms of the most contributive affiliation, Uniformed Services University from the USA was dominant and followed by two universities from the Netherlands namely, VU University Medical Centre and the Netherlands Defence Academy. For the most contributive authors, Cole Rebekah and Rudinsky Sherri L were identified as the most productive authors. In this case, the author production over time analysis indicates Cole Rebekah, and Rudinsky Sherri L, are the most productive and influential authors in this research theme. In the thematic map analysis, the concepts of 'human', 'military personnel', and 'humans' emerge as well-developed and central, indicating that discussions around military professionalism are strongly anchored in the human dimension of service members. It was emphasised in the co-occurrence analysis that highlights the centrality of military personnel, humans, and humans, which appear as the most frequent and interconnected terms, indicating that research on military professionalism is predominantly framed around the human dimension and the role of personnel. Finally, the current research reveals three major military professional research directions through Multiple Correspondence Analysis namely, (1) education and social identity, (2) healthcare personnel and military health, and (3) professionalism and ethics, with demographic factors serving as a transversal element across clusters. © 2027, Malque Publishing. Title: The residential food environment, financial constraints, and dietary behavior in Dutch adults with low socioeconomic position: a test of the EnRG framework
Abstract: Socioeconomic disparities in dietary behavior are often partially attributed to differences in the residential food environment, yet evidence linking food outlet availability to diet quality remains inconsistent. The Environmental Research framework for weight Gain prevention (EnRG) proposes that environmental influences operate through both a cognitive pathway, mediated by Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) constructs, and a direct, automatic pathway. In this secondary analysis of cross-sectional data from 1033 adults with oversampling of low socioeconomic position, we tested both pathways while additionally examining the role of food insecurity and financial scarcity. Outlet density and distance to nearest fast-food and fruit and vegetable outlet were measured at the postal code level. Dietary behavior, TPB constructs, food insecurity, and financial scarcity were assessed by self-report. Path analyses tested cognitive mediation; subgroup and moderation analyses examined whether food insecurity altered food environment effects. The residential food environment showed minimal associations with dietary consumption: only one of eight direct associations reached significance (fast-food distance and fast-food consumption), and was attenuated in path analyses. All paths from food environment characteristics to TPB constructs were non-significant, indicating no support for cognitive mediation. Food insecurity did not moderate food environment effects. In contrast, food insecurity and financial scarcity were consistently associated with lower fruit and vegetable consumption and poorer diet quality, but not with fast-food consumption. These findings do not support the hypothesis that the residential food environment plays a large role in shaping dietary behavior in low-SEP populations, while financial constraints were more consistently associated with dietary outcomes supporting evaluation of policies aimed at affordability alongside environmental interventions. © 2026 The Authors. Abstract: Bibliometric analysis is a powerful means of evaluating research. Title: Should generative AI be responsible to users? Developing and validating the user-generative AI psychological contract scale
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: As GenAI becomes increasingly embedded in AI-enabled service interactions, users' evaluations of AI are extending from functional performance to expectations regarding responsibility and obligation. Drawing on Computers Are Social Actors (CASA) theory and psychological contract theory, this study defines the user–generative AI psychological contract (AIPC) as users' beliefs about the responsibilities and obligations GenAI should fulfill toward them during ongoing interaction and develops a corresponding scale. Study 1 used purposively recruited interviews (N = 26) to identify the construct content domain. Study 2 used two nonprobability online-panel samples of active GenAI users (N = 507 and N = 506) to develop the items and examine the factor structure, reliability, and construct validity. Study 3 used the same 506-case sample employed for structural validation in Study 2 to provide an initial test of the nomological network among AIPC, AI anthropomorphism, and co-creation intention. Results indicate that AIPC consists of three dimensions—the functional support contract, relational collaboration contract, and ethical safety contract—and forms a 16-item scale. Users reported the strongest expectations regarding ethical safety. Anthropomorphism was indirectly associated with co-creation intention through functional support and relational collaboration, but not through ethical safety. The findings extend psychological contract theory to user–AI relationships and provide a measurement tool for studying responsibility expectations toward GenAI. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Factors affecting public transport adoption in Riyadh- case study
Abstract: Riyadh's greenhouse gas emissions and urban climate risks are likely heightened by accelerated urbanization and profound dependence on private cars. Despite the government's investment in public transportation, societal resistance to giving up private cars and using public transit persists due to cultural and traditional factors. Within the Gulf context, this study is the first to investigate the unique socio-cultural and urban context of Riyadh to understand university students' mobility behavior, identify four factors that significantly are associated with their travel choices, and quantitatively rank the relative influence of these factors. Surveys (n = 710) were used to assess four key factors, analyzed via multiple regression, chi-square, and t-tests. Results indicate that, in descending order of influence, psychological factors (explaining 23% of the variance) have the most significant association with students' willingness to switch to public transport in Riyadh, followed by trip characteristics (13%), urban factors (12%), and socioeconomic and demographic factors (12%). The result suggests that, alongside infrastructure improvements, coordinated strategies are required to change social norms, enhance environmental awareness, and create culturally responsive incentives. Title: Using substances while playing: Players’ motivations, perceptions, and experiences with psychoactive drugs during recreational gaming
Source title: International Journal of Human Computer Studies
Abstract: Research on psychoactive substance use during video game play has traditionally adopted a medical lens, focusing on the addictive potential of licit and illicit drugs and their pathological impacts on players. This framing highlights negative outcomes of the co-occurrence between excessive gaming and substance use, leaving the motivations, meanings, and perceptions that players themselves attach to substance use during recreational play under-examined. In this article, we explore a first-person perspective on substance-involved play through a qualitative study with 24 participants (11 Italians and 13 Americans) who reported using psychoactive substances during gameplay. Semi-structured interviews were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis, which led us to develop three themes: first, adult players describe a “lost immersion”, an effortless absorption they remember from youth and no longer attain spontaneously, which leads them to deploy a repertoire of strategies, including substance use, to re-enter it; second, participants engage in “situated modulation”: they use substances as precise, context-sensitive levers for shaping experience, emotion, and cognition, aligning substance choice with game genre, in-game task, and the stakes of the session; third, participants perform legitimacy work around fairness, treating the same substance as benign in casual play and suspect in competitive play, and practicing situational rather than categorical self-restraint. Substance use also produced unintended effects that sometimes diminished, rather than enhanced, players’ agency over play and over their internal states. Authors: Zhang L.; Ma X.; Cai C.; Yu H.
Title: How institutions shape adaptation: Evolution and mechanisms of local residents’ behaviors in rural tourism
Abstract: Local residents' adaptive behavior is a key determinant of sustainable tourism. Nevertheless, the institutional mechanisms driving its formation have received insufficient scholarly attention. Using Yinxi Village in China as a case study and the Institutional Analysis and Development (IAD) framework, this research explores the evolution and mechanisms of residents' adaptive behaviors. The findings show that: first, residents' adaptive behaviors evolve from silent adaptation to supportive adaptation and then to resistant adaptation. Second, the high mobility of tourism development weakens the constraint effect of informal institutions, thereby creating an institutional environment in which residents adopt resistant adaptation as a ‘weapon of the weak.’ Based on these findings, the “mobility-institutional effect-adaptive behavior (MIEA)” framework is proposed. This study distinguishes three types of adaptive behaviors in rural tourism and offers an institutional perspective on their evolution. The results provide practical insights for improving residents' well-being and promoting the sustainable development of rural tourism. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Understanding human detection of algorithmic bias through drift-diffusion modeling
Abstract: Algorithms increasingly make high-risk decisions that impact individuals' lives, from loan approvals to medical diagnoses, but can exhibit problematic biases that require human oversight. Despite regulatory moves toward human-in-the-loop systems, little is known about a person's ability to detect algorithmic bias or how cognitive processes influence detection accuracy. Across two experiments, we show that human detection of algorithmic bias is limited, even when bias is pronounced and participants evaluate decisions across multiple trials. Detection accuracy is shaped by individual differences in gender and moral reasoning, and was not improved by a single warning ahead of time that bias may be present. Participants who are better at detecting bias tend to engage in more deliberative decision-making, taking longer to reach conclusions and requiring more evidence before responding. Modeling detection as a process of evidence accumulation allows us to locate where in the decision oversight may break down rather than only assessing whether it breaks down or not. These findings highlight the potential and limits of human oversight in algorithmic systems, suggesting that effective human-in-the-loop designs must support careful, reflective judgments and account for variability in users' monitoring abilities. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Alignments and Trade-Offs in Multidimensional Household Diversification: A Pseudo-Panel Analysis of Standard Practices and Public Programs in Rural Ethiopia
Abstract: In rural Ethiopia, multidimensional household diversification (MDHD) has become a vital element in strengthening livelihood resilience. While earlier research addressed how household-level standard practices (HLSPs) and public income-generating initiatives (PIGIs) influence diversification, their direct impact on resilience was not fully understood. This study analyzed data from five waves of the Ethiopian Living Standards Measurement Study from 2011 to 2021 to clarify these relationships. Households were classified into 15,191 cohorts based on birth year, location, and household head gender. Using a weighted Herfindahl-based method, the analysis found that 51.33% of households were highly diversified. The results indicated that public income-generating initiatives significantly enhanced diversification, increasing it by 6.88 points on a 0-100 scale. Other important factors included land tenure arrangements, gender dynamics, access to extension services, and participation in nonfarm enterprises. A key insight was that public income-generating programs are most effective when aligned with existing household strategies. Among households already engaged in traditional livelihood practices, involvement in government initiatives led to the greatest improvements, adding 6.88 points to diversification levels. For policymakers, the study suggests that the Ministry of Agriculture should require regional offices to evaluate household practices before implementing income-generating programs. Additionally, District Rural Development Offices should supplement these efforts with agricultural training and enhanced extension services. Such an integrated approach would enable rural households to develop more diverse income sources and better withstand economic shocks. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Title: Polycentric risk governance across safety and security risk logics
Abstract: The regulatory regime governing the Norwegian petroleum sector changed significantly in response to new geopolitical conditions following the war in Ukraine and the sabotage of the Nord Stream I and II pipelines. New legal security requirements and security risk logics were introduced into a sector whose traditional regulatory regime and risk logic had been intrinsically oriented toward safety. This shift altered the balance between safety and security considerations within the sector. This article explores the implications for regulatory regimes and risk logics when transitioning from safety-oriented to security-oriented regulatory models. Our ambition is primarily conceptual and theoretical, with the Norwegian petroleum industry serving as an illustrative case. The article analyses the emerging interface between safety and security, emphasizing the ontological, epistemological, and procedural divergences that complicate the integration of security concerns − focused on intentional, adversarial threats − into established safety regimes that manage unintentional harm. Anchored in a polycentric governance framework, the article examines how geopolitical developments have created tensions between rule-based and risk-based regulatory models, and the implications for organizational practices, regulatory oversight, and tripartite cooperation. It concludes by proposing a model of enforced self-regulation that reconciles safety and security logics, highlighting the need for adaptive, resilient, and knowledge-driven approaches to risk management in complex and evolving threat landscapes. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: Hungry for change: Inclusive dining for travelers with dietary restrictions
Abstract: Dining is central to tourism experiences, yet for travelers with dietary restrictions, it can become a source of exclusion rather than enjoyment. Guided by stigma theory, this study examines how dietary restrictions function as a form of concealable stigma in tourism dining contexts. Using a sequential exploratory mixed-methods design, the study combines Critical Incident Technique interviews with 32 individuals and text mining of 3,165 traveler Yelp reviews. Findings reveal that stigma manifests through internal (self-burden, anticipatory anxiety) and external (public, structural, associative) forms producing psychological and behavioral consequences that constrain participation in dining experiences. Individuals employ a range of voluntary and involuntary coping responses to navigate such challenges. Title: The development of children’s mathematics achievement in primary school: the early and longitudinal links with perceived teacher support and mathematics anxiety
Abstract: This longitudinal study investigated developmental trajectories of children’s mathematics achievement, especially the early and longitudinal effects of perceived teacher support and mathematics anxiety. The participants included 1231 Chinese children (M T1age = 8.49, SD = 0.59; 40.29% female) assessed annually across four waves from Grade 3 through Grade 6. Latent class growth models identified three trajectories of children’s mathematics achievement: a low stable group (9.3%), a medium fast rising group (81.4%), and a high stable rising group (9.3%). Relative to the low stable group, early higher levels of mathematics anxiety were associated with lower odds of membership in the latter two groups both. In terms of the developmental trajectory of perceived teacher support, a higher initial level, a smaller early decline, and faster growth during the middle-to-late period were associated with a greater likelihood of membership in the high stable rising group. In contrast, the developmental trajectory of mathematics anxiety indicated that a higher initial level of as well as a slower subsequent decline were associated with a greater likelihood of membership in the low stable group. These findings highlight the distinct predictive roles of perceived teacher support and mathematics anxiety across diverse trajectories of mathematics achievement. Practically speaking, the present study emphasizes the need for differentiated instructional interventions tailored to children’s achievement levels, with attention to both environmental support and individual academic emotions. Title: Gendered environmental leadership and the rise of biodiversity finance
Abstract: This paper examines whether gender diversity in environmental governance is associated with biodiversity-finance outcomes across the 27 European Union countries between 2012 and 2023. We distinguish between administrative, ministerial, and legislative dimensions of women's representation and evaluate their relationship with biodiversity-finance volume and intensity using fixed-effects Poisson and fractional-response models. The results provide limited evidence that gender representation alone systematically predicts biodiversity-finance outcomes. Female representation in environmental administrations is negatively associated with biodiversity-finance intensity, while female environment ministers are positively associated with intensity. No robust unconditional relationship is observed for biodiversity-finance volume. However, several conditional patterns emerge. In the later years of the sample, higher female representation in environmental administrations, ministerial positions, and parliamentary environmental committees becomes more strongly associated with biodiversity expenditure. Similarly, the positive association between female ministers and biodiversity-finance outcomes is stronger in countries characterized by higher levels of women's political empowerment. By contrast, threshold analyses provide little evidence of critical-mass effects. Overall, the findings suggest that the relationship between gender diversity and biodiversity finance is conditional on institutional and policy context rather than representation alone. These results contribute to the emerging literature on biodiversity finance by highlighting how governance structures may shape biodiversity-related public spending. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Authors: Liu R.; He X.; Lv L.
Title: Recommend or not? Investigating the effectiveness of personalized algorithmic recommendations in micro-donation advertising
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Online charitable platforms are important channels through which the public participates in micro-donations, and these platforms have increasingly leveraged algorithmic recommendation technologies to deliver personalized charitable advertisements to potential donors. Nonetheless, whether personalized algorithmic recommendations enhance or undermine consumers’ micro-donation intentions remains unclear. Drawing on moral identity theory, our research addresses this gap through five online scenario-based experiments. The results show that consumers exhibit lower micro-donation intentions when exposed to micro-donation advertisements with personalized algorithmic recommendations, and that this negative effect is driven primarily by perceived identity value threat. Furthermore, we find that the negative effect of personalized algorithmic recommendations in micro-donation advertising is attenuated in the presence of legitimization cues or among consumers with low scores on the moral identity scale. Our findings not only extend the literature on the antecedents of micro-donations and the economic consequences of algorithmic personalization in the charitable advertising context, but also offer actionable guidance for charitable platforms seeking to optimize their algorithmic recommendation strategies. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Development and application of HELDA: a multi-criteria decision analysis software tailored for sustainable energy system transitions
Abstract: Achieving sustainable energy system transitions necessitates the development of innovative technologies and systems, and their integration into complex and rapidly changing societal frameworks. In such a dynamic context, it is important to have a tool that accelerates decision-making processes, including stakeholder preferences, while maintaining scientific rigor, transparency and inclusiveness. To achieve this objective, sustainability assessments (SA) with multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) methods have been widely used. Despite the development of MCDA software tools to facilitate the implementation of MCDA methods, challenges often arise concerning the selection of a proper MCDA method and the integration of stakeholders, which often requires significant resources. This research presents HELDA, the Helmholtz Decision Analysis Tool developed following the concepts of MCDA for SA including the strong sustainability concept and stakeholders’ integration. To our knowledge, HELDA is the only free MCDA software that integrates binary relations methods (ELECTRE III and PROMETHEE I and II) with online surveys for weights elicitation of stakeholder groups (synchronous and asynchronous). The HELDA software is the result of extending the functionality of an existing MCDA software based on a previous study on the capabilities of MCDA software to conduct SA. HELDA development process was based on theories from agile software development. The functionality of HELDA is illustrated in a case study on the prospective SA of individual motorized mobility options using ELECTRE III method. Title: Perceptions of biodiversity benefits of regional food: A Q-method study from a German biosphere reserve
Abstract: Increasing consumer demand for food produced using biodiversity-friendly practices may create market incentives that support biodiversity conservation. However, there is limited understanding of consumer perspectives regarding the perceived biodiversity aspects of such products. This study represents an empirical approach to investigate how consumers perceive biodiversity-related attributes of regional products and how these perceptions influence purchase motivation in the context of the Swabian Alb Biosphere Reserve. Regional product criteria related to biodiversity protection and prevalence within the Swabian Alb Biosphere Reserve were assessed through a literature review. Key findings include the determination of three prevalent consumer perspectives consisting of Traditional Regionalists valuing local community support and cultural identity, Environmental Pragmatists appreciating criteria with direct environmental protection benefits and Quality Seekers being motivated by concerns of food safety and transparency in the food industry. The regional product criteria were revisited regarding their importance for the individual consumer perspectives, providing insights into how each group relates to criteria associated with perceived biodiversity benefits. Authors: Jia H.; Lin B.
Title: Appliance-level energy assessment and its implications for the environmental impact of household energy conservation: Evidence from urban China
Abstract: Accurate appliance-level energy judgments may help households identify and prioritize meaningful electricity-saving opportunities, with potential implications for the environmental benefits of household conservation. Using survey and experimental data from 2592 residents in Beijing, Shanghai, and Guangzhou, this paper assesses how accurately urban households estimate the electricity consumption of 11 common appliances, whether their judgments exhibit patterns consistent with availability-based reasoning, and whether a randomized heat-related information cue improves relative appliance-energy judgments. The results reveal substantial misalignment between perceived and benchmark electricity use: (1) respondents tend to overestimate the energy use of low-energy, frequently used appliances (e.g., televisions) while underestimating high-energy, infrequently interacted devices (e.g., water heaters); (2) appliance use frequency is positively associated with perceived energy consumption, a pattern consistent with greater cognitive accessibility of frequently used appliances; (3) random assignment to the heat-related cue increases perceived energy use for heat-producing appliances and improves respondents' measured relative correspondence with the benchmark; and (4) further analyses show that higher educational attainment is associated with closer benchmark alignment and that closer alignment is associated with lower reported household electricity expenditures. These findings document systematic deviations in appliance-level energy judgments and show that a targeted information cue can improve such judgments. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: What drives hybrid cultivated meat acceptance? Evidence from a controlled real-product tasting
Abstract: Despite growing interest in cultivated meat, most consumer-related evidence remains based on hypothetical assessments rather than real product exposure, limiting understanding of actual sensory-driven acceptance. Participants (n = 82) evaluated overall liking and sensory liking for appearance, smell, taste, texture, and aftertaste, completed Just-About-Right (JAR) diagnostics and were segmented according to Net Promoter Score (NPS) responses. Across sensory dimensions, oral attributes exerted a stronger influence on liking than appearance, with taste emerging as the primary driver of acceptance and texture showing a secondary contribution. Multiple regression analysis confirmed taste liking as the strongest predictor of overall liking, whereas the remaining sensory aspects showed weaker or non-significant effects. NPS segmentation further revealed clear differences in recommendation behaviour across detractors, passives, and promoters, closely mirroring hedonic liking patterns and supporting consistency between sensory evaluation and recommendation-oriented behavioural responses. Overall, this study provides an initial empirical benchmark of consumer responses to a commercially available hybrid cultivated meat product under controlled conditions, highlighting the central role of taste quality and sensory balance in shaping hedonic responses and consumer satisfaction. Title: BadLingual: Language-Triggered Anomalous Behavior in Multilingual Foundation Large Language Models
Abstract: Multilingual foundation Large Language Models (LLMs) have greatly improved accessibility for users across different regions, but they also introduce new surfaces for anomalous behavior. In this paper, we identify a new form of anomalous behavior in multilingual foundation LLMs, termed lingual-backdoor attack, in which the input language itself acts as the trigger and selectively induces attacker-desired abnormal outputs. Because language is naturally associated with specific speaker populations, lingual-backdoor enables precise targeting and may amplify social bias or misinformation risks. To study this threat, we first implement a task-specific baseline that injects the anomaly through conventional data poisoning on downstream tasks. Although effective in controlled settings, it generalizes poorly to realistic task-agnostic scenarios on instruction-tuned foundation LLMs. We therefore propose BadLingual, a task-agnostic lingual-backdoor that improves trigger robustness and cross-task generalization through PPL-constrained Greedy Coordinate Gradient-based Search (PGCG) and adversarial training. Extensive experiments across multiple models, languages, and downstream tasks show that BadLingual improves attack success rate by up to 37.35% over the baseline while preserving utility on clean inputs. Furthermore, widely used anomaly detection and recovery methods are largely ineffective against this language-triggered anomalous behavior. These findings reveal multilinguality as a previously underexplored source of anomalous behavior in foundation LLMs and highlight the urgent need for more effective anomaly-aware defenses. © 2026

Title: Digital influences on green economic participation: The role of eWOM in shaping circular consumption among young vietnamese consumers
Abstract: Circular business models (CBMs) are increasingly recognized as a strategic mechanism for advancing sustainable consumption and supporting green economic growth, particularly in emerging economies where rising consumption intensifies pressures on natural resources and waste management systems. Concurrently, the rapid expansion of social media and digital commerce has elevated electronic word-of-mouth (eWOM) to a central role in shaping how young consumers interpret, evaluate, and normalize sustainability-oriented business practices. Addressing this gap, the present study adopts a quantitative approach using survey data from 1,142 young Vietnamese consumers to examine how core dimensions of eWOM influence information acceptance and, subsequently, participation intentions in CBMs within the retail sector. A rigorous multi-stage analytical procedure was employed, including reliability testing, exploratory factor analysis (EFA), confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) to validate the measurement model, and structural equation modeling (SEM) to assess the structural relationships among latent constructs. The results indicate that all four eWOM attributes positively influence information acceptance, which in turn significantly drives participation intention. Among these factors, relevance emerges as the most influential attribute, suggesting that sustainability-related messages are most effective when aligned with consumers’ personal needs, values, and decision contexts. The findings also confirm the mediating role of information acceptance in translating eWOM quality into behavioral intention. By validating both the measurement and structural models, this study enhances the robustness of IAM-based explanations in the context of circular consumption and extends the literature on digital influence in emerging markets. Title: Urban residential cues to care in Detroit neighborhoods: A validated lot level virtual audit tool
Abstract: High-quality built environments have potential to improve the mental and physical health of residents. Qualitatively, such environments are characterized by the visible evidence of human intervention and maintenance, including cues to care (CTC). However, to date, there has not been a validated way to quantify CTC that accounts for structure-inclusive lot types (i.e., residential, commercial). We present a validated tool that allows entire urban neighborhoods to be assessed (including occupied properties and vacant lots). We validated lot-scale physical CTC against measures of neighborhood conditions that have been widely associated with residents’ health. These measures include land use amenities and resident perceptions of neighborhood cohesion, attractiveness, and safety. We developed a novel coding tool that expands current geospatial CTC tools to quantitatively assess urban residential CTC. We applied Lot Level Cues to Care (LLCTC) to 781 lots across 245 street segments in Detroit, MI. We then investigated the relationship between LLCTC (where higher values indicate more CTC) and widely used as well as validated measures of neighborhood conditions, in a survey of 214 Detroit residents. We found negative correlations between LLCTC scores and signs of disorder and area deprivation. We also found significant associations between LLCTC scores and perceived neighborhood attractiveness. Although only approaching statistical significance, higher perceived cohesion and greater perceived safety were also associated with higher LLCTC scores. In conclusion, LLCTC is a valid quantitative geospatial measure of CTC in an urban residential environment, as validated by resident perceptions of their neighborhoods. © 2026

Title: When loyalty points become donations: The effects of redeemability, point expiration, and descriptive norm information

Abstract: Although loyalty programs and checkout charity are widely implemented across retail industries, the integration of reward point donations into online checkout charity remains rare, and consumer behavior in this context is not yet fully understood. Title: A framework integrating topological potential and semantic embeddings for identifying scientific research clusters in scholarly collaboration networks
Abstract: Multi-team collaboration is essential for addressing major scientific challenges. Previous methods focus predominantly on individuals or single teams, making it difficult to capture the structure of multi-team collaborative innovation systems. To address this, this study conceptualizes a research cluster as a multi-team system formed through inter-team relationships and related research goals within complex collaborative research environments. We further introduce a four-phase Topological Potential–Semantic Embedding Research Cluster Identification (TPSE-RCI) framework to identify scientific research clusters. First, research teams are detected and a team collaboration network is constructed. Second, team feature vectors are generated via topological potential–enhanced Node2Vec and initial clusters are identified with HDBSCAN. Third, team publications are analyzed using BERTopic with BGE-M3 semantic embeddings to derive hierarchical research goals. Fourth, validity criteria are applied to filter scientific research clusters. Using medical informatics publications as a case study, we detected 4262 research teams from 81,557 publications by 269,598 authors. At the structural level, 702 initial scientific research clusters were identified. At the thematic level, 319 topics were extracted from the team publications and consolidated into 21 secondary and 7 primary research goals. By integrating structural and thematic results, we ultimately identified 239 scientific research clusters. Comparative and ablation analyses indicate that incorporating topological potential improves team representation and structural-clustering quality within this empirical setting. The identified research clusters can provide decision support for practical tasks such as organized research management, major project coordination and optimization, domain expert identification, and research resource allocation. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: The importance of language patterns in the sensory evaluation of chocolates and plant-based drinks
Abstract: Language is a central tool through which individuals communicate sensory impressions and emotional reactions to food. Yet, the response modality through which these evaluations are expressed may substantially influence the linguistic patterns that emerge. Using an exploratory approach, this study examined how response modality (written vs. spoken) shapes the characterisation of food products during sensory evaluation. Participants evaluated three chocolates and three plant-based drinks, providing open-ended descriptions that were analysed using LIWC2015. While hedonic mean scores showed a consistent preference for chocolates across modalities, linguistic patterns revealed substantial differences between written and spoken modalities. Written responses contained more affective terms, perceptual descriptors, and lexically complex words, whereas spoken descriptions were longer and relied more on cognitive and function words, typical of spontaneous speech. Across modalities, chocolates elicited more affective and descriptive language, whereas plant-based drinks prompted more analytical and perceptual vocabulary. The findings demonstrate that the written and spoken modalities capture differentially emotional and cognitive aspects of food perception, highlighting the importance of modality choice in sensory and consumer research. © 2026

Title: Repairing trust in AI: Attribution, anthropomorphism, and the illusion of difference
Abstract: Trust repair between humans and AI systems is an emerging area of inquiry that builds on a well-established literature in human–human (HH) interactions. This review examines how key HH findings, particularly the differential effectiveness of repair strategies following competence versus integrity violations, generalize to human–robot interaction (HRI). While some patterns hold, important divergences exist. The paper argues that better operationalizations of integrity violations and increased anthropomorphism can align HRI findings more closely with HH research. However, enduring challenges remain regarding the ethics of anthropomorphic design, the moral values AI should adopt, and how AI should extend trust to humans. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Yin Y.; Zhou J.; Peng K.
Title: Online dating paradox: Why lonely hearts choose to ghost
Abstract: This study examines the differential associations of state and trait loneliness with ghosting behavior in online dating, considering self-presentation strategies and dating fatigue as potential explanatory pathways. Survey data from 881 Chinese mobile dating app users were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The results showed that state loneliness was negatively associated with ghosting, whereas trait loneliness was positively associated with ghosting. Dating fatigue was positively associated with ghosting and statistically mediated the associations between both forms of loneliness and ghosting in opposite directions. Acquisitive self-presentation was positively associated with state loneliness and negatively associated with trait loneliness; unexpectedly, it was negatively associated with dating fatigue. Authentic self-presentation was not significantly associated with loneliness or dating fatigue. These findings suggest that temporary and chronic loneliness may correspond to different patterns of engagement and disengagement in online dating. The study contributes to mobile dating research by distinguishing state and trait loneliness and by identifying dating fatigue as an important correlate of ghosting behavior. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Zeng T.; Zhang R.; Ke Q.; Yu Y.
Title: Does low-carbon policy improve the environmental performance in China?
Abstract: This study examines the impacts and driving mechanisms of low-carbon policy on environmental performance, with a focus on both direct policy effects and the underlying structural drivers. Drawing on panel data from multiple regions and years, the analysis employs a combination of econometric modeling and configurational approaches to capture heterogeneous and non-linear relationships. The results indicate that low-carbon policy significantly improves environmental performance, particularly in terms of emissions reduction, energy efficiency, and pollution control. However, the magnitude and direction of these effects vary across regions depending on differences in economic development, industrial structure, and governance capacity. Further analysis reveals that technological innovation, green investment, regulatory intensity, and public participation are key driving factors that jointly shape policy effectiveness. The study also identifies multiple pathways through which these factors interact to enhance environmental outcomes, highlighting the importance of synergistic policy design. The findings contribute to a deeper understanding of how low-carbon goals translate into measurable environmental improvements and offer practical implications for policymakers seeking to optimize policy implementation in diverse socio-economic contexts. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Epistemic justice and deep-sea mining: UNCLOS’s facilitation of epistemic diversity the International Seabed Authority’s decision-making process
Abstract: The paper discusses epistemic justice as a central justice framework to be considered in the regulatory process of exploitative deep sea mining, with the aim of bringing attention to the relevance of epistemic justice and diversity to deep sea mining scholarship. Epistemic justice is here understood as deeply connected to a broader social equity, and entails the fair treatment of different ’knowers’ and a creation, sharing, and validation of knowledge that is fundamentally diverse rather than based on one dominant knowledge-tradition. The paper reflects on epistemic justice in energy- and ocean governance, and asks whether and how United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) facilitates that such justice is sought in the regulatory process of deep sea mining by focusing on procedural rules for the International Seabed Authority (ISA) and the representation of different knowers in the decision-making process, including its Council's structure, authority, and composition. It concludes that a very small number of individuals has the power to bring about a very large change in deep sea mining regulations, currently without legal requirements to include experiential, traditional or other forms of knowledges beyond the scientific method in the decision-making process. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Technostress in the age of digital transformation and AI: A bibliometric–systematic literature review for HRM research
Abstract: Digital transformation and artificial intelligence are reshaping human resource management through algorithmic recruitment, automated evaluation, predictive analytics, and generative tools. While these systems improve efficiency, they also intensify technostress through opacity, surveillance, reduced control, and digitally intensified work arrangements. Responding to a fragmented literature spanning both AI-enabled and broader digital work systems, this study provides a B-SLR that maps technostress in digital transformation while identifying AI-specific stressors as a key emerging stream for HRM research. Drawing on 194 Scopus-indexed articles, we combine performance analysis and science mapping to identify publication trends, dominant themes, and intellectual structures. The review shows how AI-specific stressors extend established technostress mechanisms and shift attention toward transparency, control, fairness, and responsible HRM design. We conclude with actionable implications for researchers and practitioners aiming to design more transparent, responsible, and sustainable digital and AI-enabled HRM systems. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Familiar faces, honest answers? The impacts of enumerator familiarity and modality on survey responses
Abstract: Survey data can be distorted through mistrust, discomfort, or demand effects on the part of respondents. We test whether familiar enumerators – those with whom a respondent has completed a prior survey – influence data quality in a panel survey with small business owners in Uganda. We randomly assign respondents to a familiar or a new enumerator and cross-cut a second randomization to an in-person or phone-based interview modality. Across a broad set of outcome types, we observe few impacts of either survey method on means, distributions, or attrition. However, respondents are significantly more likely to give norm-congruent answers to new surveyors compared to familiar ones. The effect of familiarity does not interact significantly with a prior experiment conducted with the same sample, suggesting that familiarity influences estimates of levels but not of treatment impacts. These findings suggest that surveys by familiar enumerators can improve the measurement of sensitive beliefs. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Comparing AI chatbot users and non-users in Germany: Reasons for use, addictive AI chatbot use, mental health, and loneliness
Abstract: The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) chatbots is becoming increasingly popular worldwide. To prevent potential negative consequences associated with the use at an early stage, it is crucial to understand its associations with mental health. Therefore, the present study compared people who use AI chatbots with those who do not engage in AI chatbot-interactions in terms of mental health and loneliness. Moreover, we investigated potential mechanisms associated with addictive AI chatbot use. Data of 7,312 persons (3,729 users: 42.1% men, 57.9% women; Mage = 42.23, SDage = 13.33; 3,583 non-users: 42.6% men, 57.4% women; Mage, = 54.28, SDage = 14.49) from the German adult population were collected via an online survey. AI chatbot users had significantly higher levels of loneliness, depressive, anxiety and stress symptoms, and significantly lower levels of life satisfaction than non-users. Users primarily engaged in AI chatbot-interactions for informational and practical reasons, such as obtaining information and inspiration, and receiving text-related assistance. The frequency of AI chatbot use to escape negative emotions was significantly positively associated with addictive tendencies. Loneliness statistically mediated the association between addictive AI chatbot use and the mental health variables. Most observed effect sizes were small. The present findings show that using AI chatbots for emotion regulation is positively associated with higher addictive tendencies and lower levels of mental health. Further experimental longitudinal research is urgently needed to clarify causal mechanisms of these associations. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Divergent relationships between moral disengagement and cyberbullying bystander response behaviors: Examining the amplifying roles of humor and anonymity
Abstract: While bystander response behaviors are pivotal for cyberbullying (CB) intervention, prior research has yielded inconsistent findings regarding their correlates, partly because it has often treated diverse bystander responses as a monolithic construct and failed to distinguish constructive defense from aggressive defense. Furthermore, few empirical studies have examined how digital affordances interact with individual factors in relation to diverse bystander responses within a Social Cognitive Theory (SCT) framework. To address these gaps, this study examined the main and interactive associations of individual moral disengagement (MD), perceived anonymity, and humor of CB with four distinct online bystander responses (constructive defense, aggressive defense, inaction, and reinforcement). A final analytic sample of 1201 Chinese secondary school students, selected via multi-stage random sampling, completed a survey assessing MD, CB contexts, and real online bystander responses. Multilevel analysis indicated that MD, perceived anonymity and humor were consistently and negatively associated with constructive defense but positively associated with inaction. Conversely, MD and anonymity were positively associated with aggressive defense, whereas humor showed no significant link. Regarding reinforcement behaviors, perceived anonymity and humor were positive predictors, whereas MD exerted a non-significant association. Moderation analyses revealed that anonymity strengthened MD's positive associations with inaction and reinforcement, whereas humor amplified MD's association solely with reinforcement. These findings underscore the necessity of distinguishing constructive from aggressive defense and integrating individual moral cognition with contextual cues for both exploring correlates of online bystander response and designing CB interventions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Emotional Stability and within-person Big Five profile dispersion: Evidence for a U-shaped association in adolescents
Abstract: Personality traits are typically studied as independent predictors of behavior and well-being, yet less attention has been paid to their configuration within individuals. One approach to capturing this configuration is through intra-subject variance across traits which could reflect the consistency or divergence across the five traits. We operationalized intra-subject variance (Vi) as the within-person variance of direct Big Five scores. Across N = 3785 adolescents (14–17 years), we observed a robust U-shaped association between Emotional Stability (ES) and Vi: profiles were most homogeneous at moderate–high ES and more dispersed at both low and very high ES. This pattern held in polynomial regression models including a significant quadratic term. A robust non-linear (U-shaped) association was found between Emotional Stability and Vi: both low and very high levels were linked to greater dispersion, whereas moderate-to-high levels showed more homogeneous profiles. Other traits showed weaker nonlinear associations, with substantially lower explanatory capacity than Emotional Stability. Emotional Stability emerged as the strongest predictor. Findings suggest that Emotional Stability plays a distinctive role in the internal organization of personality and highlights the relevance of within-person approaches. However, the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation, and further longitudinal and multi-method research is needed. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Han X.; Li S.; Liu H.; Zhang M.
Title: When GAI backfires: Understanding the process mechanism of consumers’ avoidance of generative AI conversational recommendation agents from a misaligned affordance perspective
Abstract: Generative AI-enhanced conversational recommendation agents (GCRAs) are being widely deployed on e-commerce platforms; however, consumers increasingly avoid these advanced recommendation tools. Prior research has not systematically identified which specific features of GCRAs drive such avoidance, nor has it clearly articulated the underlying process mechanisms through which avoidance emerges. To address these gaps, this study draws on affordance actualization theory and misaligned affordance theory to systematically investigate consumers’ perceived GCRA misaligned affordances and to model the complete pathways from these misaligned affordances to consumer avoidance behaviors. We employed a sequential mixed-methods approach. First, a qualitative interview research (N = 19) combined with a simple experiment identified three key GCRA misaligned affordances: limited choices, iterative dialogue, and hallucinated information. Second, a quantitative research (N = 538) validated that these misaligned affordances trigger cost-based comparative appraisals (opportunity and transaction costs), which in turn lead to negative experiences (both outcome-related and process-related), ultimately driving consumer avoidance. Finally, by integrating the findings across studies, we developed a comprehensive framework explaining consumers’ avoidance of GCRAs. Theoretically, this research advances the misaligned affordance actualization theory by highlighting the novel comparative appraisal stage, moving the theory from qualitative conceptualization to process-level mechanisms. Collectively, these findings provide new theoretical insights and practical guidance for improving the design and deployment of GCRAs. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Effects of AI-based chatbot coaching on goal attainment, self-efficacy, and stress: A longitudinal randomized experiment
Abstract: Students in higher education face a range of academic challenges, which leads to high levels of stress among many students. While coaching has been shown to help students address these challenges, it is resource-intensive and therefore not broadly accessible. AI-based chatbots may help broaden access by providing interactive and personalized guidance at scale, yet empirical evidence on their effectiveness remains limited, particularly from longitudinal experimental studies. Addressing this gap, we conducted a longitudinal between-subjects experiment with four measurement points across an academic semester, randomly assigning 101 students to one of three conditions: AI-based chatbot coaching, literature-based self-study (active control), or a waitlist control condition. Students in the chatbot coaching and literature study conditions engaged in repeated interactions with the intervention, averaging approximately 100 min of cumulative interaction time accumulated across four sessions of 23–28 min each. We examined how students’ goal attainment, university-related self-efficacy, and stress developed over the course of the study. Results showed that students in the AI-based chatbot condition achieved significantly stronger increases in goal attainment over time compared to students in both control conditions. Self-efficacy also increased in the AI-based chatbot condition over time; however, between-condition differences were not consistent across time points, suggesting that the intervention had a more limited impact on self-efficacy relative to goal attainment. Furthermore, no significant effects were found for university-related stress. The findings suggest that AI-based chatbot coaching can effectively support students in achieving university-related goals and strengthening their self-efficacy, while its impact on stress reduction may be limited. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Enhancing situational awareness in health systems: A scoping review of technologies and cross-industry insights
Abstract: Background: Situational awareness technologies are increasingly utilised in healthcare systems to facilitate timely and coordinated decision-making. Reported implementation considerations include data quality, governance, and integration into everyday workflows. Objective: This scoping review aimed to map technologies, systems, and methods used to enhance situational awareness in health service delivery and to identify approaches used in other industries that could be adapted for healthcare, particularly in regional and remote settings. Methods: We followed the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) guidance for scoping reviews. Electronic databases (PubMed and Web of Science) were searched for studies published between January 2000 and October 2025. Reference lists and citation searches in Google Scholar were also examined. Records meeting the inclusion criteria were screened and reviewed, with key data extracted using a structured charting form and synthesised into seven application domains. Results: Searches identified 744 records, of which 23 studies were included. These covered diverse technologies such as dashboards, forecasting models, alert systems, and geospatial decision environments. Most studies were from high-income countries (n = 19). Studies reported potential benefits for visibility, coordination, and decision-making. However, most evidence was descriptive, with limited evidence of whether these systems improve service delivery. Recurrent implementation challenges included data fragmentation, limited interoperability, and misalignment between governance and workflow. Conclusions: This review highlights the need for more rigorous and context-sensitive evaluations of technologies used to enhance situational awareness in healthcare, especially in regional and resource-limited settings. © 2026 Fellowship of Postgraduate Medicine

Title: Conflict expression: A decade of group conflict research
Abstract: The conflict expression framework was developed to generate new practical and theoretical insights into how conflict communication affects group processes and negotiated outcomes. The framework proposes that conflict expressions vary along two dimensions: directness and oppositional intensity. The framework suggested that the effects of different types of conflict on group processes and outcomes likely depend on how the conflict is expressed, that conflict within groups is likely perceived differently by different members of the same social unit, and that conflict affects negotiation processes dynamically through reciprocated statements and responses. Title: “Can talking like you make it work?”: The role of linguistic convergence and maintenance in human–robot interaction
Abstract: As domestic robots become more integrated into everyday life, effective and socially attuned communication strategies are essential for enabling meaningful human–robot collaboration. Prior work has addressed robot errors, but less is known about handling user errors. This study investigates how domestic robots’ verbal coordination strategies shape user experiences when handling human speech errors. To establish the experimental framework, Communication Accommodation Theory (CAT) was applied to define two linguistic strategies (convergence vs. maintenance), and McGrath's Group Task Circumplex Model was utilized to establish four task types (Generate, Choose, Execute, and Negotiate). We conducted a video-based experiment using a 2 × 4 × 2 mixed factorial design, varying CAT strategy, task type, and age group. Results revealed that while convergence was generally perceived more positively, its advantage was task-dependent. In Generate and Choose tasks, convergence was associated with greater trust, while maintenance was comparably effective in Execute and Negotiate tasks. Participants’ evaluations varied by both task type and age, suggesting that communication strategies should be tailored to context and user characteristics. This study contributes design insights for adaptive, socially responsive domestic robots. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Performative narratives and destination image in cross-cultural tourism livestreaming
Abstract: Tourism livestreaming allows global audiences to encounter destinations in real time, yet how livestreamers’ expressive behaviors shape audiences’ destination evaluations across cultures remains unclear. Cross-cultural proximity further operates unevenly: cultural distance reshapes the interaction–cognition pathway, whereas linguistic accessibility improves destination image expression but does not consistently amplify performative cues. Authors: Feng M.; Li Y.; Yang Y.; Qin F.
Title: Emotional interaction and conversion value in live streaming E-commerce
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Multi-agent emotional interaction constitutes a core characteristic of live streaming e-commerce. Nevertheless, prior research has yet to build a unified analytical framework incorporating streamers, viewers and live streaming assistants, and rarely explored how emotional dynamics shape live streaming performance. Based on minute-level panel data of 4671 min retrieved from 40 Taobao live streaming sessions, this study adopts sentiment analysis to quantify the emotional expressions of streamers and viewers. Applying the Panel Vector Autoregression (PVAR) model and impulse response analysis, this study constructs a tripartite emotional interaction system among streamers, viewers and assistants, and investigates its dynamic linkage with core operational performance, including product sales and new follower growth. The empirical results are consistent with a unidirectional streamer-to-viewer emotional association, whereby streamer emotions are closely associated with viewer interaction and purchase decisions. By contrast, intra-viewer emotional association is not statistically supported, whereas viewer emotions are positively associated with new follower growth. Higher frequency of live streaming assistant intervention shows a dual association pattern: it is positively associated with viewer interaction frequency, but negatively associated with product sales. This study extends the application scope of emotional contagion theory in the live streaming context, enriches the role configuration of the live streaming e-commerce ecosystem, and offers practical and targeted operational strategies for live streaming management. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Traditional Ecological Knowledge in Sustaining Mobile Pastoralism of Türkiye
Abstract: Traditional ecological knowledge (TEK) underpins sustainable pastoralism by guiding livestock mobility, resource management, and climate adaptation. However, in Eastern Anatolia, Türkiye, TEK is increasingly marginalized by socio-economic change and restrictive land-use policies. This study documents the TEK held by mobile pastoralists in Eastern Anatolia, Türkiye, and examines how it informs herd mobility, pasture use, and weather-related decision-making. Ethnographic fieldwork was conducted between February and April 2024 across Diyarbakır and neighboring provinces, involving structured interviews, participatory observations, and focus group discussions with 20 mobile pastoralists. Qualitative and descriptive statistical analyses were used to identify patterns in decision-making related to migration, pasture selection, and weather forecasting. Within this small, purposive sample, pastoralists reported weighing pasture condition (75%), weather conditions (55%), and water availability (15%) when planning migration and grazing. Traditional forecasting relied on ecological indicators, including star density (65%), cloud formations around the moon (60%), and animal behavior (20%). These practices reveal an embedded ecological literacy that integrates environmental perception with kin-based decision-making. Yet declining interest in pastoralism among younger community members, land privatization, conservation restrictions, and other socio-economic constraints threaten TEK continuity. TEK functions not merely as inherited knowledge but as a living body of practice that supports pastoral communities within their own socio-ecological systems. Integrating TEK into contemporary rangeland management could enhance sustainability, climate preparedness, and the long-term viability of pastoral livelihoods in semi-arid environments. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Authors: Hu Y.; Wang W.; Meng Y.; Liu Z.; Tang Y.; Bai Q.
Title: Characterizing the spatial correlation network of cultivated land system resilience: Nonlinear relationships between interregional production factor flows and node centrality
Abstract: Against the backdrop of intensifying uncertainty shocks and increasingly frequent cross-regional factor flows, the spatial governance of cultivated land system resilience (CLSR) has become an increasingly important issue. Existing studies have largely treated CLSR as a localized attribute confined to specific administrative units, while paying limited attention to the evolution of its spatial correlation network. To address this gap, the Vertical and Horizontal Scatter Degree Method, Social Network Analysis, and the XGBoost-GeoShapley model were employed to examine the spatiotemporal patterns of CLSR and interregional flows of labor, capital, and technology across Chinese cities, and to identify the nonlinear relationships between interregional production factor flows and node centrality in the CLSR spatial correlation network. The results show that CLSR in China increased steadily and exhibited a clear east-west gradient, with higher levels in the east and lower levels in the west. Interregional flows of labor, capital, and technology continued to intensify, while spatial agglomeration and differentiation coexisted. The CLSR spatial correlation network in China was characterized by overall connectivity but sparse linkages. Network density fluctuated only between 0.10 and 0.14, indicating that substantive intercity linkages in CLSR remained relatively weak. All node centrality measures displayed long-tailed distributions, and cities such as Beijing, Shanghai, Tianjin, Suzhou, Chongqing, and Qingdao occupied advantageous positions in terms of connectivity, accessibility, and bridging functions. Authors: Wang L.; Li S.
Title: The temporal shift in consumer hue preferences in hotel booking
Abstract: Despite the hospitality industry's ongoing pursuit of optimal color marketing strategies, it remains unclear whether consumers respond more favorably to cool or warm hues. This research investigates how consumers' hue preferences in digital marketing imagery shift as a function of time of day. Through a case coding analysis (n = 4510), an eye-tracking experiment (n = 105), three online experiments (n = 981), and a quasi-experimental field survey with real tourists (n = 316), this research reveals temporal shifts in hue preference in hotel booking contexts, such that consumers prefer hotel room photos with cool hues in the morning and warm hues in the evening. These preferences are mediated by the need for uniqueness and the need for belonging, respectively. Furthermore, the effect is moderated by visual temporal cues (window view) and individual circadian rhythms (chronotype). Our findings challenge static perspectives on color psychology and offer actionable guidance for time-adaptive visual marketing. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Assessing the environmental–economic viability of expressway photovoltaics in China: A spatio–temporal life cycle perspective
Abstract: Expressway corridors are increasingly considered for distributed photovoltaic deployment, but their environmental–economic viability depends strongly on local solar resources, infrastructure availability, grid structure, and future decarbonization pathways. This study develops an integrated framework that combines spatio–temporal assessment with environmental life cycle costing to evaluate the deployment potential and comprehensive benefits of expressway photovoltaic systems across 351 prefecture–level cities in China. The assessment covers service areas, rest areas, and expressway slopes under business-as-usual and carbon-neutrality-by-2060 scenarios. Results indicate that expressway slopes provide the greatest installation potential, with 49.71% of cities supporting more than 200 MW. At the national-average level, expressway photovoltaic systems yield a net internal benefit of 317.05 USD/kW and a net environmental benefit of 249.48 USD/kW under the business-as-usual scenario. Inverter and monocrystalline silicon photovoltaic module production are the main contributors to environmental costs. Under the carbon-neutrality-by-2060 scenario, grid decarbonization reduces the avoided environmental burden of photovoltaic electricity and delays the transition to positive net environmental benefits from 2035 to 2037. These findings support a shift from capacity-oriented expansion to region-specific life cycle planning, prioritizing corridors where solar resources, expressway availability, grid displacement benefits, and recycling infrastructure are jointly favorable. © 2026

Authors: Liu Y.; Shi Y.; Bu W.; Liu S.
Title: A study analyzing factors retarding digital transformation and configuration pathways: Based on the perspective of digital transformation acceptors
Abstract: The high-touch service nature of the hospitality industry highlights that the success of digital transformation depends primarily on human factors rather than technology itself. Existing research indicates that approximately 80% of strategic initiatives fail due to employee resistance to change or capability deficits. Furthermore, nearly three-quarters of middle managers and staff exhibit resistance toward such transformations. This alarming trend raises a fundamental question: how can the hospitality industry navigate the inherent tension between high-touch emotional labor and digital depersonalization to transform employee resistance into proactive adoption? While traditional research frequently focuses on hotel management as change promoters, this study shifts the analytical focus to hotel employees as change recipients. Guided by cognitive appraisal and social information processing theories, within the context of hotel service scenarios, this research constructs models of resistance mitigation and antecedent condition linkages across individual, organizational, and managerial levels. Through an empirical analysis of 545 survey responses from various hotel categories and the application of fuzzy set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA), this study systematically explores the mechanisms of resistance alleviation and the synergistic effects of the identified influencing factors. Regression results indicate that digital literacy, digital strategy consensus, and perceptions of digital technology warmth and capability are negatively associated with hotel employee resistance to digital transformation. Additionally, organizational strategic flexibility and digital leadership positively moderate the relationships between these individual factors and resistance. The fsQCA results further identify two primary equifinal patterns sufficient for fostering a state of low resistance, demonstrating how strong digital leadership serves as a social cue that effectively compensates for the absence of organizational strategic flexibility. Ultimately, this research deepens the understanding of human-centered digital transformation in the hospitality sector and offers theoretical frameworks for managers to mitigate employee resistance to digital initiatives, thereby facilitating successful strategic implementation. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Zhao H.; Shi R.
Title: Why disaster experience does not always improve Preparedness: The role of disaster learning and heterogeneous effects
Abstract: The frequency and severity of natural disasters and public emergencies have continued to increase worldwide. Household preparedness plays a vital role in disaster risk reduction, yet the effect of disaster-related experience on preparedness remains inconclusive. Using survey data from 5,862 residents in China, this study separately examines the associations of past disaster experience and disaster learning with household preparedness. Conventional regression models and a causal forest approach are used to estimate average associations and explore heterogeneous effects across individuals. The results show that disaster learning, rather than past disaster experience, is positively associated with preparedness behavior, highlighting the importance of capacity building. In addition, both past disaster experience and disaster learning exhibit heterogeneous effects across individuals. Feature importance analysis further indicates that social capital, emergency awareness, and community infrastructure are important influential factors associated with preparedness behavior. By introducing a causal forest approach to distinguish the differential effects of past disaster experience and disaster learning, this study provides a more nuanced understanding of household preparedness and offers useful insights for developing more targeted household disaster risk reduction strategies. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Li M.; Yang Y.; Wang X.; Su Y.
Title: Capitalizing on positive experiences: Receiving affective empathy fosters a better mood and prosocial waiting
Abstract: Interpersonal responses to emotional disclosures have potent effects on immediate affective states, yet their capacity to shape subsequent prosocial behavior remains unclear. Across two experiments, we investigated how the perceived empathy conveyed by facial responses influences both emotional outcomes and downstream altruistic choices. In Experiment 1, participants shared imagined positive or negative life events and received either an empathic, nonresponsive, or counter-empathic facial response from ostensible partners. We observed a context-dependent affective modulation: empathic responses maximally enhanced positive affect following positive disclosures, whereas counter-empathic responses most severely worsened mood following negative disclosures. In Experiment 2, we coupled this paradigm with an experiential intertemporal choice task in which participants chose between different waiting durations for rewards benefiting themselves or a charitable cause. Empathic responses to positive disclosures selectively increased charity-benefiting decisions, indicating a greater willingness to incur personal time costs for others. Computational modeling of choice data characterized this prosocial enhancement as being accompanied by a reduction in the weight placed on waiting time relative to reward, that is, a lower subjective cost of waiting. These findings demonstrate that receiving affective empathy, particularly in the context of positive experiences, promotes downstream prosociality by recalibrating the cost–benefit computations underlying altruistic choice. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Screening out ethics: How technology enables ethical fading in negotiations
Abstract: Negotiations are rife with opportunities and temptations to engage in unethical negotiating behavior. Such behavior is not always strategic or even intentional; rather, it can emerge from situational characteristics of the negotiation environment. One psychological process through which situational characteristics influence unethical behavior is ethical fading, a process that limits one's ability to recognize the ethical aspects of the situation and behave in line with one's ethical values. As technologies such as email, video conferencing, and artificial intelligence (AI) become increasingly common in negotiations, an important question is whether these technologies facilitate ethical fading. In this review, we explore the impact that technology and AI have on ethical fading and unethical negotiating behavior. We propose that technology and AI use in negotiations promotes three cognitive processes that facilitate ethical fading: psychological distance, cognitive offloading, and displaced accountability. We review how technology may serve as an antecedent to each of these processes and explain why these processes may facilitate ethical fading in negotiation contexts. Because research on the relationship between technology and unethical negotiating behavior remains limited, we conclude by identifying promising directions for future research. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd
